quiz.stem: Put the FortiGate packet flow in order (high level).
quiz.explanation: DNAT happens before routing and policy; SNAT near the end.

quiz.stem: The panel says "Design SD-WAN for our retail chain." What should you do first?

options.text: Ask clarifying questions: sites, links, apps, availability, management
Draw a dual-hub topology with ADVPN, then ask what they'd change on it
options.why_wrong: A good design may follow, but you'd be designing before you know the requirements.

options.text: Ask which FortiOS version they run, then design for that release's features
options.why_wrong: One question isn't discovery; requirements come before versions.

options.text: Walk through the SD-WAN config blocks in order so they see your CLI depth
options.why_wrong: Commands come much later; they want design thinking.

quiz.explanation: Clarify, then draw.

quiz.stem: 'Users can't reach a server through the FortiGate.' Which first two checks follow the packet-flow method?

options.text: Sniffer to see packets arrive and leave, then debug flow for route and policy
Check the traffic logs for denies, then reboot if nothing at all shows up there
options.why_wrong: Logs help, but a reboot destroys evidence and changes nothing.

options.text: Debug flow first, then a sniffer if the debug output turns out to be empty
options.why_wrong: Close, but proving arrival first tells you whether the FortiGate is involved at all.

options.text: Disable the security profiles on the policy, then retest the server access
options.why_wrong: Changes without proof of where the packet stops.

quiz.explanation: Prove where it stops.

quiz.stem: You don't remember a default value during the panel. Best response?

options.text: Give your best understanding and say you'd verify it in the docs
Give a confident number, since the panels reward decisive answers
options.why_wrong: Panels test honesty; wrong and confident is worse.

options.text: Say you don't know it and ask to move on to the next question
options.why_wrong: Honest, but offer what you know and how you'd check first.

options.text: Explain how you'd find it in the CLI with a question mark there
options.why_wrong: Good habit, but also give your best understanding of the value.

quiz.explanation: Honest and practical.

quiz.stem: Which routing component is evaluated first on FortiGate?

options.text: Policy routes
SD-WAN rules
options.why_wrong: They come after policy routes.

options.text: Static routes
options.why_wrong: The routing table comes last.

options.text: Connected routes
options.why_wrong: Connected routes are in the routing table, checked after policy routes.

quiz.explanation: Policy routes, SD-WAN rules, then the routing table.

quiz.stem: Which failure modes are worth naming in a DC HA design? Select all that apply.

options.text: Split brain if heartbeats share one switch
Sessions dropping without session pickup
Override taking primary back after reboot
Web filter ratings changing after failover
options.why_wrong: Not an HA failure mode.

options.text: Config drift if one unit isn't in sync
options.why_wrong: Worth checking, but FGCP syncs config; it's a symptom, not a design failure mode.

quiz.explanation: Name the failure, then how you designed it out.

quiz.stem: Why end a whiteboard design with acceptance tests?

options.text: They define how the customer signs off that the design works
They let the panel see you know the FortiGate diagnostic commands
options.why_wrong: A side benefit; the point is agreed proof that it works.

options.text: They capture the low-level settings, so the LLD itself can stay short
options.why_wrong: Tests prove behaviour; the LLD still holds the settings.

options.text: They're a Fortinet requirement for PS projects before any go-live
options.why_wrong: There's no such product requirement; it's delivery practice.

quiz.explanation: Prove it works; it's what gets signed.

quiz.stem: In a debug flow, which line shows the policy decision?

options.text: Allowed by Policy-N, or Denied by forward policy check
allocate a new session, which follows the policy match
options.why_wrong: That's session creation, before the policy line.

options.text: find a route, which picks the policy by egress interface
options.why_wrong: That's routing; it sets the egress, but the policy line comes after.

options.text: received a packet, which lists the matched policy's ID
options.why_wrong: That's ingress; no policy is named there.

quiz.explanation: Policy lines name the policy ID.

quiz.stem: A panelist asks "Why A-P and not A-A?" for a mid-size DC. Strongest answer?

options.text: A-P is simpler to run and one unit's throughput fits; A-A adds complexity they don't need
A-A suits it less, as most sessions would still pass through the primary unit anyway
options.why_wrong: Partly true, but the deciding reason is that one unit fits and A-P is simpler.

options.text: A-P gives more throughput, because the secondary keeps its CPU free for the session sync
options.why_wrong: Not the point; one unit handles the traffic either way.

options.text: A-A would double throughput, but the customer can't afford licences for a second FortiGate
options.why_wrong: Both modes need two units; the real trade-off is complexity vs need.

quiz.explanation: Trade-off grounded in requirements.

quiz.stem: Which design element addresses the risk that VPN gateways are prime targets?

options.text: Fast patching, MFA, and local-in policies limiting who reaches IKE
Strong DH groups and AES-256, so that the tunnels can't be broken into
options.why_wrong: Good crypto, but gateways are breached through bugs and stolen credentials.

options.text: 3DES and DH group 2 enabled as fallbacks for partner compatibility
options.why_wrong: Weakens security without reducing exposure.

options.text: IKE on a non-standard port, so the gateway is harder for scanners
options.why_wrong: Obscurity doesn't replace patching, MFA and access limits.

quiz.explanation: Exposure, identity, patching.

scenarios.title: Whiteboard: 40 branches, 2 data centres
scenarios.situation: "We have 40 branches with two internet links each, two data centres, Microsoft 365 and an on-prem ERP. Design the network security and WAN."
scenarios.ask: Talk through it as you would at the whiteboard, in 3–4 minutes.
right_thinking: Clarify: availability, voice, compliance, team skills, existing gear
Hub-and-spoke overlays to both DCs, BGP, SD-WAN rules per app
HA pairs in the DCs, FortiManager templates, FortiAnalyzer logs
Failure modes and acceptance tests
scenarios.what: A structured design with reasons and risks.
scenarios.why: It's exactly what you'd do in a design workshop.
scenarios.model_answer: I'd start with questions: uptime target, voice at branches, compliance like PCI, and who operates it. Assuming two ISPs per branch: each branch FortiGate builds IPsec overlays to both data centres, with BGP over the overlays so the DCs are reachable over either. SD-WAN zones for underlay and overlay; health checks to the hubs and to Microsoft 365; rules: voice on Best Quality, ERP over the overlay with Lowest Cost (SLA), Microsoft 365 straight out locally using the Internet Service Database. In each DC an FGCP active-passive pair with two heartbeat links and session pickup. Everything is templated in FortiManager, logs go to FortiAnalyzer. Failure modes I'd design out: asymmetric routing between the two hubs, probes that don't reflect the app path, and split brain in the DCs. Acceptance tests: pull each ISP at a pilot branch, fail over each hub, and fail the DC primary during a call.
scenarios.best_way: Clarify, overlays to both DCs with BGP, SD-WAN rules per app, HA pairs, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer, failure modes, acceptance tests.

scenarios.title: Live troubleshooting: 'the website is slow only through the VPN'
scenarios.situation: "Branch users say the intranet is slow and file uploads fail, but only over the site-to-site VPN. Walk us through it."
scenarios.ask: Narrate your method and commands.
right_thinking: Define: which apps, since when, what changed
Tunnel state and counters
Small works, large fails → MTU/MSS
Prove, fix, verify
scenarios.what: A narrated, evidence-based diagnosis.
scenarios.why: Panels judge method and communication as much as the answer.
how: get vpn ipsec tunnel summary / diagnose vpn tunnel list
scenarios.model_answer: First I'd define it: is it all branch users, since when, did anything change, and does browsing small pages work while uploads fail? Then I'd check the tunnel: summary and tunnel list, phase 2 up and counters moving both ways. If small requests work and big transfers fail, I suspect MTU: ESP overhead means full-size packets don't fit, and if ICMP 'fragmentation needed' is blocked, hosts never adjust. I'd prove it with pings with the don't-fragment bit at decreasing sizes and a sniffer showing retransmissions. The fix is clamping TCP MSS on both tunnel policies. Then I'd verify with the users and document it, and add the MSS setting to the VPN template so the next site doesn't repeat it.
scenarios.best_way: Define it, check the tunnel, small-works-big-fails means MTU, prove with DF pings, clamp MSS, verify, template it.

scenarios.title: What if the panelist challenges your answer?
scenarios.situation: You say SD-WAN rules come after policy routes. A panelist says, "Are you sure? I think SD-WAN rules win."
scenarios.ask: How do you respond?
right_thinking: Stay calm; it may be a test
Explain your reasoning and how you'd verify
Offer the evidence: the commands that show the decision
scenarios.what: A confident, respectful correction with evidence.
scenarios.why: Customers will challenge you too.
scenarios.model_answer: I'd say: "My understanding is that policy routes are checked first, then SD-WAN rules, then the routing table. I've seen it in migrations, where a leftover policy route bypassed a new SD-WAN rule. To confirm on a live unit, diagnose firewall proute list shows the policy routes and SD-WAN rules in the order they're applied, and diagnose ip proute match shows what a given packet would use. Happy to be corrected if a newer version changed it."
scenarios.best_way: Respectfully hold your position with the reasoning and the command that proves it.

interview.question: Walk me through what happens to a packet entering a FortiGate.
interview.framework: Ordered steps → how you use it
interview.model_answer: "It arrives on an interface, DoS checks apply if configured, it's decrypted if it came through a tunnel, then destination NAT if it matches a VIP. Then the routing decision: policy routes, SD-WAN rules, routing table. Then the firewall policy lookup and session creation, security profiles, source NAT, encryption if it leaves through a tunnel, and egress. I use that order when troubleshooting: debug flow shows exactly where a packet stops."
interview.best_way: Ingress, decrypt, DNAT, route, policy, profiles, SNAT, encrypt, egress, and debug flow shows where it stops.

interview.question: A user can't reach a server through the FortiGate. Go.
interview.framework: Define → sniffer → debug flow → session → fix
interview.model_answer: "First the facts: source, destination, port, one user or all, what changed. Then the sniffer on the ingress and egress interfaces to see whether the packet arrives and leaves. If it arrives and doesn't leave, a filtered debug flow tells me the route and the policy decision, or the drop reason. If it leaves and nothing returns, I look downstream and at the return route. Then fix in a window and verify with the user."
interview.best_way: Facts, sniffer, debug flow, then downstream; fix and verify.

interview.question: How does FortiGate choose between policy routes, SD-WAN rules and the routing table?
interview.model_answer: "Policy routes first, then SD-WAN rules, then the routing table. And by default an SD-WAN rule is only consulted if the best route for the destination points to an SD-WAN member. In migrations, leftover policy routes or more specific static routes are the classic reason a new SD-WAN rule seems to be ignored."
interview.best_way: Policy routes, SD-WAN rules, routing table, with the FIB check for SD-WAN.

interview.question: Explain the order of NAT and policy matching with a VIP.
interview.model_answer: "Destination NAT happens before routing and the policy lookup, so the policy for a VIP matches the VIP object or the mapped address depending on configuration, and VIP policies take priority. Source NAT is applied after the policy. I was my TAC team's go-to for NAT, and the common customer mistake was writing the policy against the public IP instead of the VIP."
interview.best_way: DNAT before routing and policy, SNAT after; most errors are policies written against the wrong address.

interview.question: Design remote access for 500 users with MFA.
interview.model_answer: "Two options: IPsec dial-up with FortiClient, IKEv2 with EAP and MFA via FortiToken or SAML to their identity provider, or ZTNA if they want per-application access with device posture. For 500 users I'd usually start with IPsec dial-up for full-tunnel needs and plan ZTNA for sensitive apps. Either way: patch the gateway fast, limit who can reach IKE, and log to FortiAnalyzer."
interview.best_way: IPsec dial-up with IKEv2 and MFA now, ZTNA for sensitive apps, and harden the gateway.

interview.question: How would you migrate a customer from another firewall vendor to FortiGate?
interview.framework: Discover → convert → clean → test → cut over
interview.model_answer: "Discover the current config and what's actually used, convert with FortiConverter or a scripted approach, then clean up: unused objects, shadowed and overly broad rules, NAT semantics that differ between vendors. Test in a lab, write a MOP with a rollback, cut over in a window, and validate with the customer's application owners. The NAT translation is where most migrations break, so I review it line by line."
interview.best_way: Discover, convert, clean, lab-test, MOP with rollback, cut over, validate. NAT is where they break.

interview.question: What's the difference between FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer, and why deploy both?
interview.model_answer: "FortiManager is central configuration: devices, policy packages, templates, installs and revisions. FortiAnalyzer is central logging and analytics: log storage, FortiView, reports, incidents and automation. Together: you change many FortiGates consistently and you can prove what happened afterwards."
interview.best_way: FortiManager changes things consistently; FortiAnalyzer proves what happened.

interview.question: A customer's FortiGate is in conserve mode. What does that mean and what do you do?
interview.model_answer: "Memory is under pressure: by default it enters red conserve mode at 88 % memory, recovers below 82 %, and extreme at 95 %. Proxy-based inspection may stop accepting new sessions that need it. I'd check memory consumers and sessions, and look at proxy usage. At Fortinet I reduced memory pressure for customers by moving policies from proxy to flow inspection where proxy wasn't needed, which also kept more traffic on the NPU."
interview.best_way: Memory pressure at 88 %. Find the consumers; move proxy policies to flow where proxy isn't needed.

interview.question: How do you deploy SSL deep inspection without breaking users?
interview.model_answer: "Use a CA from the customer's PKI, push it by Group Policy and MDM before enabling anything, pilot with IT, exempt banking, health and pinned apps, then roll out by department with a rollback to certificate inspection. I taught customers exactly this, pushing the CA through Group Policy."
interview.best_way: CA first via GPO and MDM, pilot, exemptions, phases.

interview.question: What do you check after a cluster upgrade?
interview.model_answer: "Both units on the target version, get system ha status showing in sync with heartbeats up, the expected primary, routing and VPN tunnels up, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer connectivity, and the customer's own application test list. Then a short report. I've guided customers through HA upgrades step by step, including a manual console upgrade when the online one failed, so I always have the backup and console ready."
interview.best_way: Versions, HA in sync, routing and VPNs, FMG/FAZ, the customer's test list, then a report.

interview.question: Tell us about a Fortinet issue you escalated to development.
interview.model_answer: "SD-WAN with three ISPs over VPN was duplicating packets. I reproduced it, traced it to specific SLA settings with captures, and worked with development for almost two months with reproductions until the fix."
interview.best_way: Packet duplication over three ISPs traced to SLA settings; clean reproductions to development.

interview.question: Which logs and reports would you set up for a new deployment?
interview.model_answer: "Traffic logs on the policies that matter, all security events, and system events, sent to FortiAnalyzer with retention sized to the customer's compliance needs. Then scheduled reports for the security team and executives, and alerts for critical events. I've turned log data into SOC 2, ISO 27001 and PCI-DSS evidence for boards, so I start from what they need to prove."
interview.best_way: Log what matters to FortiAnalyzer, size retention to compliance, scheduled reports and alerts.

modules.title: Layers, Ethernet and switching: frames, MAC learning, ARP, VLANs, STP and MTU
objectives: Place protocols and problems in the right layer, and troubleshoot bottom-up
Explain MAC learning, flooding, ARP and what a switch does with unknown or broadcast frames
Configure and read 802.1Q VLAN tagging and spot native-VLAN and allowed-VLAN mismatches
Reason about STP roles and MTU/MSS problems that break only some traffic
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Administration Guide: Interfaces (p. 236+), VLANs; FortiSwitch 7.6 Administration Guide: VLANs (p. 370), STP (p. 273)
IEEE 802.1Q, 802.1D/802.1w concepts; RFC 879/RFC 6691 (MSS)

units.title: Layers as a troubleshooting tool
units.body:
The OSI model has seven layers; the TCP/IP model folds them into four (link, internet, transport,
application). In the field the model is a **troubleshooting order**: prove the lower layer before blaming the
upper one.

| Layer | Question | Evidence on a FortiGate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Physical | Is the link up, at what speed and duplex? | `get system interface physical`, CRC errors |
| 2 Data link | Do frames arrive, right VLAN, ARP resolved? | `diagnose ip arp list`, sniffer with MACs |
| 3 Network | Is there a route each way? | `get router info routing-table all` |
| 4 Transport | Does the TCP handshake complete? | sniffer flags, session table |
| 7 Application | Does the service answer correctly? | curl, logs, UTM verdicts |

A sniffer that shows SYN out and nothing back already tells you which layers are fine (the packet left) and
which aren't proven (the return path).

:::recall
Q: Why troubleshoot bottom-up?
A: Every layer depends on the one below; a perfect policy can't help a frame that never arrives.
:::

units.title: Ethernet, MAC learning and ARP
units.body:
A switch learns **source MACs** per port and forwards by **destination MAC**. Unknown unicast and broadcast
frames are **flooded** to every port in the VLAN. MAC entries age out (often 300 s).

**ARP** maps an IPv4 address to a MAC inside a subnet. A host sending to another subnet ARPs for its
**gateway**, not the destination. Classic faults:

- Wrong mask: the host thinks the destination is local and ARPs for it; nobody answers.
- Duplicate IP: ARP replies from two MACs; the session works, then breaks.
- Stale ARP after a failover: traffic goes to the old MAC until the cache updates (gratuitous ARP fixes this,
  which is why FortiGate HA sends it).

:::recall
Q: Which MAC does a host put in the frame for a packet to another subnet?
A: The gateway's MAC (the IP header still carries the final destination).
:::

:::why
Q: Why does an HA failover send gratuitous ARP?
A: So switches and hosts update their tables to the new active unit's MAC quickly.
:::

units.title: VLANs, STP and MTU
units.body:
**802.1Q** adds a 4-byte tag with a 12-bit VLAN ID (1–4094 usable). A **trunk** carries several VLANs tagged;
an **access** port carries one untagged. The **native VLAN** of a trunk travels untagged; both ends must agree,
and the VLAN must be in the trunk's **allowed** list. On a FortiGate a VLAN is a sub-interface with a `vlanid`
on a physical port.

**STP** (802.1D) and **RSTP** (802.1w) block redundant links to prevent loops: one root bridge (lowest bridge
ID), root ports toward it, designated ports per segment, the rest blocked. A misplaced root (an access switch
with a low priority) forces traffic across the wrong links. RSTP converges in seconds, classic STP in up to
~50.

**MTU and MSS.** Ethernet MTU is 1500 bytes; tunnels (IPsec, GRE, VXLAN) add overhead. When path MTU
discovery is blocked (ICMP "fragmentation needed" dropped), small packets work and large ones vanish: SSH works,
file copies hang, HTTPS pages half-load. TCP MSS clamping on the tunnel interface (`set tcp-mss`) fixes TCP.

:::recall
Q: Symptom set of a PMTU black hole?
A: Small transfers and logins work; large transfers, page loads or file copies stall.
:::

:::why
Q: Why must the native VLAN match on both ends of a trunk?
A: Untagged frames are assigned to each end's native VLAN; a mismatch silently merges two VLANs.
:::

cards.back: Link, internet, transport, application.
Bottom-up: physical, link, network, transport, application.
Source MACs per port; forwards by destination MAC.
Flooded to all ports in the VLAN.

cards.front: Host sends to another subnet: ARP for
cards.back: The default gateway.
Unsolicited ARP announcing an IP/MAC pair; used after HA failover.
4 bytes, 12-bit VLAN ID (1–4094).
The VLAN carried untagged on a trunk; must match both ends.
Lowest bridge ID (priority + MAC).

cards.front: PMTU black hole fix for TCP
cards.back: Clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel/interface (set tcp-mss).

quiz.stem: A PC at 10.1.1.20/24 pings 10.1.2.30. Which address does it ARP for?

options.text: Its default gateway's IP, since the destination is on another subnet
10.1.2.30 directly, since ARP works across routed subnets on a LAN
options.why_wrong: ARP is link-local; it never crosses a router.

options.text: The broadcast 10.1.1.255, so that the routers answer for the subnet
options.why_wrong: ARP requests are broadcast frames, but they ask for one specific IP, the gateway.

options.text: The DNS server's address, which then answers with the remote host's MAC
options.why_wrong: DNS maps names to IPs, not IPs to MACs.

quiz.explanation: Different subnet → next hop is the gateway → ARP for the gateway's IP.

quiz.stem: After an IPsec tunnel goes up, SSH to a remote server works but SCP of a 50 MB file stalls at 0%. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Large packets exceed the tunnel MTU and the ICMP that signals it is dropped
The policy allows SSH, but its service object leaves out the separate SCP protocol port
options.why_wrong: SCP runs over SSH on TCP 22; the same session works for small packets.

options.text: The tunnel phase 2 selectors exclude large flows from the encrypted path
options.why_wrong: Selectors match addresses and ports, not packet sizes.

options.text: Duplex mismatch on the WAN port drops frames once throughput goes up enough
options.why_wrong: Duplex issues cause errors and slowness, not a clean stall only on large packets.

quiz.explanation: Small works, large stalls: a PMTU black hole. Clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel or allow ICMP type 3 code 4.

quiz.stem: Two switches connect with a trunk. Users in VLAN 20 on switch B suddenly appear in VLAN 30's DHCP scope. Which misconfiguration explains it?

options.text: The trunk's native VLAN is 20 on one side and 30 on the other
VLAN 20 is missing from the trunk's allowed VLAN list on switch B
options.why_wrong: Users would lose connectivity, not land in VLAN 30.

options.text: STP blocks the trunk, so the users fall back to the management VLAN
options.why_wrong: STP blocking stops traffic; it doesn't reassign VLANs.

options.text: The DHCP server's scope for VLAN 30 overlaps the VLAN 20 address range
options.why_wrong: Overlap would confuse addressing, but the frames themselves are crossing VLANs here.

quiz.explanation: Untagged frames take each side's native VLAN; a mismatch bridges VLAN 20 into VLAN 30.

quiz.stem: Order the troubleshooting layers bottom-up.
items: Frames and ARP in the right VLAN
quiz.explanation: Each layer depends on the one below.

quiz.stem: After an HA failover, half the users lose connectivity for several minutes, then recover on their own. What most likely helped them recover?

options.text: Their ARP or switch MAC entries aged out and relearned the new active unit
STP reconverged around the failed unit's ports after its default timers ran out
options.why_wrong: Possible in some designs, but the classic minutes-long pattern after failover is stale ARP/MAC entries.

options.text: The DHCP leases expired and the clients requested new gateway addresses
options.why_wrong: The gateway IP doesn't change in HA; leases are hours long.

options.text: The session table synchronised to the new active unit after the failover
options.why_wrong: Session sync helps existing sessions; it doesn't fix L2 forwarding to the wrong MAC.

quiz.explanation: Stale MAC/ARP entries point at the old unit until they age out or a gratuitous ARP updates them.

quiz.stem: How many bits long is the VLAN ID field in an 802.1Q tag?
quiz.explanation: 12 bits: 4,096 values, 1–4094 usable.

Add a firewall policy from port2 to port3, because the echo request is being denied

scenarios.title: It works for small files
scenarios.situation: A new IPsec tunnel to a branch: users log in to the ERP fine, but report exports never finish. The branch ISP uses PPPoE.
scenarios.ask: What do you suspect and how do you prove it?
right_thinking: Small works, large stalls → MTU/PMTU
PPPoE (1492) plus IPsec overhead lowers the path MTU
Prove with ping using DF and growing sizes; sniff for missing ICMP frag-needed
Fix with TCP MSS clamping on the tunnel; document the value
scenarios.what: A PMTU problem from PPPoE plus IPsec overhead.
scenarios.why: Each encapsulation eats bytes; when ICMP feedback is lost, large TCP segments vanish.
scenarios.model_answer: "Small transactions work and big exports hang, and PPPoE plus IPsec shrinks the path MTU, so I'd test with DF pings of growing size across the tunnel. If 1400 passes and 1450 fails, I clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel interface and re-test the export."
scenarios.best_way: Small works, large hangs: prove the MTU, clamp the MSS.

interview.question: A user says 'the network is slow' only when copying big files over the VPN. What do you check?
interview.model_answer: "That pattern — small things fine, big transfers stall — is usually MTU across the tunnel with ICMP feedback blocked. I'd prove it with DF pings of increasing size, then clamp the TCP MSS on the tunnel interface and confirm the copy completes."
interview.best_way: Prove the MTU, clamp the MSS.

modules.title: Addressing and core services: subnetting, ICMP, DHCP, DNS and NTP
objectives: Subnet IPv4 quickly and read IPv6 prefixes without hesitation
Use ICMP messages as evidence (unreachable codes, TTL exceeded, fragmentation needed)
Troubleshoot DHCP (DORA, relay) and DNS (records, recursion, split DNS) on and through a FortiGate
Explain why NTP is a security control, not housekeeping
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Administration Guide: DNS (p. 405), DHCP server and relay (p. 607), IPv6 (p. 987)
RFC 792 (ICMP), RFC 2131 (DHCP), RFC 1034/1035 (DNS), RFC 5905 (NTP), RFC 4291 (IPv6 addressing)

units.title: Subnetting at interview speed
units.body:
Block size = 256 − the interesting mask octet. For a /27 (255.255.255.224) the block is 32: networks at .0,
.32, .64…; broadcast is the next network − 1; usable hosts = 2^(32−prefix) − 2.

| Prefix | Mask | Block | Usable |
|---|---|---|---|
| /24 | 255.255.255.0 | 256 | 254 |
| /26 | 255.255.255.192 | 64 | 62 |
| /27 | 255.255.255.224 | 32 | 30 |
| /29 | 255.255.255.248 | 8 | 6 |
| /30 | 255.255.255.252 | 4 | 2 |

**IPv6** in one paragraph: 128-bit addresses, /64 per LAN, link-local fe80::/10 always present, global unicast
2000::/3, unique local fc00::/7; neighbours via NDP (ICMPv6), not ARP. Blocking all ICMPv6 breaks IPv6.

:::recall
Q: Broadcast address of 172.16.5.77/27?
A: 172.16.5.95 (block 32: network .64, broadcast .95).
:::

units.title: ICMP as evidence
units.body:
ICMP messages tell you who gave up and why:

| Message | Type/code | Means |
|---|---|---|
| Echo request/reply | 8 / 0 | Reachability |
| Destination unreachable, net/host | 3 / 0, 1 | A router had no route / no ARP answer |
| Port unreachable | 3 / 3 | The host is up, nothing listens on that UDP port |
| Fragmentation needed | 3 / 4 | Packet bigger than the next hop MTU with DF set |
| Administratively prohibited | 3 / 13 | A filter rejected it (some firewalls send it) |
| Time exceeded | 11 / 0 | TTL hit zero: the basis of traceroute |

A FortiGate deny policy drops silently by default; a timeout is therefore a hint of a firewall, a quick
"unreachable" a hint of routing.

:::recall
Q: What does traceroute rely on?
A: ICMP time exceeded (type 11) from each hop as TTL increases.
:::

units.title: DHCP, DNS and NTP
units.body:
**DHCP** is DORA: Discover (broadcast), Offer, Request, Acknowledge. Broadcasts don't cross routers, so a
central server needs a **relay** on the client's gateway (`set dhcp-relay-service enable` and the server IP on
the FortiGate interface). Typical faults: relay missing, scope exhausted, wrong gateway/DNS options.

**DNS**: A/AAAA (address), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), PTR (reverse), TXT (SPF, DKIM, verification), SRV
(services such as AD's `_ldap._tcp`). Recursive resolvers ask on clients' behalf; authoritative servers own a
zone. **Split DNS** answers internal names with internal addresses. A FortiGate can be a DNS forwarder or a
server (`config system dns-server`) and hands out DNS in DHCP (`dns-service default | specify | local`).

**NTP** matters for security: Kerberos fails beyond 5 minutes of skew by default, certificates can look
not-yet-valid, and log timelines lie. Point FortiGates, DCs and SIEMs at the same time source.

:::recall
Q: Why does DHCP across subnets need a relay?
A: The Discover is a broadcast and routers don't forward broadcasts; the relay unicasts it to the server.
:::

:::why
Q: Why is NTP a security control?
A: Authentication (Kerberos), certificate validity and incident timelines all depend on correct time.
:::

cards.back: ICMPv6 (NDP), not ARP.
Port unreachable: host up, nothing on that UDP port.
Fragmentation needed (DF set, packet too big).
Time exceeded: TTL reached zero (traceroute).
Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

cards.front: DNS record for AD service discovery
cards.back: SRV (e.g. _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs).
default (system DNS), specify (dns-server1/2), local (the FortiGate itself).
5 minutes.

quiz.stem: What is the broadcast address of 192.168.40.130/26?
Clients on VLAN 30 get APIPA addresses (169.254.x.x). The DHCP server is in the data centre and works for other VLANs. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The VLAN 30 gateway interface has no DHCP relay pointing at the server
The DHCP server's scope for VLAN 30 has the wrong DNS servers in its options
options.why_wrong: Wrong options still give an address; APIPA means no offer arrived at all.

options.text: The clients' DNS suffix doesn't match the domain name the DHCP server expects
options.why_wrong: DHCP doesn't check DNS suffixes before offering an address.

options.text: A firewall policy blocks UDP 67 from the data centre back to the VLAN 30 clients
options.why_wrong: Possible in theory, but relay traffic is from the relay to the server; the missing relay is the common cause.

quiz.explanation: Other VLANs work, so the server is fine. VLAN 30's broadcasts never reach it without a relay on its gateway.

quiz.output:
C:\Users\User>tracert -d 10.50.1.20
Tracing route to 10.50.1.20 over a maximum of 30 hops
  1    <1 ms    <1 ms    <1 ms  10.10.10.1
  2     2 ms     1 ms     2 ms  10.255.0.1
  3  10.255.0.1  reports: Destination net unreachable.
quiz.stem: What do you check first?

options.text: The routing table of 10.255.0.1: it has no route toward 10.50.1.0/24
The firewall policy on 10.10.10.1, because hop 1 is the first device that filters traffic
options.why_wrong: The packet passed hop 1 and reached hop 2; the router at hop 2 answered that it has no route.

options.text: The destination host 10.50.1.20, which is probably down or blocking traceroute
options.why_wrong: A down host gives timeouts at the end, not a 'net unreachable' from an earlier hop.

options.text: The client's DNS settings, since tracert could not resolve the names of the hops
options.why_wrong: -d disables name resolution on purpose; DNS isn't involved.

quiz.explanation: 'Destination net unreachable' from 10.255.0.1 is ICMP type 3 code 0: that router has no route. Check its table (and what should advertise 10.50.1.0/24).

quiz.stem: Users can browse internal sites by IP but not by name since a new FortiGate went in. Clients use DHCP from the FortiGate with dns-service local. What is the likely gap?

options.text: The FortiGate isn't configured as a DNS server on that interface with system dns-server
The FortiGate's system DNS is set to public resolvers instead of the internal ones
options.why_wrong: Would break internal names in forwarder mode, but with 'local' the interface must first act as a DNS server.

options.text: A policy is missing for UDP 53 from the LAN to the WAN toward public DNS resolvers
options.why_wrong: Clients are told to ask the FortiGate itself; traffic to the FortiGate isn't a forward policy.

options.text: The DHCP lease time is too short, so the clients lose their DNS settings over and over again
options.why_wrong: Lease renewals keep the same options; lease time doesn't break name resolution.

quiz.explanation: 'local' hands out the FortiGate's interface IP as DNS; without `config system dns-server` on that interface nobody answers.

quiz.stem: Which can break when a domain controller's clock drifts 9 minutes? Select all that apply.

options.text: Kerberos authentication for users and services
The order of events in a SIEM investigation timeline
Validation of certificates near their start or end dates
ARP resolution between hosts on the same VLAN
options.why_wrong: ARP has no notion of time beyond cache ageing on each host.

options.text: Spanning tree root election between the core switches
options.why_wrong: STP uses bridge IDs and timers, not wall-clock time.

quiz.explanation: Time underpins Kerberos (5 min skew), certificate validity windows and every log timeline.

scenarios.title: The 9-minute clock
scenarios.situation: After a hypervisor migration, some users can't log on to file shares; others can. Event logs on the DC show Kerberos errors. The SIEM timeline for the morning looks out of order.
scenarios.ask: What do you look at and fix?

Fix the time source hierarchy, then re-check logons and log ordering
scenarios.what: Clock skew after the migration.
