scenarios.model_answer: "Kerberos errors for some users plus a scrambled SIEM timeline both point at time. I'd compare the DC's clock with a reliable source — after a VM migration the hypervisor often overrides it — fix the NTP hierarchy with the PDC emulator syncing externally, and confirm logons and log order are back."
scenarios.best_way: Kerberos and timelines both break on time: fix NTP.

interview.question: DHCP works on one VLAN and not on another behind the same FortiGate. Walk me through it.
interview.model_answer: "Same server, one VLAN fails, so I look at what's specific to that VLAN: is the relay enabled on its gateway interface with the right server IP, does the server have a scope for that subnet, and is there a route back. Then I'd run a sniffer for UDP 67/68 on the VLAN interface to see the Discover and whether an Offer comes back."
interview.best_way: What's specific to that VLAN: relay, scope, route — then sniff DORA.

modules.title: Transport, state and NAT theory
objectives: Explain TCP setup, teardown and reset, and what a stateful firewall remembers about each flow
Explain how UDP and ICMP get "state" on a firewall even though they have none themselves
Tell SNAT, DNAT, PAT and hairpin NAT apart and say when each is used
Explain MTU, MSS and why large transfers stall over tunnels while small pages work
Explain why some protocols (FTP active mode, SIP) need a session helper or ALG to survive NAT
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Policies, anti-replay, TCP MSS and session TTL (pp. 2104–2110)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: IP pool types (pp. 2166–2170), Hairpin NAT (pp. 2229–2231)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Asymmetric routing (pp. 653–655)
RFC 9293 (TCP), RFC 768 (UDP), RFC 3022 (NAT) — general knowledge

units.title: TCP from SYN to FIN, as a firewall sees it
units.body:
TCP gives applications a reliable, ordered byte stream on top of IP, which is happy to lose, duplicate or reorder packets. It does this with **sequence numbers**, **acknowledgements**, a **receive window** and a strict **connection life cycle**. A firewall engineer doesn't need to memorise every RFC detail, but must be able to read that life cycle in a capture and explain it to a customer.

## Setup: the three-way handshake

1. **SYN**: the client picks an initial sequence number and asks to open a connection. Options travel here too, most importantly the **MSS** (the largest segment it can receive).
2. **SYN/ACK**: the server answers with its own sequence number and acknowledges the client's.
3. **ACK**: the client acknowledges the server. The connection is now *established* and data flows.

If the server port is closed, the server (or a firewall in between) answers the SYN with a **RST**. If nothing answers at all, the client retries the SYN with growing back-off: that is the classic "connection timed out" a user sees when a firewall silently drops traffic.

## Teardown: FIN versus RST

A graceful close uses **FIN** in each direction, each acknowledged. The side that closes first waits in **TIME_WAIT** so late packets from the old connection can't pollute a new one. A **RST** tears the connection down immediately with no goodbye. RSTs are normal in small doses (a browser abandoning a tab) but a burst of them points at a middlebox or an application crashing.

## What a stateful firewall remembers

A stateful firewall evaluates the **first packet** of a flow against the policy table. If a policy allows it, the firewall creates a **session** keyed by the 5-tuple: source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port and protocol. Every later packet, in both directions, is matched against that session instead of the whole policy table. That is why you only write a policy for the direction that *starts* the conversation: replies ride the session.

FortiOS can also check that TCP packets make sense for the session's state. The **anti-replay** option checks TCP flags per policy, so a stray ACK that doesn't belong to a known handshake is dropped.

:::recall
Q: Why does a firewall only need a policy for the direction that opens a TCP connection?
A: The first packet creates a session (5-tuple). Replies match the session, not the policy table, so the return direction is allowed automatically.
:::

:::why
Q: Why is "connection timed out" usually a silent drop while "connection refused" is usually a RST?
A: A drop gives the client nothing back, so it keeps retrying the SYN until it gives up. A RST is an explicit answer that the port is closed or the connection was rejected.
:::

:::tip
On a support call, ask "timed out or refused?" first. It tells you whether to look for a drop (routing, policy, RPF) or for an active reject (closed port, server firewall, IPS reset).
:::

units.title: UDP, ICMP and session timers
units.body:
**UDP** has no handshake, no acknowledgements and no teardown. DNS, NTP, syslog, SNMP, RADIUS, voice media (RTP) and QUIC all run on it. A firewall still builds a session for UDP: the first packet that matches a policy creates a 5-tuple entry, and the reply matches it. The difference is how the session ends. With no FIN, the firewall relies on a **timer**: if the session sees no packets for its time-to-live, it is removed.

**ICMP** is the network's messenger: echo request and reply (ping), destination unreachable, time exceeded (traceroute), and "fragmentation needed" (path MTU discovery). Firewalls track echo using the ICMP identifier so a reply can match its request.

## Session TTL

Every protocol has a session time-to-live: how long an idle session stays in the table. FortiOS lets you change it globally and **per policy** with `set session-ttl <seconds>` (or `never` for a few special cases). Two classic problems come from TTLs:

- **Too short:** a database or ERP client keeps an idle TCP connection open for an hour. The firewall drops the idle session after its TTL, the next packet arrives with no session and is dropped, and users see "the app freezes after lunch".
- **Too long:** huge numbers of dead UDP sessions fill the table on a busy gateway.

:::recall
Q: How does a firewall know a UDP "conversation" is over?
A: It doesn't get a signal. The session expires when it has been idle for longer than its TTL.
:::

:::pitfall
Raising the TTL for one application is fine on its own policy. Raising it globally to fix one app can bloat the session table for everyone.
:::

:::cli
config firewall policy
    edit 12
        set session-ttl 7200
    next
end
:::

:::why
Q: Why might a VoIP phone lose incoming calls after a few minutes of quiet even though outgoing calls always work?
A: The phone's registration and the pinhole for incoming SIP live in a UDP session. If the session expires before the phone re-registers, inbound INVITEs find no session and are dropped.
:::

units.title: NAT, PAT and hairpin NAT
units.body:
**Network Address Translation** rewrites addresses as packets cross the firewall, and the session remembers the rewrite so replies can be translated back.

| Type | What changes | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **SNAT** | Source IP (and often port) | Users going out to the internet |
| **PAT** (overload) | Source IP *and* port, many users share one IP | Almost every office internet edge |
| **Static 1:1** | One inside IP always maps to one outside IP | A server that must always appear from the same address |
| **DNAT** | Destination IP (and optionally port) | Publishing an internal server (FortiOS calls this a VIP) |
| **Hairpin** | Both, for inside users reaching an inside server by its public address | Bookmarks with public names that must work in the office too |

## How many users fit behind one IP?

PAT distinguishes sessions by the translated source port. FortiOS documents **60,416 usable ports per IP** in an overload IP pool. The limit applies **per destination service** (same protocol, destination IP and port), so a single public IP supports far more than 60,416 total sessions as long as they go to different destinations. When many users hammer the *same* service, a pool with more IPs, or a fixed-port-range / port-block-allocation pool, is the answer.

## Hairpin NAT

A user inside the office types `portal.company.com`, which resolves to the public IP. The packet goes to the FortiGate, which sees its own external address as the destination, applies the VIP (DNAT) **and** must make the server reply back through the firewall. FortiOS's hairpin example uses a VIP plus a policy for the DNAT and a SNAT policy so the return traffic comes back through the FortiGate. Split DNS (an internal answer with the private IP) is the alternative that avoids hairpinning.

:::recall
Q: Why does PAT need to change the source port, not just the source IP?
A: Many inside hosts share one outside IP. The translated source port is what lets the firewall tell their sessions apart and send replies to the right host.
:::

:::why
Q: Why do inside users sometimes fail to reach their own published web server by its public name, while internet users can?
A: Without hairpin NAT (or split DNS) the inside user's packet to the public IP is either not translated or the server replies directly to the inside client, bypassing the firewall, so the session breaks.
:::

:::threat ref=dbir-2026-vuln-exploitation-31pct
Every DNAT/VIP publishes a service to the internet. Exploiting vulnerabilities is now the top initial access vector at 31 % of breaches (Verizon DBIR 2026). Each VIP you configure for a customer needs an owner, a patch plan and IPS on its policy.
:::

units.title: MTU, MSS and protocols that fight NAT
units.body:
## MTU and MSS

The **MTU** is the largest IP packet a link carries: 1500 bytes on standard Ethernet. The **MSS** is the largest TCP payload: MTU minus the IP header (20) and TCP header (20), so **1460** on plain Ethernet. Each side announces its MSS in the SYN.

Tunnels and encapsulations add headers: PPPoE adds 8 bytes, GRE 24, IPsec ESP typically 50–80 depending on cipher and NAT-T. If a full-size packet no longer fits and the sender set "don't fragment", a router should send back **ICMP fragmentation needed** so the sender lowers its packet size (path MTU discovery). When that ICMP is blocked somewhere, small exchanges work but full-size packets vanish. Users report: **"the page half-loads", "small emails send but attachments hang", "SSH works but file copy stalls"**.

## The fix: MSS clamping

The firewall rewrites the MSS option in the SYN so both ends agree to smaller segments that fit the tunnel. In FortiOS you can clamp per policy:

:::cli
config firewall policy
    edit 10
        set tcp-mss-sender 1350
        set tcp-mss-receiver 1350
    next
end
:::

You can also set `tcp-mss` on an interface. Clamping only helps TCP; UDP-heavy apps over tunnels still need a correct MTU.

## Protocols that carry addresses inside the payload

NAT rewrites headers. Some protocols also write IP addresses and ports **inside the payload**:

- **FTP active mode**: the client tells the server, in the PORT command, which IP and port to connect back to. Behind NAT that is a private address the server can't reach.
- **SIP** (VoIP signalling): SDP bodies carry the IP and ports for the RTP media streams.

Firewalls solve this with **session helpers / ALGs**: they read the control channel, rewrite the embedded addresses and open the expected secondary connection (a pinhole). When helpers fight with a phone system that already handles NAT itself, you get **one-way audio** or calls that drop at 30 seconds, and the fix is to decide which side does NAT traversal, not both.

:::recall
Q: What MSS does a host announce on a standard 1500-byte Ethernet link, and why?
A: 1460: 1500 MTU minus 20 bytes of IP header and 20 bytes of TCP header.
:::

:::why
Q: Why do large downloads stall over an IPsec tunnel while web pages with small objects still load?
A: Full-size packets exceed the tunnel MTU after ESP overhead. If the ICMP "fragmentation needed" messages are lost, the sender keeps sending packets that are dropped. Small packets fit and pass. MSS clamping fixes it for TCP.
:::

:::ps
In a cutover plan, add an MSS test (a large file copy and an HTTPS download through each new tunnel) to the acceptance checklist. It catches the problem before users do.
:::

cards.front: Name the three packets of the TCP handshake in order.
cards.back: SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK.

cards.front: Which TCP option, sent in the SYN, announces the largest segment a host can receive?
cards.back: MSS (maximum segment size).

cards.front: What five fields identify a firewall session?
cards.back: Source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol (the 5-tuple).

cards.front: A user says 'connection refused'. What did the client most likely receive?
cards.back: A TCP RST: the port is closed or something actively rejected the connection.

cards.front: Which TCP state does the side that closes first wait in, and why?
cards.back: TIME_WAIT, so late packets from the old connection can't be mistaken for a new one.

cards.front: What does the FortiOS per-policy `anti-replay` option check?
cards.back: TCP flags, so packets that don't fit the session's TCP state are dropped.

cards.front: How does a UDP session leave a firewall's session table?
cards.back: When it is idle longer than its session TTL; UDP has no FIN.

cards.front: FortiOS CLI to give one policy's sessions a 2-hour TTL?
cards.back: `set session-ttl 7200` under that policy in `config firewall policy`.

cards.front: Symptom of a session TTL that is too short for an app with long idle connections?
cards.back: The app freezes after being idle; the next packet finds no session and is dropped.

cards.front: Which ICMP message drives path MTU discovery?
cards.back: Destination unreachable – fragmentation needed (DF set).

cards.front: SNAT vs DNAT in one line each.
cards.back: SNAT rewrites the source (users going out). DNAT rewrites the destination (publishing a server inside).

cards.front: What does FortiOS call a DNAT object?
cards.back: A virtual IP (VIP).

cards.front: How many usable ports per IP does FortiOS document for an overload IP pool?
cards.back: 60,416 per IP, per destination service (protocol, destination IP and port).
Letting inside users reach an inside server through its public address: DNAT to the server plus SNAT so replies return through the firewall.

cards.front: Alternative to hairpin NAT for inside users?
cards.back: Split DNS: inside resolvers answer with the server's private IP.

cards.front: MSS on a standard 1500-byte Ethernet link?
Classic user symptom of an MTU/MSS problem over a tunnel?
cards.back: Small things work, large transfers stall: half-loaded pages, hanging attachments, stuck file copies.

cards.front: FortiOS policy options to clamp TCP MSS?
cards.back: `set tcp-mss-sender <n>` and `set tcp-mss-receiver <n>`.

cards.front: Why does FTP active mode break behind NAT without a helper?
cards.back: The PORT command carries the client's private IP and port inside the payload; the server can't connect back to it.

cards.front: Classic sign that SIP ALG and the phone system are both doing NAT traversal?
cards.back: One-way audio or calls that drop after about 30 seconds.

quiz.stem: A firewall allows HTTPS from LAN to WAN. Why doesn't it need a second policy for the server's replies?

options.text: Replies match the session the first packet created
Replies from port 443 are allowed by a built-in rule
options.why_wrong: There's no blanket rule for 443; replies pass because they match a session.

options.text: NAT on the outbound policy opens the return path too
options.why_wrong: NAT rewrites addresses; the session is what permits the reply, NAT or not.

options.text: Implicit deny is applied to new UDP flows alone
options.why_wrong: The implicit deny covers all traffic with no policy and no session.

quiz.explanation: The first packet is checked against policies and creates a session keyed by the 5-tuple. Replies match the session.

quiz.stem: Put the TCP connection setup in order.
items: Client sends SYN with its MSS
quiz.explanation: SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK, then data.

quiz.stem: What MSS (in bytes) will a host announce on a plain 1500-byte Ethernet link with no IP or TCP options?
Users can browse small pages over a new IPsec tunnel, but large downloads stall. Most likely cause?

options.text: Packets above the tunnel MTU are dropped and PMTUD isn't working
The IPsec phase 2 selectors leave part of the server range out
options.why_wrong: Wrong selectors break traffic by address, not by packet size.

options.text: DNS through the tunnel is slow, so the large downloads time out
options.why_wrong: Slow DNS delays the start of every connection, small or large.

options.text: The session TTL is too short, so long transfers get cut off midway
options.why_wrong: TTL ends idle sessions; an active download keeps its session alive.

quiz.explanation: The size-dependent symptom is the clue. ESP overhead lowers the usable MTU; clamp MSS or fix PMTUD.

quiz.stem: What does a FortiOS virtual IP (VIP) do?

options.text: Destination NAT from an external address to an internal one
Source NAT for outbound users to a pool of public addresses
options.why_wrong: That's an IP pool or the egress interface address.

options.text: A loopback address that the FortiGate answers on for services
options.why_wrong: Loopbacks are interfaces, not NAT objects.

options.text: Load balancing of outbound sessions between the two WAN links
options.why_wrong: VIPs can balance servers inbound, but WAN balancing is SD-WAN.

quiz.explanation: VIPs are FortiOS's DNAT objects.

quiz.stem: An app freezes whenever users leave it idle for about an hour, then works after a restart. What do you check first?

options.text: The session TTL for that traffic
The app's TCP keepalive settings
options.why_wrong: Relevant, but first confirm the firewall timer that ends the session.

options.text: The DHCP lease time on the users
options.why_wrong: A lease renewal doesn't break an open TCP connection.

options.text: Interface speed and duplex values
options.why_wrong: Duplex problems cause errors under load, not after idle time.

quiz.explanation: Idle-then-broken is the signature of a session expiring before the app sends its next packet.

quiz.stem: Which protocols carry IP addresses or ports in their payload, and often need a session helper (ALG) to cross NAT? Select all that apply.

options.text: FTP in active mode
SIP with SDP bodies
HTTPS to a web app
options.why_wrong: HTTPS carries no IP/port pairs the firewall must rewrite.

options.text: SSH with port forwards
options.why_wrong: Forwards ride inside the encrypted session; the firewall sees one TCP connection.

quiz.explanation: FTP's PORT command and SIP's SDP body embed addresses; helpers rewrite them and open pinholes.

quiz.stem: In a capture you see SYN, SYN, SYN from the client with growing gaps and nothing back. What does it mean?

options.text: Something silently drops the SYN or its reply
The server's port is closed for that service
options.why_wrong: A closed port answers with an RST.

options.text: The handshake worked but the data gets lost
options.why_wrong: No SYN/ACK came back, so the handshake never completed.

options.text: The client's MSS is too large for the path
options.why_wrong: MSS problems appear after the handshake, with full-size data.

quiz.explanation: SYN retransmissions with no answer mean a drop somewhere: routing, policy, RPF or the server's own firewall.

quiz.stem: Why can one public IP support far more than 60,416 simultaneous PAT sessions?

options.text: The port budget is per destination service, so ports get reused
FortiGate multiplexes several sessions onto each translated port
options.why_wrong: There's no multiplexing; ports are reused per destination.

options.text: UDP sessions are tracked without ports, so they don't use the pool
options.why_wrong: UDP uses ports exactly like TCP for PAT.

options.text: It can't; 60,416 is the hard total for any one public IP address
options.why_wrong: The figure is per service (protocol, destination IP and port), not a total.

quiz.explanation: FortiOS documents 60,416 ports per IP for the same service, so the real total depends on how many destinations users reach.

quiz.stem: Inside users can't open the company portal by its public name, but internet users can. The portal is published with a VIP. What do you propose?

options.text: Hairpin NAT (VIP plus SNAT for inside users) or split DNS
A longer session TTL on the VIP policy for inside traffic
options.why_wrong: Timers are unrelated; the issue is the return path.

options.text: Disable the VIP for inside sources so they reach the server
options.why_wrong: Inside users still resolve the public IP and would hit nothing.

options.text: A static route to the public IP (via the inside interface)
options.why_wrong: The public IP is the FortiGate's own; routing isn't the gap.

quiz.explanation: Inside users need either hairpin NAT so replies come back through the FortiGate, or an internal DNS answer with the private IP.

quiz.stem: A PPPoE link has an MTU of 1492. What MSS should hosts use for TCP without options?
Which FortiOS configuration clamps MSS for traffic matching policy 10?

options.text: set tcp-mss-sender and set tcp-mss-receiver
set mtu-override enable with a set mtu 1400
options.why_wrong: MTU override is an interface setting, not a policy option.

options.text: set session-ttl 1350 for that one policy
options.why_wrong: That sets a 1350-second timer, not a segment size.

options.text: set tcp-session-without-syn enable there
options.why_wrong: Allows mid-stream TCP sessions; it doesn't change segment size.

quiz.explanation: FortiOS policies support tcp-mss-sender and tcp-mss-receiver.

quiz.stem: After a firewall migration, VoIP calls connect but the caller hears nothing. The PBX already handles NAT traversal. Best first move?

options.text: Check whether the SIP ALG also rewrites the signalling, and test with it off
Increase the TCP MSS on the voice policy so the larger RTP packets get through
options.why_wrong: SIP media is RTP over UDP; MSS is irrelevant.

options.text: Open the RTP port range from the carrier to the PBX with a separate VIP policy
options.why_wrong: Pinholes matter, but with the PBX doing traversal the double rewrite is the usual cause.

options.text: Check the phones' codec list against the PBX, as a mismatch gives one-way audio
options.why_wrong: A codec mismatch usually fails the call; this started with the firewall change.

quiz.explanation: One-way audio is the classic sign of two components fighting over NAT traversal. Decide who does it.

quiz.stem: Order the life of a TCP session through a stateful firewall with SNAT.
items: First SYN is checked against the policy table
A session is created with the original and translated 5-tuples
The source is rewritten to the outside IP and port
The reply matches the session and is translated back
The session is removed after FIN/RST or the TTL
quiz.explanation: Policy lookup happens once, at the first packet. Everything after rides the session.

quiz.stem: The path to 10.50.0.10 crosses an IPsec tunnel. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: Full-size segments exceed the tunnel MTU and MSS isn't clamped
A policy denies SMB after the handshake has completed through it
options.why_wrong: Policy is checked on the first packet; the handshake passed, so it was allowed.

options.text: Asymmetric routing sends the server's replies around the firewall
options.why_wrong: The SYN/ACK came back through port2, so replies use this path.

options.text: The server's receive window is full, so it stops acknowledging data
options.why_wrong: A full window still sends ACKs advertising zero; here nothing comes back.

quiz.explanation: Handshake fine, full-size data lost, tunnel in the path: MTU/MSS. Clamp MSS (for example 1350) and retest.

quiz.stem: A customer raised the global session TTL to 24 hours to fix one ERP app. A week later the firewall is close to its session limit. What do you recommend?

options.text: Restore the global default and set a longer TTL on the ERP policy
Upgrade to a model with a larger session table for the growth
options.why_wrong: Treats the symptom; the cause is a global timer change.

options.text: Lower the TTL to 12 hours globally as a compromise for everyone else
options.why_wrong: Still far too long for every other session in the table.

options.text: Enable NAT on the ERP policy so its sessions are tracked apart
options.why_wrong: NAT doesn't change session lifetime.

quiz.explanation: Scope the change to the policy that needs it. Global timers affect every session in the table.

quiz.stem: What is the common name for 'NAT loopback' / 'U-turn NAT' in the FortiOS guide? (two words)
quiz.explanation: The FortiOS guide calls it Hairpin NAT.

quiz.stem: Which statement about UDP sessions on a stateful firewall is correct?

options.text: The first packet creates a session, which ends after its idle TTL
UDP isn't tracked, so each packet is checked against the policies
options.why_wrong: Stateful firewalls track UDP with sessions too.

options.text: UDP sessions are closed when either side sends a final FIN packet
options.why_wrong: UDP has no FIN; timers end its sessions.

options.text: UDP replies match the session, but for just the first second or two
options.why_wrong: Replies match for as long as the session's TTL keeps it alive.

quiz.explanation: UDP gets pseudo-state from the 5-tuple and a timer.

quiz.stem: A retail customer will put 9,000 users behind one public IP, all hitting the same SaaS endpoint on 443 at peak. What do you design?

options.text: An IP pool of several public IPs, since one IP gives 60,416 ports per service
One IP is enough, since PAT reuses the ports freely across all of the 9,000 users
options.why_wrong: Ports per destination service are finite: 60,416 per IP.

options.text: Port block allocation on the one IP, so each user gets a fixed port range
options.why_wrong: PBA helps logging, but the one IP still has 60,416 ports per service.

options.text: A second public IP on the interface, as two IPs double the session limit
options.why_wrong: Right direction, but size the pool from peak sessions per user to that service.

quiz.explanation: With one SaaS destination the per-service port budget matters. Size the pool from peak concurrent sessions per user to that service.

quiz.stem: Which symptom best fits an FTP active-mode transfer through NAT with no session helper?

options.text: Login works, but listings and transfers fail
The control connection on port 21 can't open
options.why_wrong: The control connection is a normal outbound TCP session and works.

options.text: Small files transfer and large files then fail
options.why_wrong: That points to MTU, not to the data channel setup.

options.text: Passive transfers fail, while active ones work
options.why_wrong: Reversed: active mode is the one that embeds the private address.

quiz.explanation: The control channel works; the data channel fails because the embedded address in PORT is private and no pinhole is opened.

labs.title: Clamp MSS for a site-to-site tunnel
labs.goal: Traffic from branch LAN to HQ over the IPsec tunnel `to-HQ` stalls on large transfers. Clamp MSS to 1350 on the policy that allows it.

worked.config:
config firewall policy
    edit 21
        set name "LAN-to-HQ"
        set srcintf "lan"
        set dstintf "to-HQ"
        set srcaddr "BRANCH-LAN"
        set dstaddr "HQ-NETS"
        set action accept
        set schedule "always"
        set service "ALL"
        set tcp-mss-sender 1350
        set tcp-mss-receiver 1350
    next
end
notes: tcp-mss-sender rewrites the MSS in SYNs from the original sender; tcp-mss-receiver does the same for the other side.
1350 leaves room for ESP, NAT-T and possible PPPoE overhead; tune after testing.
Clamping only affects TCP. Test with a large file copy before closing the change.

solo.prompt: Write the CLI to clamp MSS to 1380 on existing policy 7.
solo.solution:
config firewall policy
    edit 7
        set tcp-mss-sender 1380
        set tcp-mss-receiver 1380
    next
end

labs.title: Watch a handshake with the sniffer
labs.goal: Prove whether SYNs to 10.0.10.20:443 reach the FortiGate and leave toward the server.

worked.config: # diagnose sniffer packet any 'host 10.0.10.20 and tcp port 443' 4 20 l
notes: Format: diagnose sniffer packet <interface> '<filter>' <verbose> <count> <tsformat>.
Interface `any` shows the packet arriving on one interface and leaving on another; verbose 4 prints the interface name.
Count 20 stops after 20 packets; `l` prints local absolute time.
Seeing the SYN in on `lan` but never out on `dmz` means the FortiGate dropped it: next step is debug flow.

faded.template: # diagnose {{sniffer}} packet {{any}} 'host 10.0.10.20 and tcp port 443' {{4}} 20 l

solo.prompt: Sniff 50 packets on port1 for traffic to or from 192.168.1.10 on UDP 53, showing headers with the interface name.
solo.solution: # diagnose sniffer packet port1 'host 192.168.1.10 and udp port 53' 4 50
solo.notes: Verbose 4 = headers with interface name. The filter goes in single quotes. Stop early with Ctrl+C.

scenarios.title: The file shares are 'slow' after the SD-WAN cutover
scenarios.situation: You led the cutover of 12 branches to IPsec overlays last weekend. Monday 9:00 the customer's IT lead calls: browsing and Teams are fine, but copying files from the HQ file server "never finishes" and the ERP report export times out. It started after the cutover.
constraints: Change freeze for the rest of the week except emergency changes
stakeholders: CFO (needs the ERP exports for month-end)
scenarios.ask: What do you think is happening, how do you prove it, and how do you fix it safely?
right_thinking: Clarify: size-dependent? Only through the tunnels? All branches or some? Since exactly when?
Hypothesis from the pattern: small works, large stalls, new tunnels in the path → MTU/MSS
Prove: sniffer shows handshake fine and full-size segments retransmitted; a ping with DF and large size fails while small passes
Fix with lowest risk: emergency change to clamp MSS on the branch-to-HQ policies (or tunnel interfaces), one branch first
Validate with the IT lead: large file copy and ERP export from the pilot branch, then roll to all
Communicate and document: root cause, fix, and add an MSS test to the cutover acceptance checklist
scenarios.what: MSS clamping on the overlay policies, piloted on one branch first.
scenarios.why: ESP overhead lowered the usable MTU and PMTUD isn't working end to end, so full-size TCP segments are dropped. Clamping makes both ends agree on segments that fit.
how: Sniffer to confirm retransmitted full-size segments
set tcp-mss-sender / tcp-mss-receiver 1350 on the overlay policies
pitfalls: Changing all 12 branches at once during a freeze
Blaming the file server or the WAN provider without evidence
Forgetting that UDP-based apps need the MTU fixed, not MSS
scenarios.model_answer: "This looks like an MTU problem the new tunnels introduced: small packets pass, full-size ones don't. I'd confirm it in ten minutes with a sniffer and a large DF ping from one branch. If confirmed, I'd raise an emergency change to clamp MSS to 1350 on that branch's overlay policy, test a large file copy and the ERP export with you, and then apply it to the other eleven. Afterwards I'll send the root cause and add an MSS test to our cutover checklist so it can't happen again."
could_have_added: Offer the CFO an interim workaround timeline for month-end
Check whether the hub side also needs clamping for HQ-initiated transfers
scenarios.best_way: Small works, big stalls, new tunnels: that's MTU. I'll prove it on one branch, clamp MSS, test with your team and then roll it out, all inside an emergency change.

scenarios.title: Legacy FTP vendor can't send files anymore
scenarios.situation: After replacing the customer's old firewall with a FortiGate, a supplier says they can log in to the customer's FTP server (published through a VIP) but listings and uploads fail.
scenarios.ask: What is going on and what are your options, from best to quick-fix?
right_thinking: Clarify: active or passive mode? Which side initiates the data channel?
Recognise the pattern: control channel works, data channel fails → embedded addresses in FTP
Check the FTP session helper / protocol options are applied and the VIP maps the passive port range if passive
Best long-term option: move the supplier to SFTP or FTPS with a defined port range
Validate with the supplier on a call; document the passive range in the VIP and policy
scenarios.what: Make the FTP data channel work through NAT (helper or passive range) and plan the move to SFTP.
scenarios.why: FTP carries IPs and ports in its payload; without a helper or a published passive range the data connection has nowhere to go.
how: Confirm the mode with the supplier
Publish the passive range in the VIP or rely on the FTP helper
Propose SFTP as the target state
pitfalls: Opening a huge port range to any source
Leaving clear-text FTP as the permanent answer
scenarios.model_answer: "Login works and transfers don't, so the control channel is fine and the data channel isn't getting through NAT. I'll confirm whether they use active or passive mode, make sure the FTP helper is doing its job or publish a small passive port range limited to the supplier's IPs, and test with them on a call. Then I'll recommend moving them to SFTP, because FTP sends credentials in clear text."
could_have_added: Restrict the VIP policy source to the supplier's public IPs
Log the policy so you can show the supplier's attempts
scenarios.best_way: Control works, data doesn't: that's FTP fighting NAT. I'll fix the data path today with a tight rule, and propose SFTP so we stop sending passwords in clear text.

scenarios.title: Raid: one-way audio at the call centre
scenarios.situation: 08:05. The customer's 200-seat call centre went live on the new FortiGate at 07:00. Agents can call out and the customer hears them, but agents hear silence. The voice vendor says "it's your firewall". The call centre manager is on the bridge, angry.
scenarios.ask: Walk the bridge through your first 15 minutes.
right_thinking: Stabilise the room: acknowledge impact, give a time-boxed plan and the next update time
Gather: which direction fails (inbound RTP), all agents or some, since the cutover only
Hypothesis: SIP ALG on the firewall and the PBX/SBC both handling NAT, so the SDP advertises the wrong address/ports for return media
Test on a pilot: disable the SIP ALG for the voice traffic (or the PBX's NAT handling), place a test call
If audio returns, apply to all voice traffic; if not, roll back and look at the RTP port range policy and session timers
Document the decision of who owns NAT traversal; update the design
scenarios.what: Pick one owner for SIP NAT traversal and make the media path explicit.
scenarios.why: When two devices rewrite SIP/SDP, return media goes to the wrong address or port, which is the classic one-way audio pattern.
how: Pilot test with ALG off for voice
pitfalls: Arguing with the vendor on the bridge
Making several changes at once so you can't tell which fixed it
scenarios.model_answer: "First I tell the bridge: 'Outbound audio works, inbound doesn't; that's a NAT traversal pattern. Give me 15 minutes on one agent, next update at 08:20.' Then I test one change only: SIP ALG off for the voice traffic, one test call. If the audio comes back, we apply it to all agents; if not, we roll back and check the RTP policy and timers. After the incident I'll document who owns NAT traversal so this design can't regress."
could_have_added: Ask the voice vendor to confirm on the bridge whether their SBC does NAT traversal
Capture one call before and after the change for the report
scenarios.best_way: One change at a time, one agent first, next update in 15 minutes. One-way audio is two devices fighting over NAT; we'll make it one.

interview.question: Explain what a stateful firewall does with the first packet of a connection and with the rest.
interview.testing: Fundamentals, and whether you can say them simply
interview.framework: Anchor definition → mechanism (session, 5-tuple) → why it matters
interview.model_answer: "A stateful firewall checks the first packet of a flow against its policy table, top to bottom. If a policy allows it, it creates a session keyed by the 5-tuple: source and destination IP, source and destination port, and protocol, plus any NAT it applied. Every later packet in both directions is matched against that session, not the policy table, which is faster and is why you only write policies for the side that starts the conversation. FortiGate adds checks on top, like TCP flag validation with anti-replay and timers per protocol."
could_have_added: Mention that the session also carries the security profile decisions and offload state
interview.best_way: First packet: policy lookup. Everything after: session lookup. That's what 'stateful' means.
follow_ups: How would asymmetric routing affect this?

interview.question: A customer says: 'Small web pages load, big downloads hang, only since we added the VPN.' What do you tell them?
interview.model_answer: "That pattern, small works and big stalls after adding a tunnel, is almost always MTU. The VPN adds headers, so full-size packets no longer fit, and if the ICMP messages that tell the sender to shrink them are blocked, those packets just disappear. I'd prove it with a sniffer and a large ping with don't-fragment set, then clamp the TCP MSS on the VPN policy, for example to 1350, and test a big download with them before closing."
could_have_added: Mention you'd add it to the acceptance checklist for future tunnels
interview.best_way: Small works, big hangs after a VPN: MTU. I'll prove it in minutes and clamp MSS.

interview.question: What is the difference between SNAT, DNAT and PAT, and how does FortiGate implement each?
interview.framework: Define each → FortiOS object → typical use
interview.model_answer: "SNAT rewrites the source, usually so private users can go out to the internet. PAT is SNAT where many users share one IP and the firewall uses the source port to keep their sessions apart. On FortiGate that's NAT on the policy with the outgoing interface address or an IP pool, or central SNAT if central NAT is enabled. DNAT rewrites the destination to publish an internal server, and FortiGate does it with a virtual IP, optionally with port forwarding."
could_have_added: The 60,416 ports per IP per destination service figure, and when you need more IPs in the pool
interview.best_way: SNAT changes who's talking, DNAT changes who you're talking to, PAT lets a crowd share one address. On FortiGate: IP pools for the first, VIPs for the second.

interview.question: Why do protocols like SIP and FTP give firewalls trouble with NAT?
interview.model_answer: "Because they put IP addresses and ports inside the payload, not just in the headers NAT rewrites. FTP active mode tells the server where to connect back; SIP's SDP tells the other side where to send the audio. Behind NAT those embedded addresses are private, so the secondary connection fails. Firewalls use session helpers or ALGs to rewrite them and open pinholes. The catch is when the PBX or SBC also does NAT traversal; two rewrites give you one-way audio, so you pick one owner."
interview.best_way: They hide addresses inside the payload. Helpers fix it, unless someone else is fixing it too.

interview.question: How would you size NAT for 9,000 users going to the same SaaS service?
interview.model_answer: "PAT gives about 60,416 ports per public IP per destination service, according to the FortiOS guide. If 9,000 users each open several concurrent connections to the same SaaS endpoint, one IP can run out at peak. I'd estimate peak concurrent sessions to that service, divide by 60,416 with headroom, and build an IP pool with that many public IPs, or use port block allocation if they need predictable per-user ports for logging. Then I'd watch pool usage in the first week."
could_have_added: Ask whether the SaaS rate-limits per source IP, which also argues for more IPs
interview.best_way: Ports per IP per destination are finite: 60,416. Measure peak, add headroom, size the pool.

field_reports.title: The front door is now the vulnerability
field_reports.body: For years stolen credentials were the top way in. In the Verizon 2026 DBIR, **exploiting vulnerabilities** took first place at **31 %** of breaches with a known initial access vector, while credential abuse fell to 13 %. Only **26 %** of CISA KEV vulnerabilities were fully fixed in 2025, with a median of **43 days** to fix. Every VIP you publish is a door: put IPS on it and agree on who patches what behind it.
field_reports.source: Verizon 2026 DBIR, Key topics and findings

field_reports.title: Ransomware is half the story
field_reports.body: Ransomware appeared in **48 %** of breaches in the 2026 DBIR, up from 44 %. The good news: **69 %** of victims didn't pay. Segmentation and tight NAT/VIP design are what keep one compromised host from becoming every host.
field_reports.source: Verizon 2026 DBIR, Key topics and findings

modules.title: SOC operations: the operating model, metrics and log sources a PS consultant must design
objectives: Describe how a SOC moves an alert to a closed case, and who owns each step
Pick metrics that show whether a SOC works (and spot the vanity ones)
Choose log sources by the detections they enable, and size their quality problems
sources: Vendor-neutral SOC practice (NIST CSF 2.0 Detect/Respond functions, MITRE ATT&CK data sources)
FortiSIEM 7.6.1 User Guide: incidents, cases, CMDB and device health (as cited in M9.01–M9.04)
FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Administration Guide: log storage, Log View, FortiView (as cited in M6.01–M6.05)

units.title: From alert to closed case
units.body:
A SOC is a production line for decisions. Each alert either dies quickly (false positive, benign) or grows
into a case that ends with a written conclusion and, often, a change somewhere else (a rule, a patch, a policy).

| Step | Who | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **Alert** | Detection (rule, EDR, IPS, user report) | One event or a correlated incident |
| **Triage** | L1 analyst | Close as false positive / benign, or escalate with notes |
| **Investigation** | L2 analyst | Scope: which users, hosts, data, since when |
| **Response** | L2/L3 with IT and the business | Containment, eradication, recovery |
| **Lessons** | SOC lead, detection engineer | New or tuned detections, control gaps closed |

Three roles sit beside the line: **detection engineering** (writes and tests rules), **threat hunting** (looks
for what no rule caught) and **incident response** (leads the big ones). In a small customer one person wears
several hats; in an MSSP the tiers are separate teams with an SLA between them.

**Severity is impact × confidence.** A critical rule on a test VM with a known scanner is low; a medium rule on
the domain controller with a fresh admin logon is high. Write the matrix down with the customer before go-live,
with response times per level (for example, P1 acknowledged in 15 minutes, 24×7) — the numbers are theirs to
choose, the matrix is yours to propose.

**Handover between shifts** is where cases die. Every open case carries: what is known, what was done, what is
pending, and who owns the next step.

:::recall
Q: What does an L1 analyst produce for each alert?
A: A decision with notes: closed as false positive or benign, or escalated with what was checked.
:::

:::why
Q: Why define severity as impact × confidence instead of using the rule's severity?
A: The rule doesn't know the asset or the context; the same rule hit means different things on a lab VM and on a domain controller.
:::

units.title: Metrics that tell you the SOC works
units.body:
Good SOC metrics measure **time** and **quality**, not volume.

- **MTTD** (mean time to detect): from the first malicious action to the first alert. Long MTTD means
  detection gaps.
- **MTTA** (to acknowledge): from alert to an analyst opening it. Long MTTA means staffing or alert fatigue.
- **MTTR** (to respond / contain): from alert to containment. Long MTTR often means unclear authority to act.
- **True-positive rate per rule**: the share of a rule's incidents that were real. The weekly tuning list is
  sorted by this.
- **Coverage**: which ATT&CK techniques the SOC can detect *and has tested*. Untested coverage is a guess.
- **Log source health**: sources sending, parsing correctly, on time. A source that goes quiet is itself an
  incident.

**Vanity metrics** look good on a slide and say little: "2 million threats blocked", total events per day,
number of rules enabled. Use them only next to a quality metric.

**Reading the numbers together.** MTTA rising while incidents per day rise points to alert fatigue: tune, don't
hire. MTTR high with MTTA low points to authority: analysts see it fast but can't isolate a host without a
change ticket — fix the runbook, pre-approve containment for defined cases.

:::recall
Q: Which metric exposes alert fatigue first?
A: MTTA (time to acknowledge) rising, together with incidents per analyst per shift.
:::

:::why
Q: Why is "number of rules enabled" a weak metric?
A: Enabled is not tested or tuned; a rule that never fires on the real technique, or fires 500 times a day, adds no detection.
:::

units.title: Log sources, chosen by the detections they enable
units.body:
Start from the detections the customer needs, then pick sources. "Send everything" fills the disk and the
licence and still misses the one log that matters.

| Detection need | Source | Key events |
|---|---|---|
| Password attacks, odd logons | Domain controllers | 4624, 4625, 4768, 4769, 4771, 4776 |
| Privilege changes | Domain controllers | 4720, 4728, 4732, 4756, 4662 |
| What ran on endpoints | EDR (FortiEDR), Sysmon, 4688 with command line | process, parent, hash, user |
| Traffic and threats at the edge | FortiGate traffic and UTM logs | deny, IPS, AV, web, DNS, app control |
| Remote users | FortiSASE / VPN logs | logins, posture, policy hits |
| Cloud and SaaS identity | IdP sign-ins (e.g. Entra ID) | impossible travel, MFA fatigue, consent |

**Quality problems to plan for:**

- **Time.** Every source on NTP and one time zone in the SIEM, or timelines lie.
- **Parsing.** A log that arrives but doesn't parse can't trigger a rule. Test one sample event per source
  type before calling a source "onboarded".
- **Volume.** Firewall traffic logs dominate. Decide what to keep hot (searchable) and what to archive; in
  FortiAnalyzer that is the analytics vs archive split, in FortiSIEM the online event database vs archive.
- **Health.** Alert when a source stops sending or drops below its usual rate.

:::recall
Q: What makes a log source "onboarded"?
A: It sends, it parses into the right event types and fields, its time is right, and a test event triggers the expected rule.
:::

:::why
Q: Why can a perfectly running SIEM miss a Kerberoasting attack?
A: If the DCs don't send 4769 (or the audit policy doesn't log it), no rule can see the ticket requests.
:::

units.title: The SOC in a Fortinet PS engagement
units.body:
When the SOW says "deploy FortiSIEM/FortiAnalyzer and onboard the SOC", success is not the appliance being up.
It is the customer's analysts closing real cases with it.

**Discovery questions that change the design**

1. Who works the alerts, when? In-house 8×5, in-house 24×7, or an MSSP?
2. Which threats keep the CISO awake (ransomware, fraud, data leak, OT)? These pick the first use cases.
3. Which sources exist, who owns each, and can they change audit policy?
4. Retention: legal or contractual minimums, and how far back investigations usually go.
5. Authority: who may isolate a host, disable an account or block an IP, and at what hour?

**RACI that avoids the classic fight.** Fortinet PS builds and tunes; the customer (or MSSP) operates; source
owners fix their own audit settings. Write it in the SOW, not in an email after go-live.

**Handover package.** Use-case list with the test that proved each, runbooks for the top incidents, the
severity matrix, the tuning log (every exception: who asked, why, review date), source inventory with owners,
and a 30/60/90-day tuning plan.

:::ps
Offer a weekly 30-minute tuning session for the first month. It's cheap, it builds trust, and it is where the
customer learns to own the SIEM instead of resenting it.
:::

:::recall
Q: Name three items in a SOC handover package.
A: Tested use-case list, runbooks, severity matrix, tuning log, source inventory with owners, 30/60/90 tuning plan.
:::

:::why
Q: Why ask "who may isolate a host at 3 a.m.?" during discovery?
A: Without pre-approved authority, MTTR is set by whoever answers the phone, not by the SOC.
:::

quiz.stem: Over two weeks, a customer's SOC shows MTTA doubling while incidents per day tripled. Analysts and shifts didn't change. What is the first thing to do?

options.text: Rank rules by incident volume and true-positive rate, then tune the top ones
Add a second L1 analyst per shift until MTTA returns to the old level
options.why_wrong: Treats the symptom; the noise that caused it keeps growing and new staff burn out too.

options.text: Lower the severity of the rules that fired more than 50 times a week
options.why_wrong: Blanket severity cuts also bury the real incidents inside those noisy rules.

options.text: Extend the SLA for medium incidents so the weekly dashboards show the SOC as compliant
options.why_wrong: Changes the target instead of the cause; the SOC is still drowning.

quiz.explanation: Volume grew without a staffing change: classic alert fatigue. Measure which rules generate the noise and how often they're right, then tune those with exceptions or thresholds.

quiz.stem: MTTA is 6 minutes but MTTR for confirmed malware on laptops is 9 hours. The analysts say they 'wait for IT'. Which fix targets the cause?

options.text: Pre-approve EDR isolation of infected laptops in the SOC runbook
Add an automation that emails IT the moment malware is confirmed
options.why_wrong: Faster notification still leaves the decision with someone outside the SOC.

options.text: Escalate the malware incidents to P1 so IT has to answer faster
options.why_wrong: Inflates severity across the board and teaches IT to ignore P1.

options.text: Tune the malware rules so fewer incidents need a response from IT
options.why_wrong: These are confirmed infections; tuning won't shorten the wait for authority.

quiz.explanation: Fast acknowledgement with slow containment points to authority, not detection. Agree in advance which cases the SOC may contain alone.

quiz.stem: Which of these are metrics that show whether detections actually work? Select all that apply.

options.text: True-positive rate of each correlation rule over the last 30 days
Number of ATT&CK techniques with a rule that passed an emulation test
Count of correlation rules enabled in FortiSIEM across all organizations
options.why_wrong: Enabled rules can be untested or permanently silent.

options.text: Mean time from first malicious action to first alert in exercises
Total events per second ingested by the collectors during business hours
options.why_wrong: A capacity number; it says nothing about catching attacks.

quiz.explanation: Quality metrics: per-rule precision, tested coverage and time to detect. Rule counts and EPS are capacity or vanity figures.

quiz.output:
Log source health — last 24 h            events/h (7-day avg)   events/h (now)   last event
FGT-HQ  (FortiGate, syslog)              41,200                 40,950           08:14:02
DC01    (Windows, agent)                  3,900                  4,020           08:13:58
DC02    (Windows, agent)                  3,750                      0           02:11:47
FEDR    (FortiEDR, syslog)                  610                    590           08:13:40
quiz.stem: It is 08:15. What is the best first step?

options.text: Open a case for DC02 going silent and investigate before touching it
Restart the FortiSIEM agent service on DC02 and confirm events arrive again
options.why_wrong: Restoring the feed first may erase the trace of why it stopped (an attacker stopping logging).

options.text: Raise a capacity ticket because the FortiGate is close to its seven-day average
options.why_wrong: The FortiGate is normal; nothing in its numbers asks for action.

options.text: Wait for the next hourly report to see whether DC02 recovers on its own
options.why_wrong: A DC that stopped logging at 2 a.m. is already six hours of blindness on a crown-jewel asset.

quiz.explanation: A domain controller that stops logging in the middle of the night is a potential incident (log clearing, agent stopped) before it is an IT problem. Open a case, then investigate before you 'fix' it.

quiz.stem: A rule fires 'Excessive logon failures' on a lab VM used by the red team, and the same rule fires on DC01 from a laptop at 03:00. How should the two compare in severity?

options.text: The domain controller, because the asset and the 03:00 timing raise impact
Both equal, because severity should come from the rule definition and its tuning
options.why_wrong: Rule severity ignores asset value and context; impact differs hugely.

options.text: Lab VM higher, because red-team tooling is the more advanced threat
options.why_wrong: Known, authorised red-team activity is benign by definition if documented.

options.text: Both low until a second rule confirms the activity on either host
options.why_wrong: Waiting for a second signal on a DC wastes the window to contain.

quiz.explanation: Severity = impact × confidence. The asset and the context change the impact.

quiz.stem: A customer wants to detect Kerberoasting. Their DCs send 4624 and 4625 to FortiSIEM. What is missing?

options.text: Auditing of Kerberos service ticket operations, so DCs log event 4769
Auditing of Kerberos authentication service, so DCs log event 4768
options.why_wrong: 4768 covers TGT requests (useful for AS-REP roasting), not the service tickets Kerberoasting asks for.

options.text: Auditing of credential validation on the DCs, so they log NTLM event 4776
options.why_wrong: Kerberoasting uses Kerberos, not NTLM validation.

options.text: Auditing of directory service access, so DCs log event 4662
options.why_wrong: 4662 catches object access such as DCSync, not ticket requests.

quiz.explanation: Kerberoasting is a burst of service-ticket (TGS) requests, often with RC4 encryption. Those are event 4769, which needs the 'Audit Kerberos Service Ticket Operations' subcategory.

quiz.stem: Put the onboarding of a new log source in order.
items: Agree which detections the source must enable
Configure the source to send (audit policy, syslog target)
Confirm events arrive with correct time
Confirm events parse into the right types and fields
Trigger a test event and see the expected rule fire
quiz.explanation: From need to proof: why, send, arrive, parse, detect.

quiz.stem: FortiGate traffic logs are 85% of the customer's log volume and they want 365 days of retention. Which design keeps investigations fast without buying three times the storage?

options.text: Keep 30–90 days searchable and the rest in compressed archive, restoring when needed
Send the deny logs alone from the FortiGate, so the year fits in the searchable store
options.why_wrong: Accepted traffic is what exfiltration and beacons look like; dropping it blinds investigations.

options.text: Keep all 365 days searchable but lower the log level on the FortiGate policies
options.why_wrong: Cutting log detail to fit storage removes fields the investigations need.

options.text: Forward traffic logs to a syslog server and keep UTM logs in the analyzer
options.why_wrong: Splits the evidence across tools and still stores the same volume elsewhere.

quiz.explanation: Hot vs archive: most investigations look back weeks, not a year. Archive satisfies retention; the hot window keeps search fast.

quiz.stem: In discovery, the customer says the MSSP 'handles the SOC' but the MSSP can't change AD audit policy or isolate hosts. Where should that land in the SOW?

options.text: A RACI naming who changes audit policy and who may contain, with an escalation path
An assumption that the MSSP will request the access rights it needs during the project
options.why_wrong: An assumption is not an owner; it turns into a blocker in week 3.

options.text: A change in scope so Fortinet PS operates the SOC until the MSSP is ready
options.why_wrong: PS builds and hands over; taking operations hides the real gap and creates a dependency.

options.text: A risk entry noting that response times may be longer than expected
options.why_wrong: Records the problem without assigning anyone to solve it.

quiz.explanation: Name owners in the SOW: source owners fix audit settings, and containment authority is explicit.

quiz.stem: Which Windows event ID means 'A Kerberos service ticket was requested'?
quiz.explanation: 4769. 4768 is the TGT request; 4771 is a failed Kerberos pre-authentication.

quiz.stem: Which of these would NOT help you trust a timeline built from FortiGate, DC and EDR logs?

options.text: Raising the FortiGate log level from notification to information
Putting all sources on the same NTP servers and checking drift
options.why_wrong: This does help: clock drift is the first thing that breaks timelines.

options.text: Normalising all events to one time zone when they are stored
options.why_wrong: This does help: mixed local and UTC times reorder events.

options.text: Checking that each source's timestamps parse into the event time field
options.why_wrong: This does help: an unparsed timestamp falls back to receive time.

quiz.explanation: Timeline trust is about time: sync, zone and parsing. More log detail doesn't fix ordering.

quiz.stem: After go-live, the CISO asks for one number in the monthly report that shows the SIEM is worth it. Which is the most defensible?

options.text: Tested ATT&CK coverage this month vs last, with incidents closed as true positive
Threats blocked by the FortiGates this month, shown next to last month's figure
options.why_wrong: The firewall would have blocked those without the SIEM; it doesn't measure the SIEM.

options.text: Events correlated per day this month, compared with the vendor's original sizing estimate
options.why_wrong: Volume shows load, not value.

options.text: Number of incidents raised this month, with the critical ones highlighted in red
options.why_wrong: Raw incident counts reward noise; without true-positive rate they can mean the opposite.

quiz.explanation: Value = what you can now detect (tested) and what you actually caught. Pair coverage with confirmed cases.

labs.title: A severity matrix the customer can sign

scenarios.title: The SIEM nobody opens
scenarios.situation:
A retail customer bought FortiSIEM a year ago. The two analysts open it once a week. 1,400 incidents are
"Active". The CISO wants to know if it was a waste of money before renewal.
scenarios.ask: What do you propose in the first 30 days?
right_thinking: Measure first: incidents per rule, true-positive rate, MTTA, source health
Bulk-close or tune the noisiest rules with documented exceptions
Pick 5 use cases tied to the CISO's top risks and test each end to end
Weekly tuning ritual and a monthly value report (tested coverage, true positives)
scenarios.what: A 30-day reset: measure, tune, focus on tested use cases, report value.
scenarios.why: A SIEM fails from noise and no ownership more often than from missing features.
scenarios.model_answer:
"Before deciding it was a waste, I'd measure it: which rules make the 1,400 incidents, how many were real, and
whether the key sources even arrive and parse. Most of that backlog is usually five or six rules. We tune those
with documented exceptions, then pick five use cases from your top risks — say ransomware and privileged
account abuse — and prove each one end to end with a test. From week two there's a 30-minute tuning session
every Friday. At renewal you'd see tested coverage and real cases caught, not just a number of events."
scenarios.best_way: Measure, cut the noise, prove five use cases, then report value.

scenarios.title: Who presses the button at 3 a.m.?
scenarios.situation:
A hospital's SOC is an MSSP. FortiEDR detected ransomware behaviour on a nursing station at 03:10. The MSSP
called the hospital's IT on-call, who didn't answer until 04:40. By then two more stations were encrypted.
scenarios.ask: How do you change the operating model?
right_thinking: Pre-approved containment for defined cases (EDR isolation of non-critical endpoints)
Exceptions for life-critical devices: who decides, how fast, and the fallback (network quarantine of a segment)
Escalation chain with timers and a second on-call
Test the runbook with a tabletop and a timed drill
scenarios.what: Pre-approved, scoped authority for the SOC plus a tested escalation path.
scenarios.why: In ransomware, the hour lost waiting for permission is the damage.
scenarios.model_answer:
"The detection worked; the authority didn't. I'd agree with the hospital a runbook where the MSSP may isolate
administrative and nursing workstations immediately for confirmed ransomware behaviour, and must call the
clinical engineering lead within 10 minutes for anything attached to patient care, with segment quarantine on
the FortiGate as the fallback. On-call gets a second contact after 15 minutes without an answer. Then we run a
tabletop with both teams and a timed drill to prove it."
scenarios.best_way: Detection worked, authority didn't: pre-approve it, carve out clinical devices, drill it.

scenarios.title: Send everything
scenarios.situation:
In the kickoff, the customer's infrastructure lead says: "Just send every log from every device to the SIEM,
we'll figure out detections later." Their licence covers 5,000 EPS; a quick estimate of 'everything' is 18,000.
scenarios.ask: How do you answer him in the meeting?
right_thinking: Agree with the goal (visibility), reframe the approach (use-case first)
Show the cost: licence, storage, and noise that delays detections
Propose a prioritised source list by risk, with a phase 2 for the rest
Keep raw logs that aren't analysed in cheaper storage if retention requires it
scenarios.what: Use-case-driven onboarding with a phased source list.
scenarios.why: Sources without detections cost money and attention and still miss the event that matters.
scenarios.model_answer:
"I agree we want visibility, and I'd get there in an order that pays off. Everything is about 18,000 EPS
against a 5,000 licence, and most of it would never feed a rule. Let's start from your top risks: DCs, the
FortiGates, EDR and VPN cover password attacks, malware and remote access — roughly 3,500 EPS. Phase 2 adds
servers and SaaS once those use cases are tested. If you need the rest for retention, we archive it raw
without paying to analyse it."
scenarios.best_way: Same goal, smarter order: use cases first, everything else archived.

interview.question: How would you measure whether a customer's SOC is effective?
interview.model_answer:
"I look at time and quality, not volume. Time is MTTD, MTTA and MTTR, and the pattern between them tells me
where it hurts: high MTTA is fatigue, high MTTR with low MTTA is authority. Quality is the true-positive rate
per rule. Coverage is the ATT&CK techniques we can detect and have actually tested. And source health, because
a domain controller that goes quiet is either a broken pipeline or an attacker."
interview.best_way: Time, quality, tested coverage, source health.

interview.question: You haven't run a SOC. Why should we trust you to deliver SOC projects?
interview.framework: Honest gap → real evidence → how I close it
interview.model_answer:
"I haven't worked as a SOC analyst, and I won't pretend I have. What I bring: at Fortinet support I worked
FortiSIEM, FortiEDR and FortiSOAR cases and saw how deployments break; at Netskope I set up log streaming into
customers' SIEMs; and my OSCP, CRTP and CRTE work means I know what the attacks look like from the other side,
down to the events they leave. For SOC delivery I pair that with a method: use cases first, tested end to end,
tuned weekly with the customer."
interview.best_way: No SOC title, but the attacker's view, the product cases and a delivery method.

interview.question: A customer says their SIEM generates too many alerts. Walk me through your first week.
interview.model_answer:
"Day one I pull 30 days of incidents per rule with how many were true positives. Usually five rules make most
of the noise. For each, I find why: a known scanner, a service account, a threshold that ignores the
environment, or bad parsing. I fix with narrow exceptions or thresholds based on the baseline, never by
disabling, and log who asked, why and a review date. By Friday we review the numbers with the SOC lead and set
the weekly session."
interview.best_way: Find the five rules, fix the cause narrowly, document, review weekly.

interview.question: Which logs would you onboard first for a mid-size company, and why?
interview.model_answer:
"Domain controllers first, for password attacks and privilege changes — 4624, 4625, 4769, 4771, the group
changes. Then the FortiGates for edge threats and egress, EDR for what runs on endpoints, and remote access —
VPN or FortiSASE — because that's where external logins happen. Each one is only done when a test event fires
the expected rule."
interview.best_way: Identity, edge, endpoint, remote access — proven with a test event.

interview.question: How do you hand over a SOC project so the customer doesn't call you every week afterwards?
interview.model_answer:
"A package, practice and a plan. The package is the tested use-case list, runbooks, severity matrix, tuning log
and source inventory with owners. The practice is that their analysts ran the weekly tuning sessions in the
last two weeks, not me. The plan is 30/60/90 days of tuning with named owners. If they still call, it's
usually because one of those three was skipped."
interview.best_way: Package, practice, plan.

modules.title: Detection engineering: from the attacker's technique to a rule that fires and stays quiet
objectives: Turn an ATT&CK technique into a hypothesis, a data source and testable rule logic
Name the Windows and Linux evidence that Active Directory attacks leave (the ones you practised on the offensive side)
Spot lateral movement, web-shell and tunnelling patterns in endpoint and FortiGate logs
Test, tune and retire rules with replay, baselines and exceptions that expire
