units.title: The detection lifecycle
units.body:
A detection is a small product with a lifecycle, not a checkbox:

1. **Hypothesis.** "An attacker who has a domain user will request service tickets for many SPNs to crack
   them offline" (ATT&CK T1558.003, Kerberoasting).
2. **Data source.** Which log proves it? Here: DC event 4769 with the ticket encryption type.
3. **Logic.** Filter, group by, threshold, window, and what makes it different from normal.
4. **Test.** Emulate the technique in a lab or with an approved purple-team run. A rule that has never fired
   on the real technique is a guess.
5. **Deploy and tune.** Watch it for a week against real traffic; add narrow exceptions with expiry dates.
6. **Maintain or retire.** Re-test after OS or product upgrades; retire rules that no longer fit.

**Atomic vs behavioural.** An atomic rule matches one indicator (a hash, a domain). It is precise and dies
the day the attacker changes the file. A behavioural rule matches what the technique *must* do (many
service tickets with RC4 from one account). It survives tool changes but needs tuning.

**Precision vs recall.** Precision is "when it fires, is it real?"; recall is "when it happens, does it
fire?". Tuning trades one for the other; write down which one this rule optimises.

**Portable logic.** Sigma is a vendor-neutral rule format; FortiSIEM can import Sigma rules, which lets you
start from community logic and adapt fields to the customer's parsing.

:::recall
Q: What turns a written rule into a detection you can count as coverage?
A: A successful test against the real technique (emulation or purple team), plus a tuning week.
:::

:::why
Q: Why do behavioural rules survive longer than hash rules?
A: Attackers change files cheaply, but the technique still has to do the same things (request tickets, read LSASS), which the behaviour rule watches.
:::

units.title: Credential attacks against Active Directory: what they leave behind
units.body:
These are the attacks behind CRTP/CRTE-style paths to Domain Admin, seen from the defender's chair.

| Technique | What the attacker does | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Password spraying** (T1110.003) | One or two passwords against many accounts | Many 4625 (or 4771 with failure code 0x18) for **distinct users** from one source; on the VPN, FortiGate SSL-VPN/IKE login failures across users |
| **Kerberoasting** (T1558.003) | Requests TGS tickets for SPN accounts to crack offline | Burst of 4769 from one account for many service names, ticket encryption type **0x17 (RC4)** where AES is normal |
| **AS-REP roasting** (T1558.004) | Asks for TGTs of accounts without pre-authentication | 4768 with **pre-authentication type 0** for those accounts |
| **DCSync** (T1003.006) | Asks a DC to replicate secrets | 4662 with the replication rights GUIDs (`1131f6aa-…` Get-Changes, `1131f6ad-…` Get-Changes-All) by an account that is **not a DC** |
| **LSASS dump** (T1003.001) | Reads LSASS memory for hashes and tickets | Sysmon 10 (process access) with target `lsass.exe` and read access from an unusual process |
| **NTDS.dit theft** (T1003.003) | Copies the AD database via shadow copy or `ntdsutil ifm` | 4688/Sysmon 1 with `vssadmin create shadow` or `ntdsutil`, on a DC |
| **Pass-the-hash** (T1550.002) | Uses an NTLM hash instead of a password | 4624 logon type 9 with logon process `seclogo` on the attacker's host; NTLM 4624 type 3 from hosts that never log on that way |
| **AD CS abuse (ESC1)** | Requests a certificate that names another user | 4886/4887 on the CA with a subject alternative name that differs from the requester |
| **mitm6 / IPv6 DNS takeover** | Rogue DHCPv6 makes itself the DNS server, then relays NTLM | DHCPv6 advertisements from a workstation, WPAD lookups answered internally, NTLM authentications to an unexpected host |

Two lessons for rule logic: count **distinct** things (users, SPNs), and compare to **who normally does it**
(DCs replicate, admins log on to servers, nobody asks for 40 service tickets in a minute).

:::recall
Q: What makes a 4769 event look like Kerberoasting?
A: Many service names requested by one account in a short window, with RC4 (0x17) tickets.
:::

:::why
Q: Why must a DCSync rule exclude domain controllers?
A: DCs replicate with each other all day using exactly those rights; only a non-DC account asking for them is suspicious.
:::

units.title: Execution, lateral movement and persistence on hosts
units.body:
**Parent–child process pairs** are the cheapest high-value behaviour rules:

| Pair | Means |
|---|---|
| `w3wp.exe` → `cmd.exe` / `powershell.exe` | A web shell or exploited IIS app (T1505.003) |
| `sqlservr.exe` → `cmd.exe` | `xp_cmdshell` abuse |
| `WmiPrvSE.exe` → `powershell.exe` | Remote WMI execution |
| `wsmprovhost.exe` → anything | Remote PowerShell (WinRM) session |
| `services.exe` → unknown binary after a 7045 | Service-based execution (PsExec-style, T1569.002) |
| `php-fpm` / `apache2` → `sh` | Web shell on Linux |

**Lateral movement** shows on both ends: a 4624 logon type 3 on the target, a 5145 access to `ADMIN$` or
`C$`, then a 7045 service install (`PSEXESVC` for PsExec) or a 4698 scheduled task.

**Privilege escalation** examples you exploited in labs, and their tells: a service account
(IIS AppPool, MSSQL) suddenly spawning processes as SYSTEM (the Potato family abusing SeImpersonate);
on Linux, `sudo` use outside the admin group, new SUID binaries, edited cron jobs or systemd timers, a member
of the `docker` group starting a privileged container that mounts `/`.

**Reverse shells** are an outbound connection followed by an interactive shell: Sysmon 3 (network
connection) from `bash`, `sh`, `powershell.exe` or `nc` to an external address, often on 4444, 443 or 53.

:::recall
Q: Which two events on a target show a PsExec-style lateral move?
A: An ADMIN$ share access (5145) and a service install (7045, PSEXESVC), after a network logon (4624 type 3).
:::

:::why
Q: Why are parent–child rules cheaper to keep accurate than command-line regexes?
A: The pair itself is rare in normal operations (IIS doesn't start shells); command lines change with every tool and obfuscation.
:::

units.title: Network tells in FortiGate and FortiAnalyzer logs
units.body:
The FortiGate sees what endpoints can hide: who talked to whom, how often, how much.

- **Scanning**: one source, many destination ports or hosts, mostly denied, in minutes. Count **distinct**
  ports or IPs per source.
- **Beaconing** (T1071): one internal host, one external destination, connections at a near-fixed interval
  (say every 60 s ± 10 %) with small, similar byte counts, for hours. Long duration + low variance is the
  signal; volume is not.
- **DNS tunnelling** (T1071.004): many unique, long subdomains under one parent domain, TXT or NULL
  queries, high entropy labels. FortiGate DNS filter logs and DNS server logs both show it.
- **Exfiltration** (T1048): bytes sent far larger than bytes received, to a destination the host never used,
  often at night.
- **Tunnels for pivoting** (T1572), like the ligolo-ng or chisel you used to pivot in labs: a long-lived
  TLS or WebSocket session from a server to a rare external host, carrying traffic in both directions.
- **Web attacks** against published servers: IPS signatures for SQL injection, path traversal and command
  injection on VIP traffic, or requests to cloud metadata (`169.254.169.254`) from an app server (SSRF).

FortiAnalyzer's Log View filters and FortiView rankings surface most of these; periodicity and entropy need
an analytic query or an export.

:::recall
Q: What distinguishes a beacon from a busy app?
A: Regular intervals with low variance and small, similar payloads over a long period, to a single destination.
:::

:::why
Q: Why count distinct subdomains rather than DNS query volume for tunnelling?
A: A busy client makes many queries to few names; a tunnel encodes data in the name, so almost every query is a new subdomain.
:::

units.title: Testing, tuning and retiring rules
units.body:
**Replay before production.** Keep two streams: the attack (from an emulation run) and a normal week. A good
rule fires on the first and stays quiet on the second. FortiTatake's detection labs grade exactly this.

**Exceptions are narrow and expire.** Except one source, one account or one host, never "any source on this
subnet". Record who asked, why, and a review date. An exception without an expiry becomes the attacker's
hiding place.

**Thresholds come from data.** Look at the 30-day maximum for the grouping key (per user, per host) and set
the threshold above it with a margin, not at a round number someone liked.

**Rule health.** Track per rule: last fired, true-positive rate, last tested. A rule that hasn't fired in a
year and was never tested is either perfect or broken; find out which.

**Purple teaming turns findings into rules.** Every pentest finding that says "the EDR didn't alert on X"
(unprotected LSASS, unflagged tooling, an undetected reverse shell) becomes a detection backlog item with an
owner and a test.

:::recall
Q: What two streams does a rule need to pass before production?
A: An attack replay (must fire) and a benign baseline (must stay quiet).
:::

:::why
Q: Why should every exception have a review date?
A: The reason it was granted expires (a scanner moves, a project ends) but the blind spot stays unless someone looks again.
:::

cards.front: Six steps of the detection lifecycle
cards.back: Hypothesis, data source, logic, test, deploy and tune, maintain or retire.
Atomic: one indicator (hash, domain), precise but brittle. Behavioural: what the technique must do, durable but needs tuning.
Precision: when it fires, it's real. Recall: when it happens, it fires.
Vendor-neutral detection rule format; FortiSIEM can import Sigma rules.
Failures (4625/4771 0x18) for many distinct users from one source in a short window.
Burst of 4769 for many SPNs from one account, ticket encryption 0x17 (RC4).
4768 with pre-authentication type 0 (account doesn't require pre-auth).
4662 with replication GUIDs 1131f6aa-… / 1131f6ad-… by a non-DC account.
Sysmon 10: unusual process opening lsass.exe with memory read access.
4624 logon type 9 (NewCredentials) with logon process seclogo.
CA events 4886/4887 where the certificate's SAN names a different user than the requester.
vssadmin create shadow or ntdsutil (ifm) run on a DC (4688/Sysmon 1).
DHCPv6 advertisements from a workstation, internal WPAD answers, NTLM auth to an unexpected host.
Web shell or exploited IIS application.
4624 type 3, 5145 ADMIN$ access, 7045 PSEXESVC service install.
A service account (IIS AppPool, MSSQL) spawning processes as SYSTEM.
sudo outside admins, new SUID files, edited cron/systemd timers, docker group mounting /.
Fixed interval, low variance, small similar payloads, one destination, long duration.
Many unique long subdomains of one domain, TXT/NULL queries, high-entropy labels.
Long-lived TLS/WebSocket session from a server to a rare external host, traffic both ways.

cards.front: SSRF tell from an app server
cards.back: Requests to 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata).
Attack replay must fire; benign baseline must stay quiet.
The 30-day max per grouping key, plus a margin.
Last fired, true-positive rate, last tested.

quiz.output:
Time      EventID  Account          Service name       Ticket enc.  Client address
10:02:11  4769     svc_backup$      cifs/FS01          0x12         10.20.10.15
10:14:05  4769     m.rojas          MSSQLSvc/DB01:1433 0x17         10.20.10.44
10:14:05  4769     m.rojas          HTTP/intranet      0x17         10.20.10.44
10:14:06  4769     m.rojas          MSSQLSvc/DB02:1433 0x17         10.20.10.44
10:14:06  4769     m.rojas          exchangeAB/EX01    0x17         10.20.10.44
10:14:06  4769     m.rojas          WSMAN/APP03        0x17         10.20.10.44
... 31 more rows for m.rojas within 4 seconds
quiz.stem: What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: m.rojas's session is being used to Kerberoast: dozens of RC4 service tickets in seconds
m.rojas is password spraying the service accounts, which is why each line is a separate SPN
options.why_wrong: Spraying produces failed logons (4625/4771); these are successful ticket requests.

options.text: A Golden Ticket is in use, because the tickets are RC4 while the backup account's are AES
options.why_wrong: Forged TGTs show up as anomalies in TGT use, not as a burst of TGS requests for many services.

options.text: The client at 10.20.10.44 runs a legacy app that supports RC4 alone, so this is normal noise
options.why_wrong: A legacy app talks to its few services; 36 different SPNs in four seconds is enumeration.

quiz.explanation: Many distinct SPNs from one account in seconds, all with RC4 (0x17) while normal tickets use AES (0x12), is the Kerberoasting pattern. The account may be compromised or the user may be the attacker.

quiz.stem: You must write a DCSync rule on 4662 events. Which condition gives the best precision without losing the attack?

options.text: Replication GUIDs in the properties, and the subject is not a domain controller account
Replication GUIDs in the properties, and the subject is a member of Domain Admins or Enterprise Admins
options.why_wrong: DCSync works with any account granted the rights; attackers often grant them to a quiet user.

options.text: Any 4662 on the domain object outside business hours, from any account at all
options.why_wrong: Catches noise and misses daytime DCSync, which is just as common.

options.text: Replication GUIDs in the properties, and the source host is not on the server VLAN
options.why_wrong: Attackers run it from servers too; the account (non-DC) is the reliable signal.

quiz.explanation: DCs replicate with these rights constantly. The tell is a non-DC account asking for Get-Changes/Get-Changes-All.

quiz.stem: Spraying against the domain: which grouping key and condition separate it from a user who keeps mistyping a password?

options.text: Group by source address; distinct target users ≥ 10 within 30 minutes
Group by target user; failed logons ≥ 10 within 30 minutes from any source
options.why_wrong: That is brute force on one account; spraying spreads few attempts over many users and stays under per-user lockout.

options.text: Group by source address; failed logons ≥ 10 in 30 minutes for the same account
options.why_wrong: Same-account repeats are the mistyping user or classic brute force, not spraying.

options.text: Group by domain controller; account lockouts (4740) ≥ 3 within one hour
options.why_wrong: Sprayers deliberately stay below the lockout threshold, so lockouts may never occur.

quiz.explanation: Spraying is breadth: one source, one or two passwords, many accounts. Count distinct users per source.

quiz.stem: On a file server you see, within one minute: 4624 logon type 3 from 10.20.10.44, 5145 access to ADMIN$, then 7045 service 'PSEXESVC'. Which conclusions are justified? Select all that apply.

options.text: A remote execution tool was used against the file server from 10.20.10.44
The account used holds administrative rights on the file server
The account's password was cracked offline from a Kerberos service ticket
options.why_wrong: Possible, but nothing in these events says how the credentials were obtained.

options.text: 10.20.10.44 should be scoped next: what ran there before this logon
The file server was the first host compromised in this intrusion
options.why_wrong: It is a target of lateral movement; the earlier activity is on the source.

quiz.explanation: ADMIN$ + PSEXESVC means admin rights and remote execution from the source. How the credentials were obtained and which host was first are open questions.

quiz.stem: Which parent–child pair is the strongest sign of a web shell on an IIS server?

options.text: w3wp.exe starting cmd.exe, which then runs whoami and ipconfig
svchost.exe starting w3wp.exe after the application pool recycles
options.why_wrong: That is how IIS starts worker processes normally.

options.text: explorer.exe starting powershell.exe for an administrator at the console
options.why_wrong: Interactive admin work; suspicious only with other context.

options.text: services.exe starting w3wp.exe with the identity of an application pool
options.why_wrong: Normal service plumbing; no shell is involved in that chain at all.

quiz.explanation: IIS worker processes don't start shells in normal operation. Recon commands right after confirm it.

quiz.output:
FortiAnalyzer — traffic, srcip=10.30.5.21 (APP-SRV-03), last 6 h, grouped by destination
dstip            dstport  sessions  avg_interval  stdev_interval  sent_bytes(avg)  rcvd_bytes(avg)
52.96.12.40      443      1,904     n/a           n/a             18,220           242,610
185.77.31.9      443        358     60.2 s        1.9 s              612              418
10.30.1.10        53      2,113     n/a           n/a                 74              148
quiz.stem: What do you do first?

options.text: Open a case for 185.77.31.9 and look on APP-SRV-03 for the process holding that connection
Block 185.77.31.9 on the FortiGate at once, then open a case to find the process later
options.why_wrong: Blocking first tips the attacker off and loses the live process you need to scope the intrusion.

options.text: Open a case for 52.96.12.40 because it has the most sessions and the most received bytes
options.why_wrong: High volume with irregular intervals looks like a busy SaaS app, not a beacon.

options.text: Open a case for the DNS server because APP-SRV-03 sends more DNS queries than HTTPS sessions
options.why_wrong: Many queries to the internal resolver are normal; nothing here suggests tunnelling.

quiz.explanation: A 60-second interval with a 1.9-second deviation and tiny constant payloads for six hours is a beacon. Identify the process (EDR) before containing, so you know what else it touched.

quiz.stem: Which DNS pattern most strongly suggests tunnelling through the resolver?

options.text: Thousands of unique 50-character subdomains under one domain, mostly TXT queries
Thousands of queries per hour from one host, all for the same Microsoft update host name
options.why_wrong: Repeated queries for one name are a chatty client, not data encoded in names.

options.text: A few queries per day to a newly registered domain with a short random name
options.why_wrong: Worth a look (phishing, C2 setup) but too little volume to carry data.

options.text: Queries for many different domains that each resolve to the same CDN address
options.why_wrong: CDNs host many names on shared addresses; that is normal web traffic.

quiz.explanation: Tunnels encode data in the query name, so almost every query is a new, long, random-looking subdomain of one parent domain.

quiz.stem: An app server opens a TLS session to a rare external host that stays up for 9 hours, with steady traffic in both directions. A week ago a pentest used ligolo-ng from a similar server. What is the best detection logic for this class of activity?

options.text: Long-lived outbound sessions from servers to destinations not seen in 30 days, with sustained two-way bytes
A hash rule for the ligolo-ng agent binary found in the pentest, pushed to FortiEDR as a blocklist entry
options.why_wrong: Catches that exact file only; a recompiled agent or chisel walks past it.

options.text: An application-control block on the category 'Proxy' for traffic leaving the server VLAN on TCP 443
options.why_wrong: Without SSL inspection the tunnel looks like ordinary TLS, so the category rarely matches.

options.text: Any session longer than one hour from any internal host to any external destination at all
options.why_wrong: Streaming, VPNs and SaaS keep long sessions; without rarity and the server scope it is pure noise.

quiz.explanation: Behaviour over tool: servers rarely hold long two-way sessions to new destinations. Rarity + duration + direction survives the tool changing.

quiz.stem: Order the detection lifecycle.
items: Write a hypothesis from the technique
Identify the data source and events
Test against an emulated attack and a benign baseline
quiz.explanation: Hypothesis, data, logic, test, deploy and tune, maintain.

quiz.stem: A rule for LSASS access (Sysmon 10, target lsass.exe) fires 300 times a day. Which tuning keeps it useful?

options.text: Exclude the known security agents by signed image path and keep read-access masks in scope
Exclude the processes under C:\Program Files, since attackers usually run their tools from user folders
options.why_wrong: Attackers can drop tools in Program Files or use signed binaries like the Task Manager dump; the exclusion is too wide.

options.text: Raise the threshold to 50 accesses per host per hour before raising an incident at all
options.why_wrong: A credential dump needs one access; a threshold hides exactly the event you want.

options.text: Keep the rule but lower its severity to informational, reviewing the list each Friday
options.why_wrong: A dump reviewed days later is a breach already in progress; fix precision instead.

quiz.explanation: Security products touch LSASS legitimately. Exclude them precisely (signed path), and keep the access masks that mean memory read.

quiz.stem: A pentest report says 'the EDR raised no alert when we dumped LSASS on WS-12'. What is the right detection-engineering response, and why?

options.text: Add a backlog item with an owner, write the rule, and re-test with the same technique
Ask the EDR vendor for a signature update and close the finding once the update lands
options.why_wrong: Without a re-test nobody knows if the update detects that technique in this environment.

options.text: Enable LSASS protection (RunAsPPL) on WS-12 and mark the detection finding as remediated
options.why_wrong: Prevention is good, but the finding was about missing detection; the gap remains on every other host.

options.text: Accept the risk, because the pentesters had local admin rights, which a real attacker lacks
options.why_wrong: Real attackers get local admin routinely; that's why the technique exists.

quiz.explanation: A finding becomes a tracked detection item: owner, logic, and the same test repeated to prove it now fires. Prevention is a parallel control, not a substitute for detection.

quiz.stem: A 4624 event on a workstation shows logon type 9 and logon process 'seclogo'. What does it most likely indicate?

options.text: Alternate credentials were used for network access, as with runas /netonly or pass-the-hash
A user unlocked the console with a smart card after a short screen saver timeout
options.why_wrong: Unlocks are logon type 7, not type 9.

options.text: A remote desktop session was opened to this workstation from another machine on the network
options.why_wrong: RDP logons are type 10 (RemoteInteractive).

options.text: A scheduled task ran under a stored service account during the night
options.why_wrong: Batch logons from scheduled tasks are type 4.

quiz.explanation: Type 9 (NewCredentials) keeps the local identity and uses other credentials for network access: what runas /netonly and pass-the-hash tooling produce.

quiz.stem: During an AD CS review you see 4887 (certificate issued) where the requester is 'jperez' and the certificate's subject alternative name is 'administrator'. What is the most likely issue?

options.text: The certificate template accepts an enrollee-supplied subject, enabling impersonation
The CA itself is compromised and is issuing certificates on its own for the privileged accounts
options.why_wrong: The CA did what the template allowed; the misconfiguration is the template, not a CA compromise.

options.text: jperez enrolled for a smart card for the administrator as a delegated enrolment agent
options.why_wrong: Enrolment agents leave different evidence and need an agent certificate; nothing shows that here.

options.text: The certificate was renewed automatically and kept the subject of a previous holder
options.why_wrong: Renewal keeps the requester's own identity; it does not swap in another user.

quiz.explanation: A SAN that names someone else than the requester is the ESC1 pattern: a template allowing enrollee-supplied subject plus client-authentication use.

quiz.stem: Which ticket encryption type value in 4769 means RC4-HMAC (the one Kerberoasting rules look for)?
quiz.explanation: 0x17 (decimal 23) is RC4-HMAC. AES256 is 0x12, AES128 0x11.

labs.title: Kerberoasting rule on paper
labs.goal: Write a correlation rule for Kerberoasting and its exceptions.

worked.config:
# Name:        Kerberoasting - many RC4 service tickets from one account
# Technique:   T1558.003
# Source:      Domain controllers, event 4769 (Audit Kerberos Service Ticket Operations)
# Filter:      TicketEncryptionType = 0x17 AND ServiceName not ending in '$' AND ServiceName != krbtgt
# Group by:    TargetUserName (the requester), IpAddress
# Condition:   COUNT(DISTINCT ServiceName) >= 10
# Window:      300 s
# Severity:    High; incident attributes: user, source IP, service count
# Exceptions:  none at start; legacy app accounts reviewed weekly
# Test:        request TGS for 20 SPNs from a test user (lab) -> fires; normal week replay -> quiet
notes: Computer accounts ($) and krbtgt are filtered out: they are not roastable targets.
Distinct service names is what separates enumeration from one app using one service.

solo.prompt: Write the five fields of the rule, one per line: event, filter, group, condition, window.
solo.solution:
event 4769
filter encryption 0x17
group by requesting user and IP
count distinct service names >= 10
window 300 s
solo.notes: Then the test plan: attack replay fires, baseline stays quiet.

labs.title: From pentest finding to detection backlog
labs.goal: Turn three pentest findings into detection items with data source, logic and test.

worked.config:
# Finding 1: LSASS dumped on WS-12 without alert
#   Detection: Sysmon 10, TargetImage=lsass.exe, read access, SourceImage not in signed security agents
#   Test: dump LSASS with a test tool in the lab -> incident within 2 min
# Finding 2: reverse shell from WEB-01 to 203.0.113.50:4444 not detected
#   Detection: Sysmon 3 from sh/bash/powershell to external; FortiGate rule: server VLAN -> any:4444 allowed? (should be denied)
#   Test: lab reverse shell -> incident; egress policy denies non-approved ports
# Finding 3: BloodHound collection not flagged
#   Detection: one host making LDAP queries for all users/groups/sessions in minutes (DC LDAP logging or EDR)
#   Test: run the collector in the lab -> incident
notes: Each finding also gets a prevention control, tracked separately.

faded.template:
# LSASS dump -> Sysmon event {{10}}
# Reverse shell -> Sysmon event {{3}} from a shell to an external address

solo.prompt: Write the four fields of a detection backlog item, one per line.
solo.solution:
finding
data source
logic
test
solo.notes: And an owner with a date.

scenarios.title: The pentest report lands on your desk
scenarios.situation:
A bank's annual pentest reached Domain Admin in two days: password spray on the VPN, Kerberoasting of a SQL
service account, then DCSync. The SOC (FortiSIEM + FortiEDR) raised one low incident during the whole test.
The CISO asks Fortinet PS: "What do we fix in detection, and by when?"
scenarios.ask: What do you propose?
right_thinking: Map each step of the chain to a technique, a data source and the reason it wasn't detected
Check the sources first: are 4769 and 4662 even audited and sent? VPN logs parsed?
Write and test rules for each step, prioritising the ones that come earliest in the chain
Re-run the same chain (purple team) to prove detection, then measure time to detect
Pair with prevention: AES-only service accounts with long passwords, MFA on VPN, limit replication rights
scenarios.what: A chain-by-chain detection plan proven by a purple-team re-run.
scenarios.why: Detecting the first step (spray) buys the most time; proving it with the same chain is the only evidence that counts.
scenarios.model_answer:
"I'd take their chain step by step. For the spray, the VPN logs must reach FortiSIEM parsed with user and
source, and a rule counts distinct users per source. For Kerberoasting, the DCs must audit service tickets
and we alert on many RC4 tickets from one account. For DCSync, 4662 with the replication rights from a non-DC
account. Earliest steps first, because catching the spray stops the rest. In four weeks we re-run the same
chain with the pentesters and measure how fast each step raises an incident. In parallel, prevention: MFA on
the VPN and AES-only, long-password service accounts."
scenarios.best_way: Same chain, step by step: fix the source, write the rule, re-run it.

scenarios.title: The exception that ate the subnet
scenarios.situation:
During a FortiSIEM health check you find an exception on 'Excessive Logon Failures': srcIpAddr in
10.20.0.0/16, created 14 months ago, no comment. The SOC lead says it was added because 'the scanners were
noisy'.
scenarios.ask: What do you do?
right_thinking: Treat it as a blind spot covering almost every internal source
Find the scanners' real addresses and replace the /16 with those hosts
Replay the last 30 days without the exception to see what it hid
Add who/why/review date to every exception; schedule a quarterly review
scenarios.what: Replace the broad exception with host-level ones and check what it hid.
scenarios.why: An undocumented /16 exception is exactly where an internal attacker hides.
scenarios.model_answer:
"That exception means the rule is off for almost every internal machine. I'd replace it with the two or three
scanner addresses, replay the last 30 days without it to see whether anything real was hidden, and add the
who, why and review date to it and to every other exception. Then a quarterly review goes in the runbook."
scenarios.best_way: Narrow it, look at what it hid, document it.

scenarios.title: IOC feed vs behaviour
scenarios.situation:
A customer's SOC lead wants to spend the detection budget on threat-intel IOC feeds ('we'll block every known
bad hash and IP'). Their last incident was a contractor laptop using legitimate admin tools to move laterally.
scenarios.ask: How do you advise them?
right_thinking: IOCs catch known, reused infrastructure; they miss living-off-the-land and fresh infrastructure
Their own incident would not have matched any IOC
Balance: IOC feeds for cheap blocking, behaviour rules for the techniques in their incidents
Measure with the pyramid of pain: hashes and IPs are easy for attackers to change
scenarios.what: IOCs as a cheap layer, behaviour detections as the investment.
scenarios.why: Attackers change hashes and IPs in minutes; techniques like admin-tool lateral movement stay.
scenarios.model_answer:
"IOC feeds are worth having because they're cheap and they block reused infrastructure, and FortiGuard
already gives you a lot of that on the FortiGates. But your last incident used admin tools and a valid
account, so no IOC would have fired. I'd put most of the effort into behaviour: remote service installs,
admin logons from workstations that never do that, unusual ADMIN$ access. Then we measure coverage on the
techniques you've actually seen."
scenarios.best_way: IOCs for the cheap wins, behaviour for the attacks you actually had.

interview.question: How would you detect Kerberoasting?
interview.testing: AD attack knowledge from the defender side
interview.model_answer:
"Kerberoasting is requesting service tickets for accounts with SPNs and cracking them offline. The DCs log
those requests as 4769, if the service ticket auditing is on. The tell is one account asking for many
distinct service names in a short window, with RC4 encryption — 0x17 — when the environment normally uses
AES. So: group by requester and source IP, count distinct service names, exclude computer accounts and
krbtgt, and test it by actually roasting in a lab. I did this attack in my CRTP and CRTE labs, which is why
I know exactly what it leaves behind."
interview.best_way: 4769, many distinct SPNs, RC4, one account, tested.

interview.question: What's the difference between an atomic and a behavioural detection, and which would you invest in?
interview.model_answer:
"Atomic detections match one indicator — a hash, an IP — so they're precise but the attacker changes them in
minutes. Behavioural ones match what the technique has to do, like a web server spawning a shell or a
non-DC account asking for replication. They need tuning but they survive tool changes. I'd let threat intel
cover the atomic layer cheaply and put the engineering time into behaviour."
interview.best_way: Atomic is cheap and brittle; behaviour is the investment.

interview.question: Tell me about a time your offensive background helped a defensive outcome.
interview.framework: STAR from lab and report work
interview.model_answer:
"In my CRTE and OSCP work every finding had to go into a full report with remediation. One recurring finding
was that the endpoint monitoring didn't flag things it should — LSASS wasn't protected, tooling ran without
alerts, reverse shells went unnoticed — and for each one I documented the fix. That's the habit I bring to a
SOC project: every gap becomes a detection item with a data source, logic and a test that proves it now
fires. These were lab and exam environments, not a customer SOC, and I say that openly."
interview.best_way: Every gap in my reports came with a fix; in a SOC that becomes a tested detection.

interview.question: How do you tune a noisy rule without creating a blind spot?
interview.model_answer:
"I find why it's noisy first — a scanner, a service account, a threshold below normal behaviour. Then the
narrowest fix: an exception for that host or account, or a threshold set above the 30-day maximum for that
key. Every exception gets who asked, why and a review date, and I replay a known attack through the tuned rule
to make sure it still fires."
interview.best_way: Narrow, documented, expiring, and re-tested.

modules.title: Incident response: scoping, containment decisions and recovery with the Fortinet stack
objectives: Choose containment (EDR isolation, FortiGate quarantine, account disable, segment block) by trade-off
Plan eradication and recovery for AD compromise and ransomware, including credential resets
Lead the post-incident review and turn it into detections and control changes
sources: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (2025): incident response recommendations aligned with CSF 2.0; classic phases from Rev. 2
FortiEDR and FortiGate response features as covered in M10.03, M10.04, M4.12 and M8.01
Microsoft guidance on krbtgt reset after domain compromise (reset twice, allowing replication between resets)

units.title: Frameworks and the first hour
units.body:
**The phases you will hear.** NIST SP 800-61 (Rev. 2) described preparation; detection and analysis;
containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity. SANS teaches the same as PICERL (prepare,
identify, contain, eradicate, recover, lessons). Rev. 3 (2025) reorganises the guidance around the CSF 2.0
functions (govern, identify, protect, detect, respond, recover), so IR is part of risk management, not a
separate playbook. In a customer meeting, use whichever vocabulary their policy uses.

**The first hour, in order:**

1. **Confirm and classify.** Is it real? What type (malware, account compromise, data exposure)? Initial
   severity.
2. **Assemble.** Incident lead, scribe, technical leads, a business owner with authority. One bridge.
3. **Scope questions.** Which hosts, users, data? Since when? Is it still active?
4. **Preserve.** Volatile evidence first: memory and live connections, then disk and logs. Don't reboot
   first.
5. **Contain the bleeding** proportionately (next unit).
6. **Communicate.** Next update time on every message. Facts, not guesses.

**The scribe matters.** A timeline written live (time, who, what, why) is your legal record, your
post-incident input, and the thing executives ask for at 2 a.m.

:::recall
Q: Why preserve memory and live connections before rebooting an infected server?
A: A reboot destroys running processes, injected code and live C2 connections, which are often the best evidence of what the attacker did.
:::

:::why
Q: Why should every incident update state the time of the next update?
A: It stops stakeholders interrupting the responders for news and sets a rhythm the team can keep.
:::

units.title: Choosing containment
units.body:
Containment is a trade-off between stopping the attacker and keeping the business running. Know your options
and what each costs:

| Option | Fortinet tool | Stops | Cost / risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Isolate host** | FortiEDR isolation (only EDR core traffic allowed) | Lateral movement, C2 from that host | The user can't work; on servers, the service stops |
| **Quarantine at the network** | FortiGate address group in a deny policy, FortiSwitch/FortiAP quarantine via automation | That host's traffic through the fabric | Doesn't stop traffic inside the same L2 segment unless the switch enforces it |
| **Block destination** | FortiGate deny policy, DNS filter, threat feed | C2 / exfil to known infrastructure | Attacker switches infrastructure; tips them off |
| **Disable / reset account** | AD, IdP; FortiAuthenticator | Use of stolen credentials | Kerberos tickets already issued stay valid until expiry; tips them off |
| **Segment block** | FortiGate policy between zones, SD-WAN rule | Spread between sites or VLANs | Broad business impact |

**Decision rules:**

- **Scope before you show your hand** when the attacker is quiet and you don't yet know all footholds: block
  one host and they move to the next one you didn't see. When damage is active (ransomware encrypting, data
  leaving), contain now and scope in parallel.
- **Prefer the narrowest action that stops the harm**, and widen it when it fails.
- **Disabling an account isn't instant on its own.** Existing Kerberos tickets remain valid until they
  expire; combine with isolating the hosts using them, and for domain-level compromise plan the krbtgt reset.
- **Life and safety first.** Medical, OT and safety systems need a pre-agreed alternative (segment
  quarantine, manual operation) instead of isolation.

:::recall
Q: When should you contain immediately instead of scoping quietly first?
A: When the harm is active: encryption spreading, data leaving, or safety at risk.
:::

:::why
Q: Why might quarantining a host on the FortiGate not stop it from attacking its neighbours?
A: Traffic between hosts in the same VLAN doesn't cross the FortiGate unless the switch forwards it there (FortiLink/quarantine VLAN) or EDR isolates the host.
:::

units.title: Eradication and recovery after AD compromise and ransomware
units.body:
**Eradication removes every foothold**, not just the one you found: persistence (services, scheduled tasks,
run keys, new accounts, added group memberships), web shells, implants on other hosts, and the initial access
path (the unpatched VPN, the phished account without MFA).

**Credential reset order after domain compromise:**

1. Accounts the attacker is known to hold (and their sessions in the IdP).
2. Privileged accounts: domain admins, service accounts with SPNs, accounts with replication rights.
3. **krbtgt twice**, with replication between the two resets (Microsoft's guidance is to wait at least the
   maximum ticket lifetime, typically 10 hours). Twice, because the DC keeps the previous key; a forged
   golden ticket signed with the old key works until both are gone.
4. Everyone else, if the NTDS database was taken.

**Rebuild or clean?** Rebuild domain controllers and servers where the attacker had SYSTEM, unless you can
prove what they changed. Clean only what EDR evidence fully explains.

**Ransomware specifics.** Isolate first, keep encrypted systems for evidence, restore from backups known to
predate the intrusion (not just the encryption), check the backups weren't touched, and expect
exfiltration: most ransomware crews steal data before encrypting.

**Recovery is monitored.** Restored systems go back with extra watch: EDR in prevention mode, the indicators
from this case in the SIEM, and a named owner watching for 30 days.

:::recall
Q: Why is krbtgt reset twice?
A: The DC accepts tickets signed with the current and the previous krbtgt key; both must change to kill forged tickets.
:::

:::why
Q: Why restore from a backup that predates the intrusion rather than the encryption?
A: The attacker was inside before encrypting; a backup taken in between contains their persistence.
:::

units.title: Communication and the post-incident review
units.body:
**Three audiences, three messages.**

- **Responders:** facts, tasks, owners, next sync.
- **Executives:** impact on the business, what is being done, decisions needed from them, next update time.
  No jargon, no guesses presented as facts.
- **External** (customers, regulators, insurer): through legal and the communication owner only. Deadlines
  depend on jurisdiction and contracts (for example, GDPR expects notification to the authority within 72
  hours of becoming aware of a personal-data breach); know the customer's obligations before the incident.

**The post-incident review** is blameless and specific:

1. Timeline with times of first malicious action, first alert, acknowledgement, containment.
2. What worked, what didn't, what we got lucky with.
3. Detection gaps → new rules with tests (M13.02).
4. Control gaps → owners and dates (MFA, patching, segmentation).
5. Process gaps → runbook changes (authority to contain, escalation).

Publish the actions with owners and dates, and check them at 30 days.

:::recall
Q: Four times to record in every incident timeline?
A: First malicious action, first alert, acknowledgement, containment.
:::

:::why
Q: Why keep the post-incident review blameless?
A: People hide mistakes when they expect blame, and hidden mistakes are the gaps the next attacker uses.
:::

cards.back: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity.
Prepare, identify, contain, eradicate, recover, lessons learned (SANS).
Organises IR around the CSF 2.0 functions as part of risk management.
Volatile first: memory and live connections, then disk and logs.
Time, who, what, why.
All network traffic from the host except to the EDR core: lateral movement and C2.
Doesn't stop same-VLAN traffic unless the switch enforces it.

cards.front: Disabling an AD account isn't instant because
cards.back: Kerberos tickets already issued stay valid until they expire.
Active harm (encryption, exfil, safety) → contain now. Quiet attacker, unknown footholds → scope first.
Twice, with replication (and the max ticket lifetime, ~10 h) between resets.
Known-compromised, privileged and service accounts, krbtgt twice, everyone if NTDS was taken.
A backup from before the intrusion, checked untouched.
Rebuild where the attacker had SYSTEM, unless EDR evidence fully explains the changes.
Business impact, actions, decisions needed, next update time.
72 hours from awareness of a personal-data breach, to the supervisory authority.
Detection gaps, control gaps, process gaps — each with owner and date.

quiz.stem: FortiEDR shows ransomware-like file renaming on FS01 right now, spreading to shares on two other servers. What comes first?

options.text: Isolate FS01 and the affected servers now, and scope from the EDR events in parallel
Scope quietly for an hour first, so the attacker doesn't learn that you have seen them
options.why_wrong: Right for a quiet intrusion, wrong when encryption is spreading: every minute costs data.

options.text: Reboot FS01 into safe mode so that the encryption process stops and can be removed
options.why_wrong: Destroys memory evidence and the process may come back at boot; isolation stops spread without losing evidence.

options.text: Disable the user account seen on FS01 in AD, then wait for the sessions to expire
options.why_wrong: Existing sessions and tickets keep working; the encryption continues meanwhile.

quiz.explanation: Active harm means contain now. EDR isolation stops spread and keeps the host's evidence intact.

quiz.stem: A threat hunt finds a quiet beacon from one server, no other alerts, no data loss seen yet. The CISO wants the server blocked today. What do you recommend?

options.text: Scope the other footholds first with a set deadline, then contain them all at once
Block the C2 domain on the FortiGate today and keep watching the server for a week
options.why_wrong: Tips the attacker off while leaving every other foothold you haven't found in place.

options.text: Isolate the server today and rebuild it, because a known-bad host cannot stay online
options.why_wrong: Cleans one host and teaches the attacker to use the others; scoping first is the safer order here.

options.text: Leave it until the next maintenance window, because nothing harmful is happening right now
options.why_wrong: No visible harm is not the same as no harm; scoping must start now with a deadline.

quiz.explanation: With a quiet attacker, a premature block makes them change behaviour. Scope fast with a deadline, then contain all known footholds together.

quiz.stem: A laptop is quarantined with a FortiGate address group in a deny policy, but it still reaches a file server in the same VLAN. Why?

options.text: Same-VLAN traffic is switched locally and never crosses the FortiGate's policies
The deny policy sits below an allow policy for that VLAN in the policy order
options.why_wrong: Order matters for routed traffic, but this traffic never reaches the policy table at all.

options.text: Existing sessions were kept because the policy change didn't clear the session table
options.why_wrong: A real effect for routed sessions, but same-VLAN traffic isn't in the FortiGate's sessions.

options.text: Address groups are evaluated after the first packet, so the quarantine misses replies
options.why_wrong: Addresses are matched on the first packet of a session; that's not how they work.

quiz.explanation: L2 traffic within a VLAN is switched. Use EDR isolation or switch-level quarantine (FortiSwitch via FortiLink) to stop it.

quiz.stem: Order the credential resets after a confirmed domain compromise with NTDS.dit stolen.
items: Accounts known to be held by the attacker
krbtgt, second reset after replication and ticket lifetime
quiz.explanation: Cut the attacker's known access, then the most powerful accounts, then kill forged tickets with two krbtgt resets, then everyone (NTDS had every hash).

quiz.stem: After the first krbtgt reset, the team wants to do the second one ten minutes later 'to be safe'. What is the risk?

options.text: Tickets signed with the first new key fail before replication completes
The second reset is ignored, because a DC accepts one krbtgt password change per day
options.why_wrong: There is no such limit; the issue is tickets and replication timing.

options.text: Golden tickets signed with the original key keep working until the DCs are next rebooted
options.why_wrong: After two resets the original key is gone; the problem with rushing is breaking legitimate tickets.

options.text: The DCs fall out of sync and need re-promotion before users can log on again
options.why_wrong: Overstated; the realistic impact is authentication failures, not re-promotion.

quiz.explanation: Both keys are kept so in-flight tickets keep working. Resetting twice too quickly invalidates valid tickets before all DCs and clients catch up.

quiz.stem: Ransomware hit a hospital's admin network. Which steps belong in recovery? Select all that apply.

options.text: Restore from backups that predate the intrusion and check they were not altered
Assume data was stolen before encryption and involve legal on notification
Restore the most recent backup to cut downtime, then scan it with antivirus
options.why_wrong: The latest backup may hold the attacker's persistence; a clean scan doesn't prove absence of access.

options.text: Return systems with EDR in prevention mode and the case indicators watched
Delete the encrypted copies right away to free storage for the restores
options.why_wrong: They are evidence (and sometimes decryptable later); keep them.

quiz.explanation: Restore point before intrusion, assume exfiltration, monitor what you restore, keep evidence.

quiz.stem: It's 02:30. The CFO joins the bridge and asks 'are we breached?'. You know one account is compromised and two laptops are isolated; scope is ongoing. What do you say?

options.text: What is confirmed, what we are doing, what we don't know yet, and when the next update is
That it is too early to say, and that you will call back once the investigation is complete
options.why_wrong: Leaves the executive with nothing to act on and no time for the next update.

options.text: The full technical timeline so far, including the Kerberos tickets and the EDR events
options.why_wrong: Right facts, wrong audience; executives need impact and decisions, not event IDs.

options.text: That it is contained, since both laptops are isolated and the account is now disabled
options.why_wrong: Scope isn't finished; claiming containment is a guess presented as fact.

quiz.explanation: Executive updates: confirmed facts, actions, unknowns, decisions needed, next update time.

quiz.stem: An infusion-pump management server on the clinical VLAN shows the same beacon as an infected admin PC. Isolating it would stop pump drug-library updates. What is the best first step?

options.text: Call the clinical engineering lead and apply the pre-agreed segment-level control for that VLAN
Isolate it with FortiEDR immediately, because the same beacon means the same compromise and risk
options.why_wrong: Correct for the admin PC; for a clinical system safety comes first, with a pre-agreed alternative.

options.text: Leave it untouched until the vendor confirms the beacon, because it is a medical device
options.why_wrong: Waiting with a known compromise on a clinical network is the bigger safety risk.

options.text: Block the C2 destination on the FortiGate and keep monitoring the server for further signs
options.why_wrong: A useful layer, but it skips the clinical owner and the agreed plan for this device class.

quiz.explanation: Life-safety systems get a pre-agreed alternative to isolation, decided with their owner: involve them first, then apply the planned control.

quiz.stem: Which item is the most important output of the post-incident review?

options.text: Detection, control and process gaps, each with an owner and a due date
A report that names who made the mistake that allowed the initial access
options.why_wrong: Blame makes people hide errors; the review is blameless by design.

options.text: A full export of the logs that were collected during the incident response
options.why_wrong: Evidence is preserved separately; the review produces actions.

options.text: A list of the indicators of compromise, added as blocks on the FortiGates
options.why_wrong: Useful but short-lived; gaps with owners prevent the next incident.

quiz.explanation: Actions with owners and dates are what make the next incident shorter.

quiz.stem: How many times must the krbtgt password be reset to invalidate forged golden tickets?
quiz.explanation: Twice, with replication and the maximum ticket lifetime between the two resets.

labs.title: The first-hour checklist
labs.goal: Write the first-hour checklist for an account-compromise incident.

worked.config:
# 00-10 min  Confirm (EDR + SIEM evidence), classify (account compromise), initial severity P1/P2
# 00-15 min  Bridge: incident lead, scribe, AD admin, EDR admin, business owner with authority
# 10-30 min  Scope: hosts used by the account (4624 by user), processes run (EDR), data touched (file server logs)
# 10-30 min  Preserve: EDR forensic collection on the hosts, export FortiGate logs for the account's IPs
# 20-40 min  Contain: isolate the hosts in active use, disable the account, revoke IdP sessions
# every 30 min  Update: facts, actions, unknowns, decisions needed, next update time
notes: Disable + isolate together: tickets outlive the disabled account.

faded.template:

# Every update ends with the {{next update}} time

solo.prompt: Write the six first-hour steps, one per line.
solo.solution:
confirm and classify

scope

contain

solo.notes: The scribe starts the timeline at minute zero.
