scenarios.title: Monday after the ASA cutover
scenarios.situation: Saturday's ASA → FortiGate cutover passed the acceptance tests. Monday 08:30: payroll can't reach the bank's SFTP and the IT manager asks for 'any/any until you fix it'.
scenarios.ask: What do you do?
right_thinking: Decline any/any politely; offer a fast specific fix
Filter deny logs for the payroll host, find the flow (likely a level-based allow or an object missing)
Add the specific policy, test with the user, update the workbook and acceptance tests
scenarios.what: Specific fix from logs in minutes.
scenarios.why: An any/any rule hides every other gap and tends to stay.
scenarios.model_answer: "I'd rather fix it properly in the next ten minutes. I'll filter the deny logs for the payroll PC, find the SFTP flow — probably something the ASA allowed by security level — and add a policy just for it. Then I'll test with the user and add the flow to our acceptance tests so the remaining sites don't hit it."
scenarios.best_way: Specific policy from deny logs, added to the tests.

interview.question: What goes wrong most often when migrating from Cisco ASA to FortiGate?
interview.model_answer: "The things the ASA does without config: traffic from higher to lower security levels is allowed with no ACL, so the converter produces nothing for it. Second, NAT: ASA's three NAT sections and real-IP ACLs map best onto FortiGate central NAT, and mixing models causes mismatches. I clean the rulebase with hit counts first, test with app owners, and watch deny logs after cutover."
interview.best_way: Implicit allows and NAT model, then a clean-test-watch process.

modules.title: Design documents and customer handling: HLD, LLD, status, scope and escalations
objectives: Write a high-level and a low-level design the customer can approve and an engineer can build from
Apply four design principles and name the failure modes in common Fortinet patterns
Run status reporting with a RAID log and RAG status that nobody is surprised by
Handle scope creep, difficult stakeholders and escalations without losing the relationship
sources: PS delivery practice (curriculum M11.4 Design patterns and M11.5 Customer handling, merged)
FortiTatake modules M4.09, M4.10, M8.03 and I3 for the technical patterns
Your evidence: escalation save, sponsor change, merger health checks, executive QBRs (super-cv)

units.title: HLD, LLD and four design principles
units.body:
## High-level design (HLD): for approval

Who reads it: the customer's architect, security lead and sponsor. Contents: **requirements and assumptions**, current state, the **target architecture diagram**, key decisions with **reasons and alternatives considered**, security zones, HA and resilience, management and logging, migration approach, risks.

## Low-level design (LLD): for building

Who reads it: the engineer who implements, maybe you at 2 a.m. Contents: **every interface, VLAN, IP, zone, route, VPN parameter, HA setting, SD-WAN member, health check and rule, policy matrix, NAT table, security profiles, admin access, logging**, naming conventions, and the acceptance tests.

If the LLD is good, the MOP almost writes itself.

## Four principles to justify any choice

1. **Segmentation and least privilege:** zones and policies that allow only what's needed; no `any any`.
2. **Resilience:** no single point of failure the customer can't accept (links, units, heartbeats, hubs).
3. **Manageability:** templates in FortiManager, naming standards, logs in FortiAnalyzer; the customer's team must be able to run it.
4. **Visibility and response:** logging, reports and alerts sized to what they must prove (compliance) and react to.

## Failure modes to design out (from the modules you've studied)

- SD-WAN: asymmetric routing, probes not reflecting the app path, leftover policy routes.
- HA: split brain from shared heartbeat paths; no session pickup for long sessions; override surprises.
- VPN: overlapping subnets, MTU, weak proposals, exposed gateways.
- Inspection: CA not distributed, pinned apps, proxy where flow would do.

:::recall
Q: Who is the HLD for, and who is the LLD for?
A: HLD for approval (architects, sponsor); LLD for building (the implementing engineer).
:::

units.title: Status, RAID and scope
units.body:
## Weekly status that prevents surprises

One page: **RAG status** (red/amber/green) for scope, schedule and budget; done this week; next week; **decisions needed** from the customer; risks and issues. Send it at the same time every week. Amber early is a gift; red at the end is a failure of communication.

## The RAID log

- **Risks:** might happen (a change freeze could delay cutover). Owner, likelihood, impact, mitigation.
- **Assumptions:** what you're relying on (the customer provides console access).
- **Issues:** happening now (ISP circuit not delivered). Owner and due date.
- **Dependencies:** what you need from others (partner VPN parameters by Friday).

## Scope creep

Requests will come: "while you're here, can you…". The pattern:

1. **Acknowledge** the request positively.
2. **Check the SOW.**
3. If out of scope: explain, estimate, and raise a **change request**, or park it for a follow-up project.
4. Never do unbilled work silently: it sets an expectation and hides the real cost.

At Netskope you kept reporting rhythms for a whole portfolio: weekly status on open issues, quarterly business reviews in three languages. PS status is the same discipline on a project scale.

:::pitfall
"Green, green, green, red" is the worst status pattern. If something might slip, show amber with the reason and what you need.
:::

units.title: Difficult moments and storytelling
units.body:
## Difficult stakeholders

- **The hostile sponsor:** treat it as a problem to solve, not a person to win. Find the technical cause behind the anger. Your evidence: a hostile escalation where you fixed the underlying technical issue first, and the customer exchanged licences instead of leaving: more than USD 900k in contract value kept.
- **The new team that inherits you:** start with something useful to them. After a whole security team was replaced, you opened with a health check; more than half the seats were in use within six weeks.
- **Two merged companies:** one shared view. After customer mergers you presented a health check and adoption dashboards so the combined team agreed on priorities.
- **The customer's architect who disagrees:** listen, compare options against their requirements, bring evidence (lab, docs), and if it's their risk to take, document the decision.

## Escalations

Escalate **early, factually, to the right level**, with options. Before a rollout at Netskope you escalated a support backlog to the director of support and set an AI agent to alert on every case update or idle case: the issue was visible and moving.

## Storytelling that lands

**Problem → impact → approach → proof.** "Branches lost voice quality at peak (problem); it cost them complaints from stores (impact); we moved voice to Best Quality on jitter with probes to the voice platform (approach); jitter fell and complaints stopped in the pilot stores (proof)." Use their words and their numbers.

:::ps
The relationship is built in the bad moments. Customers forgive problems; they don't forgive surprises.
:::

cards.back: Requirements and assumptions, current state, target diagram, decisions with reasons, zones, HA, management/logging, migration approach, risks.
Every interface, IP, route, VPN, HA, SD-WAN, policy matrix, NAT table, profiles, admin, logging, naming, acceptance tests.
Segmentation/least privilege, resilience, manageability, visibility and response.

cards.front: SD-WAN failure modes to design out?
cards.back: Asymmetric routing, probes not on the app path, leftover policy routes.
Risks, Assumptions, Issues, Dependencies.
A risk might happen; an issue is happening now.
RAG for scope/schedule/budget, done, next, decisions needed, risks and issues.
Acknowledge, check SOW, explain and estimate, change request or park it. No silent unbilled work.
Fix the technical cause first; the escalation became a licence exchange, more than USD 900k kept.

cards.front: New team inherits you: what do you open with?
cards.back: Something useful to them: a health check. More than half the seats in use within six weeks.
Early, factual, to the right level, with options.
Problem → impact → approach → proof, in the customer's words and numbers.

quiz.stem: Which document should contain the full NAT table and every VPN parameter?

options.text: The low-level design (LLD)
High-level design (HLD)
options.why_wrong: The HLD is for approval; details go in the LLD.

options.text: The statement of work (SOW)
options.why_wrong: The SOW defines scope, not configuration.

options.text: The acceptance test plan (ATP)
options.why_wrong: The ATP tests results; it doesn't hold the build parameters.

quiz.explanation: LLD is the build document.

quiz.stem: "The ISP circuit for the branch wasn't delivered and cutover is next week." In a RAID log, this is…

options.text: An issue, since it's happening now
Risk, since cutover hasn't failed
options.why_wrong: The missing circuit already happened; that makes it an issue.

options.text: An assumption that the ISP will deliver
options.why_wrong: It's a fact now, not something you rely on.

options.text: A dependency to add to the project plan
options.why_wrong: The circuit was a dependency; once missed it's tracked as an issue.

quiz.explanation: Issue, with owner and due date.

quiz.stem: The cutover might slip because the customer's change board meets monthly. What status do you report this week?

options.text: Amber on schedule, with the reason and the decision needed
Green until it slips, to avoid alarming the sponsor early
options.why_wrong: That creates a surprise later.

options.text: Red now, since any slip means the date can't be met at all
options.why_wrong: It's a risk, not yet a failure.

options.text: Green, with the change board listed in the risk log instead
options.why_wrong: Logging it is right, but the status should reflect the risk too.

quiz.explanation: Amber early.

quiz.stem: The customer asks: 'While you're here, can you also set up the guest Wi-Fi?' It's not in the SOW. Good responses? Select all that apply.

options.text: Acknowledge the request positively
Explain it's outside the SOW, estimate it
Offer a change request or follow-up
Do it quietly tonight as a favour
options.why_wrong: Unbilled work sets expectations and hides cost.

options.text: Decline it to protect the timeline
options.why_wrong: Protects scope but damages the relationship; offer the path instead.

quiz.explanation: Helpful and controlled.

quiz.stem: Put the customer-story structure in order.
quiz.explanation: Problem, impact, approach, proof.

quiz.stem: The customer's architect insists on A-A HA where you recommended A-P. Best approach?

options.text: Compare both against their requirements with evidence, then document the choice
Decline to build A-A, as your company's design standard requires A-P for this case
options.why_wrong: It's their risk to take, with information.

options.text: Build A-A as asked and note your preference in the as-built for the record
options.why_wrong: You owe them your reasoning before the build, not after.

options.text: Escalate to their CIO so a senior decision-maker settles the disagreement
options.why_wrong: Try the technical discussion with evidence first.

quiz.explanation: Evidence, then a documented decision.

quiz.stem: Which principle does "templates in FortiManager and naming standards" serve?

options.text: Manageability
Resilience
options.why_wrong: Resilience is about surviving failures.

options.text: Standardisation
options.why_wrong: Templates do standardise, but the design principle served is manageability.

options.text: Visibility
options.why_wrong: Visibility is logging and alerts, not templates.

quiz.explanation: The customer must be able to operate it.

quiz.stem: A sponsor is angry about repeated outages and threatens to cancel. First move?

options.text: Listen, get the facts, find the cause behind the anger, then present a plan
Offer a service credit straight away to show that you take the outages seriously
options.why_wrong: May come later, but it doesn't fix the cause.

options.text: Explain the outages came from their changes, with the logs to prove it
options.why_wrong: Defensive; even if true, lead with listening and a plan.

options.text: Give them a day to calm down, then book a meeting to talk it through
options.why_wrong: Silence makes it worse; respond now.

quiz.explanation: Solve the problem, and the relationship follows.

scenarios.title: Raid: the project is drifting
scenarios.situation: Week 5 of an 8-week SD-WAN rollout for 25 branches. Only 6 branches are done. The customer's network lead is on leave, two ISP circuits are late, and the sponsor has just asked for "a quick status" before tomorrow's board meeting.
scenarios.ask: What do you send the sponsor tonight, and what do you change in the plan?
right_thinking: Honest RAG: schedule red or amber with clear reasons
Separate causes: customer dependency (lead on leave), third party (ISPs), your own pace
Offer options to recover: parallel branches, temporary delegate, re-sequence by circuit availability
Ask for the decisions you need
scenarios.what: A one-page status with options and decisions requested.
scenarios.why: The board will ask; the sponsor needs facts and a plan, not reassurance.
pitfalls: Reporting green
Blaming the customer
No options
scenarios.model_answer: I'd send a one-page status tonight. Schedule: red, 6 of 25 branches done against a plan of 15. Causes, factually: two ISP circuits late (owner: ISP, escalated), and approvals slowed while the network lead is on leave. Recovery options: re-sequence so we do branches with circuits ready first, run two branches per window instead of one, and a temporary delegate for approvals. With those, the new forecast is week 10, or week 9 if we get a delegate by Monday. Decisions needed: approve the delegate and the double windows. That gives the sponsor a clear story for the board and a plan, not just bad news.
scenarios.best_way: Red, with causes, options and a new forecast, and the two decisions we need from you.

scenarios.title: The design review that turns hostile
scenarios.situation: In your HLD review, the customer's security lead says: "This design is too complex, our team can't run it. Why did Fortinet sell us this?"
scenarios.ask: How do you respond in the meeting?
right_thinking: Don't defend the sale; engage with the concern
Manageability is a design principle: it's a valid requirement
Simplify where possible; offer knowledge transfer and runbooks
scenarios.what: A respectful, constructive reply and a design adjustment.
scenarios.why: A design the team can't run will fail after handover.
scenarios.model_answer: "That's an important point: if your team can't run it, it's not the right design. Which parts worry you most?" Then I'd look for simplifications, like fewer SD-WAN rules, A-P instead of A-A, templates in FortiManager, and add knowledge transfer and runbooks to the plan. I'd update the HLD with those changes and the reasons, so the decision is clear for everyone.
scenarios.best_way: If your team can't run it, it's not right. Tell me which parts worry you, and we'll simplify and plan knowledge transfer.

interview.question: How do you keep a project's stakeholders informed?
interview.model_answer: "A one-page weekly status at the same time each week: RAG for scope, schedule and budget, done and next, decisions needed, and the RAID highlights. I show amber early with the reason, so nobody is surprised. At Netskope I kept that rhythm across a portfolio: weekly status on open issues and quarterly reviews with executives in three languages."
interview.best_way: Weekly one-pager with RAG, decisions and RAID. Amber early, no surprises.

interview.question: Tell me about a time you had to deliver bad news to a customer.
interview.model_answer: "[Use a real case: for example, telling an account that the support backlog was blocking their rollout, while escalating it to the director of support.] Show: you told them early, with facts and a plan, you followed up visibly, and the relationship held because there were no surprises."
interview.best_way: Early, factual, with a plan, and visible follow-up.

interview.question: How do you handle a customer who keeps changing requirements?
interview.model_answer: "I welcome the change and make its cost visible. Check it against the SOW, explain the impact on time and effort, and raise a change request, or park it for a later phase. And I write down each decision. Customers usually appreciate it, because they can prioritise with real information."
interview.best_way: Welcome it, show the impact, change request or later phase, and write it down.

interview.question: What's the difference between an HLD and an LLD?
interview.model_answer: "The HLD is for approval: requirements, target architecture, key decisions and why, risks. The LLD is for building: every interface, IP, route, VPN, HA, SD-WAN, policy and NAT detail, plus the acceptance tests. A good LLD makes the MOP straightforward."
interview.best_way: HLD for approval, LLD for building.

interview.question: Tell me about turning around an unhappy customer.
interview.model_answer: "A named enterprise account escalated and was ready to leave. I treated it as a technical problem first: diagnosed and fixed the underlying issue, and with that credibility we restructured the agreement as a licence exchange instead of a cancellation, keeping more than 900 thousand dollars in contract value. Learning: fix the real problem and the relationship follows."
interview.best_way: Fixed the technical cause first; the escalation became a licence exchange, more than USD 900k kept.

field_reports.title: Speed of response is money
field_reports.body: IBM's 2026 report found organizations using security AI and automation extensively saved **USD 1.93 million** and **65 days** per breach. Good designs include the logging, alerting and runbooks that make fast response possible.
field_reports.source: IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026

modules.title: Executive storytelling with threat data: readouts, risk registers and saying no well
objectives: Structure an executive readout as bottom line, evidence, options and the ask
Turn the customer's own logs (FortiAnalyzer, FortiSIEM, FortiEDR) into risk statements, not counts

objectives.Use industry reports honestly: cite them, scope them, never let them replace the customer's data

objectives: Keep a risk register and handle scope creep and escalations without losing the customer
sources: PS practice; Verizon DBIR and IBM Cost of a Data Breach as public reference reports (cite the edition you use)
FortiAnalyzer and FortiSIEM report and dashboard features (FortiOS-family admin guides)

units.title: The shape of a readout
units.body:
Executives read the first sentence and decide whether to read the second. So:
1. **Bottom line** (one sentence): where they stand and what you need.
2. **Evidence** (three points at most), from *their* environment.
3. **Options** with cost, effort and the risk each one leaves.
4. **The ask**: a decision, an owner and a date.

Translate counts into consequences. "4.2 million blocked events" says nothing. "Two finance laptops talked to a
known command-and-control domain; the EDR stopped it on one, the other has no agent" is a risk they can act on.

:::recall
Q: What turns a log statistic into a risk statement?
A: Saying which business asset is exposed, how, and what happens if nothing changes.
:::

units.title: Using threat data honestly
units.body:
Industry reports are context, not proof. Use them to show a pattern is common, then show the customer's own
evidence that it applies to them.
- **Cite** report, edition and the exact figure; never round up to sound scarier.
- **Scope**: a global average cost doesn't predict a 300-person company's loss in another country.
- **Prefer their data**: FortiAnalyzer reports, FortiSIEM incidents, FortiEDR events, pentest findings.
- **No fear selling**: if their posture is good, say so; credibility is what gets the next project funded.

:::why
Q: Why lead with the customer's logs instead of a breach-cost statistic?
A: Their own evidence is specific and hard to dismiss; a global average invites "that's not us".
:::

units.title: Risk registers, scope creep and escalations
units.body:
A **risk register** row: risk, likelihood, impact, owner, mitigation, due date, status. Review it in every status
meeting; a risk with no owner is a risk you own.

**Scope creep** ("while you're here, can you also..."): say yes to the goal, route the work through **change
control** (effort, cost, date impact), and let the sponsor decide. Small favours that aren't recorded become
expected.

**Escalations**: facts first (what happened, impact, what's being done, next update time), no blame, one owner
for communication. Escalate early to your own manager; surprises are worse than bad news.

:::recall
Q: What four things go in the first message of an escalation?
A: What happened, the impact, what's being done, and when the next update comes.
:::

cards.back: Bottom line → evidence → options → the ask.
Name the asset, the exposure and the consequence.
Cite and scope it; let the customer's data carry the argument.
Risk, likelihood, impact, owner, mitigation, due date, status.
Yes to the goal, change request for the work, sponsor decides.
What happened, impact, actions, next update time.

quiz.stem: Which opening line best starts a five-minute readout to a CFO after a SOC assessment?

options.text: "Your detection covers the common attacks; one gap puts payroll at risk, and I need a decision on it."
"FortiSIEM processed 38 million events this month and raised 412 incidents across your sites."
options.why_wrong: Real data, but counts without consequence give the CFO nothing to decide.

options.text: "Industry studies put the average breach cost in the millions, so investment here pays back fast."
options.why_wrong: A global average isn't their risk; it invites 'that's not us'.

options.text: "Let me walk you through our methodology first, so that the findings that follow have the right context."
options.why_wrong: Method belongs in the appendix; executives need the bottom line first.

quiz.explanation: Bottom line first: where they stand, what's at stake, what you need.

quiz.stem: A FortiAnalyzer report shows 9,000 blocked malicious URLs a month. How do you present it to the board?

options.text: As proof the web filter is working, plus the few users who clicked through and why that matters
As 9,000 attacks stopped each month, which shows the value of the security budget they approved
options.why_wrong: Blocked URLs aren't attacks; inflating them costs credibility when questioned.

options.text: As a trend chart over twelve months with the top categories and the top users for each of them
options.why_wrong: Useful in the appendix; the board needs what it means, not the chart.

options.text: As a sign of rising risk that justifies adding sandboxing and DNS filtering at the branch sites
options.why_wrong: Maybe true, but a recommendation needs evidence of a gap, not a count of blocks.

quiz.explanation: Blocks show a control working; the risk lives in what got through.

quiz.stem: Mid-project, the customer's IT manager asks you to 'also set up the new branch while you're on site' — not in the SOW. First step?

options.text: Say you'd like to help, estimate the effort, and raise a change request for the sponsor
Do it this week as goodwill, since it's small and it builds the relationship with the IT team
options.why_wrong: Unrecorded favours become expected and hide the real effort from your own team.

options.text: Decline politely, as the SOW is signed and the branch isn't part of this project
options.why_wrong: Saying no to the goal damages the relationship; route it through change control instead.

options.text: Ask your sales rep to quote a new project, then pause until the paperwork arrives
options.why_wrong: Sales may help later; the first step is the change process with the sponsor.

quiz.explanation: Yes to the goal, change control for the work, the sponsor decides.

quiz.stem: Order the parts of a first escalation message after a failed cutover.
items: What is being done and by whom
When the next update will come
quiz.explanation: Facts, impact, action, next update. Causes and blame wait for the review.

quiz.stem: Which belong in a risk register row? Select all that apply.

options.text: A named owner for the risk
The mitigation and its due date
Likelihood and impact ratings
The engineer who found the risk
options.why_wrong: Nice to know, but the owner is who acts; finders aren't tracked.

options.text: The vendor's product SKU to buy
options.why_wrong: A mitigation isn't a purchase order; that belongs in a proposal.

quiz.explanation: Owner, mitigation, due date, likelihood and impact make a risk manageable.

scenarios.title: The CISO wants scary numbers
scenarios.situation: A CISO asks you to put a slide in the board deck saying 'we face 1,000 attacks a day', based on IPS blocks. Most are internet scans.
scenarios.ask: How do you handle it?
right_thinking: Support the goal (budget) without inflating
Offer a stronger, true message: what was blocked that mattered, what got through, what the gap costs
Point out the credibility risk if a board member asks
scenarios.what: A truer message that still makes the case.
scenarios.why: Inflated numbers get questioned and cost the CISO credibility.
scenarios.model_answer: "I want to help you get the budget, and I think we can make a stronger case. Most of those blocks are internet-wide scans, so if someone on the board asks, the number won't hold. What will hold is this: two exploit attempts against the VPN that IPS stopped, the unpatched server that one of them targeted, and what an outage there would cost. I can draft that slide for you today."
scenarios.best_way: Same goal, true evidence, offer to draft.

interview.question: Tell me how you'd present security findings to an executive who isn't technical.
interview.model_answer: "I start with one sentence: where they stand and what I need from them. Then three pieces of evidence from their own environment, in business terms — which asset, what could happen. Then two or three options with cost and the risk each leaves, and a clear ask with a date. My QBRs with C-level customers at Netskope taught me that executives read the first line and decide whether to keep reading."
interview.best_way: Bottom line first, their evidence, options, a dated ask.

modules.title: IPsec VPN on FortiGate: build, verify and troubleshoot
objectives: Explain phase 1 and phase 2 in plain words and say which settings must match on both sides
Build a route-based site-to-site tunnel with routes, blackhole route and policies in both directions
Choose modern proposals and DH groups, and justify IKEv2
Read diagnose vpn output and an IKE debug to find the failing step
Talk a customer through a tunnel that is up but passes no traffic
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: General IPsec VPN configuration, phase 1 (pp. 3128–3143), phase 2 (pp. 3168–3171)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: FortiGate-to-FortiGate site-to-site with the VPN Wizard (pp. 3247–3252)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: VPN IPsec troubleshooting, logs and diagnose commands (pp. 3754–3768)

units.title: Two phases, one tunnel
units.body:
An IPsec tunnel is built in two steps.

**Phase 1 (IKE SA)** is the two gateways agreeing to talk securely: who the peer is (`remote-gw`), how they authenticate (pre-shared key or certificates), which **IKE version**, and the **proposals** (encryption + hash) and **Diffie-Hellman groups** they accept (pp. 3129–3140). IKE uses **UDP 500**, and **UDP 4500** when NAT traversal is in use.

**Phase 2 (IPsec SA, "quick mode")** is the agreement for the actual traffic: the **selectors** (which local and remote networks), the phase 2 proposals, **PFS**, replay detection and key lifetime (pp. 3168–3170). In tunnel mode the original packet is encrypted inside ESP with a new IP header.

## Must match on both sides

- Phase 1: IKE version, at least **one proposal**, at least **one DH group**, the authentication method and key.
- Phase 2: at least one proposal and DH group (if PFS), and **mirror-image selectors** (my local = your remote).

## IKEv1 or IKEv2

Both are supported. IKEv1 uses XAuth for user authentication; IKEv2 uses EAP and can run over TCP. **New tunnels default to IKEv2** (p. 3142). Use IKEv2 unless the peer can't.

## Strong choices

The guide marks NULL, DES, 3DES, MD5 and SHA1 as **not recommended**; AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are IKEv2-only; Fortinet recommends **DH groups 15–21 and 28–32** (pp. 3169–3170). By default the CLI only shows recommended IKE proposals (`ike-proposal-visibility`, p. 3139).

:::recall
Q: Phase 1 is up but phase 2 never comes up. What's the first thing to compare?
A: The phase 2 selectors (local/remote subnets must mirror each other) and the phase 2 proposals/PFS groups.
:::

units.title: Route-based site to site, the complete build
units.body:
On FortiGate the normal design is **route-based**: phase 1 is an interface (`phase1-interface`), and routing decides what enters the tunnel. The VPN Wizard's site-to-site template creates everything a working tunnel needs (pp. 3250–3251):

1. `config vpn ipsec phase1-interface`: interface, `ike-version 2`, `remote-gw`, `psksecret`, proposals.
2. `config vpn ipsec phase2-interface`: proposals and selectors.
3. **A static route** to the remote subnet with `device` = the tunnel interface.
4. **A blackhole route** to the same subnet with **distance 254**, so that when the tunnel is down the traffic is dropped instead of leaking out the default route in clear text.
5. **Two firewall policies**: LAN → tunnel and tunnel → LAN.

Forgetting steps 3–5 is the most common reason a tunnel is "up" but nothing works: IPsec builds the pipe, **routing and policy** decide whether anything uses it.

## Keeping it alive

- **DPD (dead peer detection):** `set dpd on-idle | on-demand`, with `dpd-retrycount` and `dpd-retryinterval` (p. 3140), so a dead peer is detected and the tunnel renegotiates.
- **add-route** (enabled by default) adds routes to the peer's selectors automatically, mainly useful for dial-up tunnels (p. 3141).
- `auto-negotiate` keeps phase 2 up without waiting for traffic.

:::cli
config router static
    edit 20
        set dst 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set device "to-branch"
    next
    edit 21
        set dst 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set blackhole enable
        set distance 254
    next
end
:::

:::pitfall
An MTU problem looks like a VPN problem: small pings work, file copies and web pages hang. ESP adds overhead, so clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel policy (`tcp-mss-sender` / `tcp-mss-receiver`), exactly as in the transport module.
:::

units.title: Reading what the FortiGate tells you
units.body:
Work bottom-up: is IKE reaching the peer, did phase 1 come up, did phase 2 come up, does traffic use it?

## Summary first

- `get vpn ipsec tunnel summary`: every tunnel, up/down, selectors up.
- `diagnose vpn ike gateway list`: **phase 1**: peer address and port (`:4500` means NAT-T), IKE version, negotiated **proposal**, `status: established`, DPD counters (pp. 3757–3758).
- `diagnose vpn tunnel list`: **phase 2**: `status=up`, the proxy ID **selectors** (`src:` / `dst:`), packet counters `rxp`/`txp`, DPD and NAT-T state (pp. 3758–3759).

If `txp` grows and `rxp` stays at zero, you're sending into the tunnel and nothing comes back: check the peer's routes and policies, not your phase 1.

## The IKE debug

:::cli
diagnose vpn ike log filter rem-addr4 203.0.113.10
diagnose debug application ike -1
diagnose debug enable
...bring the tunnel up...
diagnose debug disable
diagnose debug reset
:::

Always filter by the peer (p. 3761); on a busy hub an unfiltered IKE debug is unreadable. In the output, look for the **negotiation result** and **proposal** lines, `PSK authentication succeeded`, NAT detection, then the phase 2 **selectors** (p. 3762). A proposal mismatch typically shows as *no proposal chosen*; a wrong key fails at authentication.

## Logs

VPN event logs mirror the steps: *Progress IPsec phase 1* (negotiate → DONE), *IPsec connection status changed* (tunnel-up), *Progress IPsec phase 2*, *IPsec SA installed* with the SPIs, and tunnel-down or *phase 1 SA deleted* when it fails (pp. 3755–3756).

Sniff the control plane when nothing arrives: `diagnose sniffer packet any 'host 203.0.113.10 and (port 500 or port 4500)' 4`.

:::recall
Q: Which command shows the phase 2 selectors and packet counters?
A: diagnose vpn tunnel list.
:::

units.title: Remote access, and the consultant's view
units.body:
## Remote access in FortiOS 8.0

In 8.0 the browser-based SSL VPN portal is called **Agentless VPN**, and full-tunnel remote access is covered under **IPsec VPN** (dial-up, typically with FortiClient). Use IKEv2 for FortiClient 7.4.4 and later (p. 3142). Dial-up tunnels create a **dynamic instance per client** (`name_0`, `name_1` in `diagnose vpn ike gateway list`).

## Questions to ask before you build

- What's on each side: subnets, overlaps (overlapping subnets need NAT), and who manages the far end?
- Third-party peer? Agree a written parameter sheet: IKE version, proposals, DH groups, lifetimes, selectors, PSK delivery method.
- Redundancy: one tunnel per ISP? Then it belongs in **SD-WAN** (next module) with health checks.
- Security: which services cross the tunnel? A tunnel is a trust path; policies on it should be as tight as on the internet edge.

:::threat
Internet-facing VPN gateways are prime targets. In the 2026 DBIR, exploitation of vulnerabilities was the top initial access vector (31 %), and only 26 % of known-exploited vulnerabilities were fully remediated. Patch edge devices quickly, limit who can reach IKE with local-in policies (p. 3242), and keep strong proposals.
:::

:::ps
In a third-party tunnel the problem is usually a mismatch nobody wrote down. The parameter sheet is the deliverable that prevents the 2 a.m. call.
:::

cards.back: The IKE SA: peer identity, authentication, IKE version, proposals and DH group.
The IPsec SA for traffic: selectors, proposals, PFS, replay detection, key lifetime.
UDP 500; UDP 4500 with NAT traversal.
IKEv1 uses XAuth; IKEv2 uses EAP. New FortiGate tunnels default to IKEv2.

cards.front: Algorithms the guide marks not recommended?
cards.back: NULL, DES, 3DES, MD5, SHA1.
AES128GCM, AES256GCM, CHACHA20POLY1305.

cards.front: Five parts of a working route-based site-to-site VPN?
cards.back: Phase 1 interface, phase 2, static route via tunnel, blackhole route (distance 254), two policies.

cards.front: Why a blackhole route with distance 254?
cards.back: When the tunnel is down, traffic for the remote subnet is dropped instead of leaking out the default route unencrypted.
on-idle or on-demand (or disable), with dpd-retrycount and dpd-retryinterval.

cards.front: What does add-route do, and its default?
cards.back: Adds routes to the peer's selectors (mainly dial-up); enabled by default.

cards.front: Small pings work, big transfers hang over the VPN?
cards.back: MTU/MSS. Clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel policies.

cards.front: Quick list of all tunnels and their state?
cards.back: get vpn ipsec tunnel summary

cards.front: Command for phase 1 status and negotiated proposal?
cards.back: diagnose vpn ike gateway list

cards.front: Command for phase 2 selectors and rxp/txp counters?
cards.back: diagnose vpn tunnel list
diagnose vpn ike log filter rem-addr4 <peer IP>

cards.front: txp increasing, rxp stuck at 0. Meaning?
cards.back: You send into the tunnel but nothing returns: check the peer's routes, policies and selectors.

cards.front: FortiOS 8.0 name for browser-based SSL VPN?
cards.back: Agentless VPN. Full-tunnel remote access is under IPsec VPN.

cards.front: What should a third-party tunnel always have?
cards.back: A written parameter sheet: IKE version, proposals, DH, lifetimes, selectors, PSK handling.

quiz.stem: Which phase negotiates the selectors (local and remote subnets)?

options.text: Phase 2, quick mode or CHILD_SA
Phase 1, along with the IKE SA
options.why_wrong: Phase 1 builds the IKE SA; selectors belong to phase 2.

options.text: Routing, via the tunnel interface
options.why_wrong: Routing decides what enters the tunnel; selectors are negotiated in phase 2.

options.text: The firewall policy for the tunnel
options.why_wrong: Policies allow traffic; they aren't negotiated with the peer.

quiz.explanation: Selectors are phase 2.

quiz.stem: A route-based site-to-site tunnel is up, but no traffic passes. Which could be missing? Select all that apply.

options.text: A route to the remote subnet via the tunnel
A firewall policy from LAN to the tunnel
A policy from the tunnel to LAN, on both ends
A phase 2 with PFS enabled on both ends
options.why_wrong: PFS must match to negotiate, but the tunnel is already up.

options.text: A higher HA priority on the tunnel unit
options.why_wrong: HA has nothing to do with traffic through an up tunnel.

quiz.explanation: IPsec builds the pipe; routes and policies make traffic use it.

quiz.stem: Why does the VPN Wizard add a blackhole route with distance 254?

options.text: So remote-subnet traffic is dropped, not leaked in clear, while the tunnel is down
So the tunnel route wins, since 254 is lower than the distance of the default static route
options.why_wrong: 254 is the highest usable distance; it's the fallback, not the winner.

options.text: So IKE traffic from the internet to the tunnel's local gateway gets dropped early on
options.why_wrong: Blocking IKE is a local-in policy job, not a route.

options.text: So two tunnels to the same subnet share load through ECMP at the same distance
options.why_wrong: That's SD-WAN or ECMP; the blackhole is a leak guard.

quiz.explanation: A safety net against leaks.

quiz.stem: Which DH groups does Fortinet recommend as best practice?

options.text: Groups 15–21 and 28–32
Groups 1, 2 and 5 for speed
options.why_wrong: These are old and weak groups.

options.text: Group 14 for compatibility
options.why_wrong: Allowed, but the guide recommends 15–21 and 28–32.

options.text: Groups 14 and 5 as a fallback
options.why_wrong: Group 5 is weak; a fallback to it undermines the stronger group.

quiz.explanation: Strong groups.

quiz.stem: Which UDP port does IKE move to when NAT traversal is used?
quiz.explanation: UDP 500 normally, 4500 with NAT-T.

quiz.stem: Which command shows the negotiated phase 1 proposal and whether the IKE SA is established?

options.text: diagnose vpn ike gateway list
diagnose vpn tunnel list name x
options.why_wrong: That's phase 2: selectors and counters.

options.text: get vpn ipsec tunnel summary
options.why_wrong: Summarises tunnels and selectors up or down, not the phase 1 proposal.

options.text: diagnose sys session list ike
options.why_wrong: The session table doesn't hold IKE SAs.

quiz.explanation: gateway list = phase 1.

quiz.output:
name=to-branch ver=2 serial=3 192.0.2.1:0->203.0.113.10:0 status=up
proxyid=to-branch proto=0 sa=1 ref=3 serial=1
  src: 0:10.10.0.0-10.10.0.255:0
  dst: 0:10.20.0.0-10.20.0.255:0
stat: rxp=0 txp=4821 rxb=0 txb=385680
quiz.stem: Users at HQ can't reach the branch. What does this output suggest?

options.text: Phase 2 is up and HQ sends traffic, but nothing returns: check the branch's route and policy
Phase 1 is down, so the encrypted packets are queued at HQ and don't leave the FortiGate at all
options.why_wrong: status=up, an SA exists and txb grows.

options.text: The selectors leave the branch subnet out, so the branch's FortiGate drops all of the packets
options.why_wrong: dst covers 10.20.0.0/24, which is the branch subnet.

options.text: NAT-T is failing, so ESP leaves HQ but the ISP drops it before it reaches the branch peer
options.why_wrong: The port shows :0, so no NAT-T is in use; check the far side's return path first.

quiz.explanation: txp grows, rxp is zero.

quiz.stem: Put the safe IKE debug in order.
items: diagnose vpn ike log filter rem-addr4 <peer>
quiz.explanation: Filter first, enable, reproduce, then disable.

quiz.stem: Phase 1 comes up with a third-party firewall, but phase 2 keeps failing. Most likely cause?

options.text: Selectors that don't mirror each other, or mismatched phase 2 proposals or PFS
A wrong pre-shared key, which phase 2 checks again once the IKE SA has been built
options.why_wrong: A wrong key fails phase 1 authentication.

options.text: Mismatched DH groups in phase 1, which surface during phase 2 negotiation
options.why_wrong: Phase 1 DH mismatches fail phase 1; PFS groups are the phase 2 part.

options.text: A missing blackhole route, which makes the FortiGate reject the CHILD_SA
options.why_wrong: Blackhole routes prevent leaks; they don't affect negotiation.

quiz.explanation: Phase 2 mismatch: selectors, proposals, PFS.

quiz.stem: Which IKE version do new FortiGate tunnels use by default?

options.text: IKEv2
IKEv1 main
options.why_wrong: Still supported, but not the default for new tunnels.

options.text: IKEv1 aggr.
options.why_wrong: Aggressive mode isn't the default.

options.text: Per model
options.why_wrong: New tunnels default to IKEv2 on all models.

quiz.explanation: IKEv2 by default.

quiz.stem: Over a new tunnel, ping and SSH work, but SMB file copies and some HTTPS pages freeze. Best fix?

options.text: Clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel policies, and check ICMP 'fragmentation needed'
Change the DH group on both ends so that the SAs renegotiate with fresh keys
options.why_wrong: Negotiation is fine; data flows.

options.text: Lower the tunnel interface MTU on one end and leave the other as it is
options.why_wrong: Helps one direction; clamping MSS on both directions is the reliable fix.

options.text: Add a second phase 2 for the file servers' subnet with its own selectors
options.why_wrong: Selectors are fine; this is packet size.

quiz.explanation: ESP overhead plus blocked PMTUD.

quiz.stem: Two sites both use 192.168.1.0/24 and must be connected. What do you tell the customer?

options.text: Overlapping subnets need NAT across the tunnel, or re-addressing
IKEv2 traffic selector narrowing separates the two subnets for you
options.why_wrong: Narrowing can't tell identical subnets apart.

options.text: A policy route at each end sends the remote 192.168.1.0/24 to the tunnel
options.why_wrong: Local hosts still own that subnet; routing alone can't distinguish them.

options.text: Two phase 2s with the same selectors, one for each direction of traffic
options.why_wrong: Phase 2 already covers both directions; overlap remains.

quiz.explanation: Overlap is a design problem; plan NAT or re-addressing.

quiz.stem: In FortiOS 8.0, what is the browser-based SSL VPN portal called?

options.text: Agentless VPN
ZTNA web portal
options.why_wrong: ZTNA is a different access model.

options.text: Dial-up IPsec
options.why_wrong: That's full-tunnel remote access with a client.

options.text: Web mode VPN
options.why_wrong: Close to the old name, but 8.0 calls it Agentless VPN.

quiz.explanation: Agentless VPN.

quiz.stem: In a dial-up tunnel named 'remote', what does an entry named 'remote_0' in diagnose vpn ike gateway list represent?

options.text: A dynamic instance created for one connected client
A failed negotiation that is kept for troubleshooting later
options.why_wrong: Instances are created on connection, not failure.

options.text: The tunnel's phase 2, shown with its own numbering
options.why_wrong: Phase 2 shows in tunnel list as a proxy ID.

options.text: The first of the tunnel's redundant backup peers
options.why_wrong: Dial-up instance names count clients, not backup peers.

quiz.explanation: Each client gets its own instance.

labs.title: Build the HQ side of a route-based tunnel
labs.goal: HQ (LAN 10.10.0.0/24 on port2, WAN port1) connects to a branch at 203.0.113.10 protecting 10.20.0.0/24.

worked.config:
config vpn ipsec phase1-interface
    edit "to-branch"
        set interface "port1"
        set ike-version 2
        set peertype any
        set proposal aes256gcm-prfsha384 aes256-sha256
        set dhgrp 20 19
        set remote-gw 203.0.113.10
        set psksecret <strong-shared-key>
        set dpd on-idle
    next
end
config vpn ipsec phase2-interface
    edit "to-branch"
        set phase1name "to-branch"
        set proposal aes256gcm aes256-sha256
        set dhgrp 20 19
        set src-subnet 10.10.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set dst-subnet 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set auto-negotiate enable
    next
end
config router static
    edit 20
        set dst 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set device "to-branch"
    next
    edit 21
        set dst 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set blackhole enable
        set distance 254
    next
end
config firewall policy
    edit 0
        set name "HQ-to-branch"
        set srcintf "port2"
        set dstintf "to-branch"
        set srcaddr "HQ-LAN"
        set dstaddr "BRANCH-LAN"
        set action accept
        set schedule "always"
        set service "ALL"
    next
    edit 0
        set name "branch-to-HQ"
        set srcintf "to-branch"
        set dstintf "port2"
        set srcaddr "BRANCH-LAN"
        set dstaddr "HQ-LAN"
        set action accept
        set schedule "always"
        set service "ALL"
    next
end
notes: The branch mirrors it: its src-subnet is 10.20.0.0/24 and dst-subnet 10.10.0.0/24.
Tighten service ALL to what the business needs once it works.
No NAT on the tunnel policies: both sides route real addresses.

faded.template:
config vpn ipsec {{phase1-interface}}
    edit "to-branch"
        set ike-version {{2}}
        set {{remote-gw}} 203.0.113.10
    next
end
config router static
    edit 21
        set dst 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set {{blackhole}} enable
        set distance {{254}}
    next
end

solo.prompt: Write the branch's phase 2 selectors and its two static routes (tunnel route and blackhole) for the HQ LAN 10.10.0.0/24, tunnel name to-hq.
solo.solution:
config vpn ipsec phase2-interface
    edit "to-hq"
        set phase1name "to-hq"
        set src-subnet 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set dst-subnet 10.10.0.0 255.255.255.0
    next
end
config router static
    edit 10
        set dst 10.10.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set device "to-hq"
    next
    edit 11
        set dst 10.10.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set blackhole enable
        set distance 254
    next
end
solo.notes: Selectors mirror HQ's exactly.

labs.title: Troubleshoot a tunnel that won't come up
labs.goal: The branch tunnel to 203.0.113.10 is down. Check summary, phase 1, phase 2, then debug IKE for this peer only.

worked.config:
# get vpn ipsec tunnel summary
# diagnose vpn ike gateway list name to-branch
# diagnose vpn tunnel list name to-branch
# diagnose sniffer packet any 'host 203.0.113.10 and (port 500 or port 4500)' 4 20
# diagnose vpn ike log filter rem-addr4 203.0.113.10
# diagnose debug application ike -1
# diagnose debug enable
...bring the tunnel up...
# diagnose debug disable
# diagnose debug reset

In the debug, read proposal → authentication → selectors, in that order.
Always reset debug at the end.

scenarios.title: The partner's tunnel: 'it's your side'
scenarios.situation: A customer's FortiGate must build a tunnel to a supplier's third-party firewall. Phase 1 is up. Phase 2 fails. The supplier's engineer says, "Our side is fine, it's your FortiGate."
scenarios.ask: How do you get it working without a blame game?
right_thinking: Phase 1 up means reachability, key and phase 1 proposals are fine
Phase 2 failures are selectors, proposals or PFS
Get evidence from your side (debug) and ask for theirs
Agree a written parameter sheet both sides sign off
scenarios.what: A matched phase 2 and a documented parameter sheet.
scenarios.why: Third-party tunnels fail on unwritten assumptions; evidence ends the argument.
how: Filtered IKE debug: read the phase 2 selectors and proposals we send and receive
Share the exact values; ask for their proposal and selector config
Fix the mismatch (commonly subnet mask or PFS group)
Document the final parameters for both teams
scenarios.model_answer: I'd keep it factual. Phase 1 is up, so reachability, the key and phase 1 are fine; the issue is phase 2. I'd run a filtered IKE debug and read the selectors and proposals we send and what they answer. Then I'd send the supplier a short table: our local and remote subnets, our proposals and PFS group, and ask for theirs. Usually it's a mask, like a /24 against a /23, or PFS on one side only. Once it's up, both teams sign off the same parameter sheet so the next change doesn't break it.
could_have_added: Offer a quick joint call with both screens on the debug
scenarios.best_way: Phase 1 is fine, so it's phase 2: here are our selectors and proposals from the debug, please share yours.

scenarios.title: Tunnel up, users still complaining
scenarios.situation: The tunnel shows up on both sides. Branch users can open the HQ intranet homepage, but uploading files to SharePoint on-prem hangs.
scenarios.ask: What do you suspect and how do you prove it?
right_thinking: Some traffic works, so routing, policies and selectors are fine
Large transfers failing = packet size
Prove with ping using DF and sizes, or a sniffer
Fix with MSS clamping on the tunnel policies
scenarios.what: An MTU/MSS diagnosis and fix.
scenarios.why: It's the classic "VPN works but doesn't" problem.
how: Ping with DF bit and decreasing size
Set tcp-mss on both tunnel policies
scenarios.model_answer: Since small requests work, the tunnel, routes and policies are fine. Big uploads hanging points at packet size: ESP adds overhead, so full-size packets don't fit, and if ICMP "fragmentation needed" is blocked somewhere, the hosts never learn it. I'd prove it with pings with the don't-fragment bit at decreasing sizes, then clamp the TCP MSS on both tunnel policies, for example around 1350, and retest the upload with the user.
scenarios.best_way: Small works, big hangs: packet size. Prove with DF pings, clamp MSS on the tunnel policies.

scenarios.title: What if the customer wants 3DES "for compatibility"?
scenarios.situation: An old partner device only supports 3DES-SHA1. The customer asks you to just enable it.
scenarios.ask: How do you respond?
right_thinking: Don't silently lower security; the guide marks 3DES and SHA1 not recommended
Offer options: upgrade or replace the partner device, limit the tunnel's scope, time-box the exception
Get the risk accepted in writing if they insist
scenarios.what: A risk-aware recommendation.
scenarios.why: A consultant protects the customer from quiet risk, even when it's what they asked for.
how: If accepted: narrow selectors, strict policies, review date, written acceptance
scenarios.model_answer: I'd explain that Fortinet's own guide marks 3DES and SHA1 as not recommended, so this weakens the tunnel. The best path is for the partner to upgrade their device. If that can't happen now, we can limit the risk: a separate tunnel just for that partner, narrow selectors, tight policies, and a review date. And I'd ask the customer to approve the exception in writing, so it's a decision, not an accident.
scenarios.best_way: It's not recommended. Best fix is the partner's upgrade; otherwise a narrow, time-boxed exception with written approval.

interview.question: Explain phase 1 and phase 2 to me as if I were a customer's manager.
interview.framework: Analogy → what must match → why it fails
interview.model_answer: "Phase 1 is the two firewalls proving who they are and agreeing how to talk privately, like two people agreeing a secure phone line. Phase 2 is agreeing what will travel on that line: which networks, and how it's encrypted. Both sides must agree on the details, and most tunnel failures are one detail that doesn't match, often in phase 2, like a subnet."
interview.best_way: Phase 1 is a secure line between the firewalls; phase 2 is what travels on it. Most failures are one detail that doesn't match.

interview.question: A tunnel is up but traffic doesn't pass. How do you troubleshoot?
interview.framework: Layers: routing → policy → selectors → counters → peer
interview.model_answer: "Up only means IPsec is built. I check that there's a route to the remote subnet via the tunnel, policies in both directions, and that the selectors include the hosts. Then diagnose vpn tunnel list: if txp increases and rxp is zero, I'm sending and the peer isn't answering, so I look at their route and policy back. A debug flow on our side confirms which policy and route the packet takes."
interview.best_way: Route, policies both ways, selectors, then counters. txp without rxp means look at the peer.

interview.question: Why does FortiGate add a blackhole route for VPN subnets?
interview.model_answer: "If the tunnel drops, the route via the tunnel disappears and traffic for the remote subnet would follow the default route to the internet, unencrypted. A blackhole route with distance 254 stays in the table and drops it instead. The VPN Wizard adds it automatically."
interview.best_way: So traffic is dropped, not leaked in clear text, when the tunnel is down.

interview.question: Which proposals and DH groups would you configure today, and why IKEv2?
interview.model_answer: "IKEv2 with AES-GCM, for example aes256gcm, and DH groups in Fortinet's recommended range, like 19, 20 or 21. IKEv2 is the default for new tunnels, it supports EAP and modern ciphers like GCM and ChaCha20, and it's what current FortiClient versions expect. I'd avoid 3DES, SHA1 and the old DH groups."
interview.best_way: IKEv2, AES-GCM, DH 19–21; no 3DES or SHA1.

interview.question: Tell me about a time you resolved a VPN problem for a customer.
interview.model_answer: "[Use a real Fortinet TAC case.] Structure it: situation (who, impact), the evidence you gathered (summary, gateway list, tunnel list, filtered IKE debug), the root cause in one sentence, the fix, and what you did so it wouldn't recur, such as documenting parameters or adding MSS clamping to the template."
could_have_added: Mention the customer outcome and CSAT if you have it
interview.best_way: Evidence first, one-line root cause, fix, prevention.

field_reports.title: VPN gateways are on the front line
field_reports.body: Exploitation of vulnerabilities was the **top initial access vector (31 %)** in the 2026 DBIR, and only **26 %** of known-exploited vulnerabilities were fully remediated in the period studied. Internet-facing VPN and firewall interfaces are exactly where those exploits land: patch fast and restrict who can reach IKE.
field_reports.source: Verizon 2026 DBIR

field_reports.title: Third parties extend your attack surface
field_reports.body: Third-party involvement appeared in **48 %** of breaches in the 2026 DBIR. Partner tunnels are third-party connections: narrow selectors and tight policies limit what a compromised partner can reach.
field_reports.source: Verizon 2026 DBIR

modules.title: High availability: FGCP clusters, failover and upgrades
objectives: Explain FGCP, FGSP and VRRP and when each one fits
Predict which unit becomes primary, with and without override
Design heartbeat, monitored interfaces and session pickup for a customer's real failure modes
Upgrade a cluster with the right upgrade mode and verify it afterwards
Diagnose split brain and out-of-sync clusters calmly, from the console
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: High Availability overview and FGCP (pp. 4556–4559), primary selection and override (pp. 4561–4567), A-P / A-A setup (pp. 4567–4571)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: A-A load balancing (pp. 4583–4586), heartbeat (pp. 4586–4597), session failover (pp. 4598–4615)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: management interfaces (pp. 4620–4626), upgrades (pp. 4638–4640), troubleshooting (pp. 4701–4716)

units.title: Three ways to stay up
units.body:
A FortiGate carrying critical traffic is a single point of failure. The guide lists three HA answers (pp. 4556–4557):

- **FGCP (FortiGate Clustering Protocol):** the classic cluster. Two or more FortiGates of the **same model, firmware and hardware** negotiate a cluster and share one configuration; only the **hostname and the HA priority** differ. Modes: **active-passive (A-P)** and **active-active (A-A)**.
- **FGSP (Session Life Support Protocol):** for networks that already have **external load balancers or routers** spreading sessions; FGSP only synchronizes sessions (TCP, UDP, ICMP, NAT, expectation) between peers.
- **VRRP:** standard first-hop redundancy, versions 2 and 3, also with third-party routers.

## How FGCP keeps one brain

- Members talk over **heartbeat interfaces**. Fortinet recommends **two back-to-back heartbeat links** in a two-member cluster (p. 4557).
- All synchronization runs over the heartbeat link on **TCP/703 and UDP/703** (p. 4559).
- The primary owns the cluster's **virtual MAC addresses** and IPs. After a failover the new primary sends **gratuitous ARP** so switches learn the new path (p. 4564).
- All cluster members must be registered under the **same FortiCare account**, or you get licensing issues (p. 4557).

:::recall
Q: Which two settings may differ between FGCP members?
A: The hostname and the HA (device) priority. Everything else is synchronized.
:::

:::delta
Customers with an external load balancer in front of two FortiGates don't need FGCP: that is the FGSP use case.
:::

units.title: Who becomes primary
units.body:
Primary election is the most-tested HA topic and the first thing a customer asks after a failover. The order depends on **override** (pp. 4562–4563):

| override | Order (first difference wins) | Mnemonic |
|---|---|---|
| disabled (default) | Connected **M**onitored interfaces → HA **U**ptime → **P**riority → **S**erial number | MUPS |
| enabled | Connected **M**onitored interfaces → **P**riority → HA **U**ptime → **S**erial number | MPUS |

Details that matter in the field:

- **Priority:** 0–255, **default 128**, higher wins (pp. 4561, 4576).
- **Uptime tie:** uptimes within **300 seconds** count as a tie (`ha-uptime-diff-margin` changes it). A **monitored-interface failure or a reboot resets that unit's uptime to zero** (p. 4563).
- **Override:** make it the same on all members; mixing it causes unpredictable elections (p. 4561). With override enabled, the higher-priority unit takes over again as soon as it comes back, which means a **second failover**.
- **override-wait-time** (0–3600 s, default 0, not synchronized) delays that takeover after a reboot so the returning unit can sync first. From 8.0.1, during the wait the unit with the longest uptime stays primary (pp. 4563–4564).

:::cli
# get system ha status
...
Primary selected using:
<...> vcluster-1: FG101F...7 is selected as the primary because its override priority is larger than peer member FG101F...8.
:::

"Primary selected using" is the history that answers *why* (p. 4566). `diagnose sys ha dump-by group` shows the uptime difference between members (p. 4567).

:::pitfall
With override disabled, raising the priority on the unit you want as primary does nothing while the other unit has more than 5 minutes more uptime. Uptime beats priority.
:::

:::recall
Q: Override disabled, both units have all monitored ports up, A has 2 h more uptime, B has priority 200. Who is primary?
A: A. Uptime is checked before priority when override is disabled (and the difference is above 300 s).
:::

units.title: Heartbeat, monitoring and session pickup
units.body:
## Heartbeat timing

`hb-interval` (default 2, in units of `hb-interval-in-milliseconds`, default 100 ms) and `hb-lost-threshold` (typically 6 on hardware and 20 on VMs; check with `get system ha | grep hb-lost-threshold`). The guide's example: 2 × 100 ms × 20 = **4 seconds** to declare a peer dead (p. 4593). Lower values give faster failover but more false positives.

`backup-hbdev` is used only when the secondary stops hearing the primary on the normal heartbeat links, to prevent split brain; configuration isn't synchronized while it's in use (pp. 4589–4590).

## What triggers a failover

- **Device failure:** heartbeats stop.
- **Link failure:** `set monitor port1 port2`. A monitored port going down on the primary moves the role.
- **Remote link failure:** `pingserver-monitor-interface` checks reachability of a remote IP through an interface (p. 4576).

## Session pickup

**Session failover (`session-pickup`) is not enabled by default** (p. 4598). Without it, a failover keeps the cluster up but **drops existing sessions**; users reconnect.

- `session-pickup enable`: synchronizes the TCP session table.
- `session-pickup-connectionless enable`: adds UDP and ICMP (p. 4602).
- `session-pickup-delay enable`: only sessions older than **30 seconds** are synced, which cuts load with many short HTTP sessions (p. 4607).

## Active-active

In A-A, the primary receives all traffic on the virtual MACs and uses a **load-balancing schedule** to hand sessions to the others; `load-balance-all` extends this to all TCP sessions (pp. 4583–4584). A-A adds complexity; for most customers A-P plus right-sizing is easier to operate.

:::why
Q: Why is session pickup off by default?
A: Synchronizing every session costs CPU and heartbeat bandwidth. It's a design decision per customer: enable it when long-lived sessions (VoIP, database, VPN) must survive a failover.
:::

:::tip
In a change plan, write the expected failover time and whether sessions survive, so the customer approves a measured behaviour, not a hope.
:::

units.title: Upgrades, management and the bad days
units.body:
## Upgrade modes (pp. 4638–4640)

`set upgrade-mode {simultaneous | uninterruptible | local-only | secondary-only}`

- **uninterruptible:** the subordinates are upgraded first, a new primary is chosen from the upgraded units, then the former primary is upgraded. Traffic keeps flowing. Simultaneous (interrupted) upgrade is **disabled by default**.
- **simultaneous:** all members at once. Faster, but an outage.
- **local-only / secondary-only:** advanced, manual staged upgrades (multi-version cluster) for testing one member before the rest.

Always check the supported upgrade path and book a window first.

## Managing each unit

- `execute ha manage <id> <username>` jumps to the other member's CLI (p. 4597, p. 4707).
- **Reserved management interfaces** (`ha-mgmt-status enable`, `config ha-mgmt-interfaces`) give each unit its own management IP; `ha-direct` lets services such as SNMP, syslog and FortiAnalyzer logging leave from each unit's own interface (pp. 4622–4625).

## Split brain (pp. 4702–4703)

Both units think they're primary and use the **same IP and virtual MAC**: switches flap, admin access is intermittent, traffic drops. Cause: **all heartbeat links lost**, or congested links that exceed the lost threshold.

Fix: get to the **console** (on-site if possible), check the heartbeat ports are physically up and passing heartbeats, check **mode, group-name, group-id and password** match, then confirm with `get system ha status`.

Prevent: back-to-back heartbeat cables, **redundant heartbeat interfaces**, and for geo-separated members, thresholds longer than the link latency.

## Out of sync (pp. 4707–4709)

`get system ha status` → **Configuration Status** shows in-sync / out-of-sync per serial and the checksums. The GUI HA monitor highlights the member in red; **Force resync** pushes the primary's config. `diagnose sys ha checksum cluster` is the classic CLI comparison.

`execute ha failover set <cluster_id>` forces a failover for **testing in a maintenance window only** (p. 4703).

:::threat
Downtime is a big share of breach cost: in IBM's 2026 report, detection and escalation plus lost business are 63 % of the cost of a breach. A cluster that fails over cleanly during an incident protects revenue as well as security.
:::

cards.back: Same model, same firmware, same hardware configuration; same FortiCare account. (p. 4557)

cards.front: What differs between FGCP members' configs?
cards.back: Only the hostname and the HA priority.
TCP/703 and UDP/703 over the heartbeat link. (p. 4559)

cards.front: When is FGSP the right choice?
cards.back: When external load balancers or routers already distribute sessions; FGSP only syncs sessions between peers.

cards.front: What does the new primary send after failover?
cards.back: Gratuitous ARP for the virtual MACs/IPs, so switches update their tables.

cards.front: Primary election order with override disabled?
cards.back: Monitored interfaces → uptime → priority → serial number (MUPS).

cards.front: Primary election order with override enabled?
cards.back: Monitored interfaces → priority → uptime → serial number (MPUS).
0–255, default 128; higher wins.

cards.front: Uptime difference treated as a tie?
cards.back: Less than 300 seconds (ha-uptime-diff-margin).

cards.front: What resets a unit's HA uptime?
cards.back: A monitored interface failing, or the unit restarting. (diagnose sys ha reset-uptime does it manually)
Delays a higher-priority unit's takeover after it reboots (0–3600 s, default 0, not synced) so it can sync first.

cards.front: Default heartbeat detection in the guide's example?
Is session pickup on by default?
cards.back: No. Without it, sessions drop on failover.

cards.front: Setting that adds UDP/ICMP session failover?
cards.back: session-pickup-connectionless enable.
Syncs only sessions older than 30 s, reducing load from short sessions.

cards.front: How do you fail over when a remote site is unreachable?
cards.back: Remote link monitoring: pingserver-monitor-interface.
Subordinates first → new primary chosen from upgraded units → former primary upgraded.
Console in; heartbeat ports physically up and passing heartbeats; mode, group-name, group-id and password match.

cards.front: Where do you see sync status in the CLI?
cards.back: get system ha status → Configuration Status (checksums per serial).

cards.front: Give each cluster unit its own management IP?
cards.back: Reserved management interface: ha-mgmt-status enable + config ha-mgmt-interfaces (ha-direct for services).

quiz.stem: Which pair is required for two FortiGates to form an FGCP cluster?

options.text: Same model and same firmware
Same hostname and same priority
options.why_wrong: Those are exactly the settings that can differ per unit.

options.text: Same model and same HA priority
options.why_wrong: Model yes, but priority is per unit; firmware must match.

options.text: Same firmware and one shared serial
options.why_wrong: Each unit keeps its own serial number.

quiz.explanation: Same model, firmware and hardware configuration.

quiz.stem: Put the primary-election criteria in order with override disabled (the default).
quiz.explanation: MUPS. With override enabled, priority moves above uptime (MPUS).

quiz.stem: Override disabled. Unit A: uptime 3 days, priority 128. Unit B: uptime 2 days, priority 250. Both have all monitored interfaces up. Who is primary?

options.text: A, as uptime is compared first and the gap is over 300 s
B, as priority 250 is higher than the default 128 on A
options.why_wrong: Priority decides first only when override is enabled.

options.text: A, but for 300 s, after which B takes over as the primary
options.why_wrong: Uptime keeps A primary; there's no timed handover.

options.text: The unit with the higher serial, since both links are fine
options.why_wrong: Serial is the last tiebreaker, after uptime and priority.

quiz.explanation: Uptime beats priority with override disabled.

quiz.stem: Override enabled on both units. The higher-priority primary reboots and comes back 5 minutes later. What happens by default?

options.text: It takes the primary role back, causing a second failover
It stays secondary until an admin intervenes on the cluster
options.why_wrong: That's the override-disabled behaviour, where uptime wins.

options.text: It waits for the override-wait-time of 300 s, then takes over
options.why_wrong: The override-wait-time setting defaults to 0.

options.text: Both units become primary until the heartbeats are resynced
options.why_wrong: That's split brain, a heartbeat failure, not override.

quiz.explanation: Use override-wait-time if you want it to sync before taking over.

quiz.stem: What is the default FortiGate HA device priority?
quiz.explanation: Range 0–255, default 128.

quiz.stem: After a failover, every user had to reconnect their VPN and SSH sessions. What was most likely missing?

options.text: set session-pickup enable
A second heartbeat interface
options.why_wrong: That prevents split brain; it doesn't preserve sessions.

options.text: set override enable on both
options.why_wrong: Override decides who's primary, not session survival.

options.text: set hb-lost-threshold higher
options.why_wrong: That changes detection time, not session sync.

quiz.explanation: Session failover is off by default; existing sessions drop without it.

quiz.stem: Which events can move the primary role? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heartbeats from the primary stop
A monitored port on the primary drops
A pingserver-monitored IP goes quiet
An admin logs in to the secondary
options.why_wrong: Logging in changes nothing about roles.

options.text: The secondary's uptime passes the primary's
options.why_wrong: Uptime is compared at elections; it doesn't trigger one by itself.

quiz.explanation: Device, link and remote-link failures.

quiz.stem: Both cluster units show 'Primary' in get system ha status from the console, and switches report MAC flapping. Best first step?

options.text: Check the heartbeat links pass heartbeats and group name, ID, mode and password match
Upgrade both units to the same patch release so the cluster can form again cleanly
options.why_wrong: Firmware mismatch prevents forming, but this was a working cluster; check heartbeats first.

options.text: Enable session-pickup so the users' sessions survive whichever unit ends up primary
options.why_wrong: Session pickup is unrelated to heartbeat loss.

options.text: Raise the priority on one unit with override enabled so that it wins the next election
options.why_wrong: They can't see each other, so priority isn't compared.

quiz.explanation: Split brain is a heartbeat problem first.

quiz.stem: In an uninterruptible cluster upgrade, which unit is upgraded first?

options.text: The secondary units
Primary unit first
options.why_wrong: The primary goes last, after a new primary is chosen.

options.text: All of them at the same time
options.why_wrong: That's the simultaneous (interrupting) mode.

options.text: The lowest serial number
options.why_wrong: Order is by role, not serial.

quiz.explanation: Subordinates, new primary from upgraded units, then the former primary.

quiz.stem: Which CLI command shows why the current primary was selected? (three words after 'get')
quiz.explanation: Look at "Primary selected using".

quiz.stem: A customer has many short HTTP sessions and session pickup is overloading the cluster. Which option helps most?

options.text: session-pickup-delay, syncing sessions older than 30 s
session-pickup-connectionless, to sync UDP and ICMP too
options.why_wrong: That adds more sessions to sync.

options.text: A lower hb-interval so sync messages go out more often
options.why_wrong: Faster heartbeats don't reduce sync load.

options.text: A dedicated session-sync link separate from the heartbeat
options.why_wrong: Moves the load off the heartbeat but still syncs every short session.

quiz.explanation: Short sessions aren't worth syncing.

quiz.stem: Two members are in different buildings over a shared fibre. Heartbeats are lost during backups and both go primary. Which design change does the guide recommend?

options.text: Longer heartbeat lost interval and threshold than the latency, plus redundant links
A lower hb-lost-threshold so a real failure is detected sooner during the backups
options.why_wrong: That makes false failovers more likely.

options.text: QoS on the shared fibre for heartbeats, keeping the default heartbeat timers as they are
options.why_wrong: Helps, but the guide's fix is timers matched to latency plus redundant heartbeat paths.

options.text: Override on the preferred unit, so the same one wins once the heartbeats come back
options.why_wrong: Decides the winner afterwards but doesn't stop both going primary.

quiz.explanation: Tune timers to the link, add redundant heartbeat paths.

quiz.stem: In active-active FGCP, who receives packets sent to the cluster?

options.text: The primary, which hands out sessions by schedule
Each member equally, via ECMP from the switches
options.why_wrong: That's closer to FGSP with an external load balancer.

options.text: The secondary, which forwards them to the primary
options.why_wrong: The primary owns the virtual MACs.

options.text: Each member for its own VLANs, set per virtual cluster
options.why_wrong: Virtual clustering splits VDOMs; plain A-A still has the primary receive.

quiz.explanation: The primary receives and hands out sessions.

quiz.stem: The monitoring team needs SNMP and syslog from each cluster member separately. What do you configure?

options.text: Reserved HA management interfaces with ha-direct
Separate SNMP communities per unit on the cluster IP
options.why_wrong: Communities don't give each unit its own source address.

options.text: FGSP between the units instead of an FGCP cluster
options.why_wrong: FGSP is for session sync with external load balancers.

options.text: A loopback per unit as the syslog source interface
options.why_wrong: Loopbacks are synced cluster config; each unit needs its own reserved port.

quiz.explanation: Each unit keeps its own management IP; ha-direct sends services from it.

quiz.stem: The GUI shows a member highlighted red as Not Synchronized. What's the right next step?

options.text: Check which tables differ, fix the cause, then force a resync if needed
Force a resync from the primary straight away, then check whether it holds
options.why_wrong: May clear it, but without the cause it'll drift again.

options.text: Fail over to the out-of-sync member to see whether its config is better
options.why_wrong: Failover doesn't fix sync and may change behaviour in production.

options.text: Wait for the next sync cycle, as the checksum mismatch usually clears
options.why_wrong: Brief mismatches clear; a persistent red member needs investigation.

quiz.explanation: Find the differing tables, then resync.

labs.title: Build an active-passive cluster
labs.goal: Configure the first unit of an A-P cluster with two heartbeat links, session pickup and two monitored ports, preferring this unit.

worked.config:
config system global
    set hostname FGT-HQ-A
end
config system ha
    set mode a-p
    set group-id 10
    set group-name "HQ-CLUSTER"
    set password <shared-secret>
    set hbdev "ha1" 50 "ha2" 50
    set session-pickup enable
    set monitor "port1" "port2"
    set override disable
    set priority 200
end
notes: group-id, group-name, mode and password must match on both units.
Two heartbeat links, cabled back to back.
With override disabled, priority 200 only decides on a tie in uptime.
