scenarios.title: "Just disable the certificate check, it works"
scenarios.situation:
During go-live, LDAPS fails with a certificate error because the LDAP server is set to the DC's IP. The customer's
admin says: "Disable server-identity-check, we're inside our own network."
scenarios.ask: What do you do and say?
right_thinking: Explain the risk: without the check, any host with a certificate can impersonate the DC and harvest passwords
Offer the fix that keeps the check: use the FQDN on the certificate and import the AD CA
If they still choose to disable it, record the risk acceptance in the change
scenarios.what: A secure fix proposed in minutes, and the decision documented.
scenarios.why: PS engineers own the quality of what they leave behind.
scenarios.model_answer:
"We can make it work without lowering security. The certificate is issued to dc01.andes.local, and we're
connecting by IP, so the name check fails. If I point the FortiGate at the FQDN and import your AD CA, LDAPS works
with the check on. Turning it off means any machine with a certificate could pretend to be your DC and see every
password. If you still prefer to disable it today, I'll note it in the change record as an accepted risk."
scenarios.best_way: Keep the control, fix the name.
rubric: explains the risk in business terms

scenarios.title: Monday morning, nobody can log in
scenarios.situation:
100 users fail firewall authentication since 7:00. The FortiGate config hasn't changed in a month. AD admins
rotated service-account passwords on Sunday.
scenarios.ask: Your first three moves?
right_thinking: Everyone at once points to something shared: the bind account or the DC
diagnose test authserver with a known-good account; fnbamd debug for the bind result
Update the bind password; add the account to the rotation runbook
scenarios.what: Root cause in minutes, not a password reset storm.
scenarios.why: Pattern recognition saves hours.
scenarios.model_answer:
"If everyone fails at once, it isn't their passwords. I'd run diagnose test authserver with a test account and
the fnbamd debug: if the bind as svc-fortigate fails with invalid credentials, the rotation changed it. Update
the password on the FortiGate, retest, and ask the AD team to add this account to their rotation checklist."
scenarios.best_way: Shared failure → shared component.

interview.question: How would you integrate a FortiGate with Active Directory for user-based policies?
interview.testing: LDAP vs FSSO judgement and correct settings
interview.model_answer:
"If users must log in explicitly, LDAP: regular bind with a least-privilege service account, cnid
sAMAccountName, the domain as the base DN, LDAPS. Then a user group matched on the AD group DN and identity
policies. If they want transparency, FSSO with the collector agent, ideally polling or DC agents on every DC,
and fsso-service groups. Either way I prove it with diagnose test authserver and two test users before go-live."
interview.best_way: Two options, the trade-off, and how you'd test.

interview.question: Users authenticate fine but still can't reach the application. How do you troubleshoot?
interview.model_answer:
"If the password is accepted, I look at authorization. diagnose firewall auth list shows which group the user
landed in; the fnbamd debug shows whether group matching passed; diagnose test authserver lists the real group
DNs to compare with the match entry. Then debug flow shows which policy the traffic hits, in case another
policy matches first."
interview.best_way: Name the split, then the tools in order.

interview.question: RADIUS authentication times out. What could it be?
interview.model_answer:
"A timeout means no answer, so: is there a route from the FortiGate to the server on UDP 1812, and is the
FortiGate's source IP, the egress interface or source-ip, configured as a RADIUS client? NPS drops unknown
clients silently. A wrong secret or password usually gives a reject instead."
interview.best_way: Timeout vs reject is the key.

field_reports.title: Credentials are the front door
field_reports.body:
Stolen or guessed credentials are one of the most common ways attackers get in. A firewall that can tie every
session to a named user turns "an IP on the LAN" into "Juan from Finance", in policies and in the logs your SOC
reads. That's the business case for identity-based policies, and MFA on remote access is the second half of it.
field_reports.source: General industry knowledge; see the DBIR for current figures

modules.title: Cryptography and PKI: what the algorithms do, how trust chains work, and what breaks in projects
modules.stage_title: S3 · Security, crypto, identity and the threat landscape
objectives: Tell symmetric, asymmetric and hash functions apart by job, and explain Diffie-Hellman and PFS
Read a certificate chain and diagnose untrusted, expired, wrong-name and revoked certificates
Plan certificate work in FortiGate projects (VPN, admin GUI, SSL inspection CA)
Explain post-quantum migration in one minute without hype
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Administration Guide: Certificates (p. 4411), cipher suites (p. 4504), post-quantum cryptography (p. 3898)
NIST FIPS 203/204/205 (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, 2024); RFC 5280 (X.509), RFC 6960 (OCSP)

units.title: Three tools, three jobs
units.body:
| Tool | Job | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Symmetric cipher** | Encrypt bulk data fast with one shared key | AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 |
| **Asymmetric** | Key exchange and signatures with a key pair | RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519; ECDH |
| **Hash / MAC** | Integrity fingerprint; with a key (HMAC) proves origin | SHA-256, HMAC-SHA256 |

Real protocols combine them: asymmetric to agree on keys and authenticate, symmetric for the data, hashes for
integrity. **AEAD** modes (GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) encrypt and authenticate in one step.

**Diffie-Hellman** lets two parties derive a shared secret over an open channel. **Perfect forward secrecy
(PFS)** uses fresh (ephemeral) DH keys per session, so stealing a server's long-term key later doesn't decrypt
recorded traffic. In IPsec, PFS is the extra DH exchange in phase 2; in TLS 1.3 it is always on.

:::recall
Q: What does PFS protect against?
A: Decrypting recorded sessions after the long-term private key is stolen.
:::

units.title: Certificates and chains
units.body:
A certificate binds a **public key** to a **name** (Subject / SAN), signed by an issuer. Clients trust it if
they can build a chain to a **root CA** they already trust, every certificate is in its validity window, the
name matches (the **SAN**, not the CN, in modern clients), and it isn't **revoked** (CRL or OCSP).

Four errors you'll meet and their causes:

| Error | Usual cause |
|---|---|
| Untrusted issuer | Private CA not installed on clients, or the server doesn't send the intermediate |
| Name mismatch | Users connect by IP or a name missing from the SAN |
| Expired / not yet valid | Renewal missed, or clock skew |
| Revoked / status unknown | CA revoked it, or the client can't reach the CRL/OCSP URL |

On a FortiGate: import the server cert with its chain for SSL VPN or the admin GUI, and for **deep
inspection** use a CA certificate the FortiGate can sign with — which every client must trust.

:::recall
Q: Which field do modern browsers use for the name check?
A: Subject Alternative Name (SAN).
:::

:::why
Q: Why can a perfectly valid server certificate fail on some clients only?
A: The server doesn't send the intermediate CA, and only clients that cached it can build the chain.
:::

units.title: Post-quantum in one minute
units.body:
A large quantum computer would break RSA and elliptic-curve key exchange and signatures; symmetric ciphers and
hashes mostly survive with larger sizes. The threat today is **harvest now, decrypt later**: record
encrypted traffic now, decrypt it when the computer exists.

NIST standardised **ML-KEM** (key encapsulation, FIPS 203) and **ML-DSA / SLH-DSA** (signatures, FIPS 204/205) in
2024. The near-term move is **hybrid key exchange** (classical + ML-KEM), so a session is safe if either holds.
FortiOS supports post-quantum options for IPsec (see the admin guide's PQC section).

Customer message: inventory where long-lived secrets travel (VPNs between sites, backups), plan hybrid key
exchange there first, don't rip out RSA certificates in a panic.

:::recall
Q: Why does PQC start with key exchange rather than signatures?
A: Harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks target recorded traffic, which only key exchange protects.
:::

cards.back: Symmetric: one shared key, fast bulk encryption. Asymmetric: key pair for exchange and signatures.
Encrypt and authenticate in one mode (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305).
Ephemeral DH per session; a stolen long-term key can't decrypt old traffic.
Chain to trusted root, validity dates, SAN name match, not revoked.

cards.front: Some clients trust a cert, others don't
cards.back: Server isn't sending the intermediate CA.
A CA cert the FortiGate signs with; every client must trust it.
Record encrypted traffic today, decrypt with a future quantum computer.
NIST post-quantum key encapsulation (FIPS 203, 2024).

quiz.stem: Which property means a stolen VPN gateway private key can't be used to decrypt last month's recorded tunnel traffic?

options.text: Perfect forward secrecy from ephemeral Diffie-Hellman keys per session
Strong hashing of each packet with SHA-256 in the integrity check value
options.why_wrong: Integrity proves packets weren't changed; it doesn't protect confidentiality of recorded traffic.

options.text: AES-256 encryption, since its key is long enough to resist brute force
options.why_wrong: Strong ciphers don't help if the session keys can be derived from the stolen long-term key.

options.text: Certificate revocation, which invalidates the stolen key for older sessions
options.why_wrong: Revocation stops future trust; it can't change how past sessions were keyed.

quiz.explanation: With PFS, session keys came from ephemeral DH and are gone; the long-term key only authenticated.

quiz.output:
$ openssl s_client -connect vpn.andes.com.co:443 -servername vpn.andes.com.co
depth=0 CN = vpn.andes.com.co
verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate
verify error:num=21:unable to verify the first certificate
---
Certificate chain
 0 s:CN = vpn.andes.com.co
   i:C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R11
quiz.stem: Windows laptops connect fine; Android phones show an untrusted-certificate warning. What do you fix first?

options.text: Import the intermediate CA and send the full chain from the SSL VPN certificate
Add vpn.andes.com.co as a SAN entry and reissue the certificate with the CA
options.why_wrong: The name matches already (depth 0 CN and SNI); the chain is the problem.

options.text: Install the Let's Encrypt root on the Android phones through the MDM platform
options.why_wrong: The root is already trusted; the phones can't reach it without the intermediate.

options.text: Switch the VPN to a self-signed certificate and push it to all of the devices
options.why_wrong: Replaces a public chain with a private one everyone must trust; more work, same lesson.

quiz.explanation: Only the leaf is sent (chain depth 0). Windows often fetches the missing intermediate itself; Android doesn't. Send the full chain.

quiz.stem: After enabling deep inspection, users get certificate warnings on every HTTPS site. What did the rollout miss?

options.text: Distributing the FortiGate's inspection CA to the clients' trusted root stores
Adding exemptions for the categories that pin their certificates, such as banking
options.why_wrong: Needed for pinned apps, but warnings on every site mean the CA isn't trusted at all.

options.text: Enabling certificate inspection instead of deep inspection on the same policy
options.why_wrong: That avoids warnings by not decrypting, which isn't the requirement.

options.text: Renewing the FortiGate's admin GUI certificate, which inspection reuses to sign
options.why_wrong: Inspection signs with its own CA certificate, not the GUI's server cert.

quiz.explanation: The FortiGate re-signs every site with its CA; clients must trust that CA.

quiz.stem: A customer asks what to do about quantum computing this year. Which advice is most defensible?

options.text: Inventory long-lived sensitive traffic and plan hybrid key exchange there first
Replace all RSA certificates with post-quantum signature certificates now
options.why_wrong: Signatures matter less for harvest-now risk, and ecosystem support is still maturing.

options.text: Move bulk encryption from AES-128 to AES-256 to offset Grover's speed-up first
options.why_wrong: Reasonable hygiene, but symmetric ciphers are the least affected; key exchange is the urgent part.

options.text: Wait for a working quantum computer, since recorded traffic stays safe until then
options.why_wrong: Harvest-now-decrypt-later means recorded traffic is the risk today.

quiz.explanation: Key exchange protects recorded traffic; hybrid ML-KEM where secrets live long is the pragmatic first step.

quiz.stem: Which checks must pass for a client to trust a server certificate? Select all that apply.

options.text: A chain to a root CA in the client's trust store
The name used to connect matches an entry in the SAN
The current time falls within each certificate's validity
The key length matches the cipher suite negotiated
options.why_wrong: Key types must be usable, but key length isn't matched to the cipher suite.

options.text: The certificate was issued by the same CA as the client's
options.why_wrong: Clients trust any CA in their store, not just their own issuer.

quiz.explanation: Chain, name, time (and revocation status) are the trust checks.

scenarios.title: The certificate that expired on a Saturday
scenarios.situation: Saturday 08:00: remote staff can't connect to SSL VPN; the error says the certificate expired. Nobody owns certificate renewals.
scenarios.ask: What do you do now and what do you leave behind?
right_thinking: Restore: issue/import a new certificate with full chain, assign it to the VPN
Verify from outside with a client and openssl
Leave a certificate inventory with owners and expiry alerts (FortiGate certificate expiry warnings, monitoring)
scenarios.what: Restore now, then fix ownership.
scenarios.why: Expiry is a process failure, not a technical one.
scenarios.model_answer: "First restore: get a new certificate with its full chain, import it and assign it to the VPN, then test from outside. Then I'd leave them a certificate inventory — VPN, GUI, inspection CA, LDAPS — with owners and alerts at 60 and 30 days, so this never depends on someone remembering."
scenarios.best_way: Renew with the chain, then give certificates an owner and an alert.

interview.question: Explain perfect forward secrecy to a customer's network manager.
interview.model_answer: "Each session gets its own temporary key that's thrown away afterwards. So even if someone steals the VPN gateway's private key next year, the traffic they recorded today stays encrypted, because those temporary keys are gone. In IPsec it's the PFS option in phase 2; in TLS 1.3 it's always on."
interview.best_way: Temporary keys per session, thrown away — a stolen key can't unlock the past.

modules.title: TLS and inspection theory: the handshake, what a middlebox can see, and why apps break
modules.stage_title: S3 · Security, crypto, identity and the threat landscape
objectives: Walk through a TLS 1.2 and 1.3 handshake and say what is visible on the wire in each
Explain certificate inspection vs full (deep) inspection and what each can and can't see
Predict which applications break under inspection (pinning, mutual TLS, QUIC) and plan exemptions
Scope an inspection rollout as a project, including privacy categories and performance
sources: RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3), RFC 9000 (QUIC), RFC 9849 draft / Encrypted Client Hello
FortiOS 8.0.2 Administration Guide: SSL/SSH inspection profiles (certificate vs deep inspection, exemptions)

units.title: The handshake and what leaks
units.body:
TLS 1.2: ClientHello (with **SNI**, the server name) → ServerHello + **certificate in clear text** → key exchange →
encrypted data. A passive device sees the SNI and the full certificate.

TLS 1.3: ClientHello (SNI still clear) → ServerHello → everything after, **including the certificate, is
encrypted**. One fewer round-trip, PFS always on, old ciphers gone.

So a firewall that doesn't decrypt identifies sites from the **SNI** (both versions) and the **certificate**
(TLS 1.2 only). **Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)** hides the real SNI too, leaving only the front server's name.

:::recall
Q: What does a passive device see in a TLS 1.3 handshake that identifies the site?
A: The SNI in the ClientHello (unless ECH is used); the certificate is encrypted.
:::

units.title: Certificate inspection vs deep inspection
units.body:
| | Certificate inspection | Deep (full) inspection |
|---|---|---|
| How | Reads SNI / certificate, no decryption | FortiGate terminates TLS, re-signs with its CA, opens a second session to the server |
| Sees | Domain name → web filter category, app guess | URLs, content, files → AV, IPS, DLP, full app control |
| Client impact | None | Clients must trust the CA; pinned or mutual-TLS apps break |
| Cost | Low | CPU-heavy; size the box for decrypted throughput |

Things that break under deep inspection and the usual fix:
- **Certificate pinning** (banking apps, some update services, Microsoft 365 endpoints): exempt by address or
  category.
- **Mutual TLS** (client certificates): the FortiGate can't present the client's certificate → exempt.
- **QUIC / HTTP/3** on UDP 443: no TLS-over-TCP to intercept → block QUIC so browsers fall back to TCP, or use
  a release that inspects QUIC.
- **Privacy categories** (health, finance) are usually exempted by policy or law.

:::why
Q: Why is blocking UDP 443 a common step when deploying deep inspection?
A: Browsers fall back from QUIC to TLS over TCP, which the FortiGate can inspect.
:::

units.title: Inspection as a project
units.body:
Inspection projects fail on people and process, not CLI. A sensible plan:
1. **Agree scope** with legal / HR: which users, which categories exempt, how users are told.
2. **Distribute the CA** (GPO, MDM, EMS) and check BYOD / guest networks separately.
3. **Pilot** a group with certificate inspection first, then deep inspection, collecting breakages.
4. **Build the exemption list** from evidence (logs, tickets), not guesses.
5. **Size** with the vendor's SSL inspection throughput figure, not firewall throughput.
6. **Hand over** a process for new exemption requests.

:::recall
Q: Which throughput figure sizes a deep-inspection design?
A: The SSL inspection throughput, not the firewall or IPS figure.
:::

cards.back: Server name in the ClientHello, visible without decryption (unless ECH).
Encrypted; only the SNI identifies the site passively.
No decryption; category from SNI/cert, no content scanning.
Pinned apps, mutual TLS, QUIC (unless blocked or supported).
Forces the browser back to TLS over TCP, which can be inspected.
Scope with legal → distribute CA → pilot → evidence-based exemptions → size → handover.

quiz.stem: Without decryption, how does a FortiGate assign a web filter category to a TLS 1.3 session?

options.text: From the server name in the ClientHello, the part sent before encryption starts
From the server certificate, which it reads as the handshake passes through it
options.why_wrong: True for TLS 1.2; in TLS 1.3 the certificate is encrypted.

options.text: From the URL path of the request, which is sent in clear inside the TLS records
options.why_wrong: The path is inside the encrypted HTTP request; it needs decryption.

options.text: From a reverse DNS lookup of the destination address once the session opens
options.why_wrong: Reverse DNS of a CDN address rarely names the site; SNI is what's used.

quiz.explanation: TLS 1.3 encrypts the certificate; the SNI is the remaining clear-text identifier.

quiz.stem: After deep inspection goes live, the bank's mobile app fails on Wi-Fi while browsers work fine. Most likely cause?

options.text: The app pins its server certificate and rejects the FortiGate's re-signed copy
The FortiGate's CA wasn't pushed to phones, so the app sees an untrusted issuer
options.why_wrong: Then the phone's browser would fail too; the app alone failing points to pinning.

options.text: The app uses QUIC over UDP 443, which the inspection profile silently drops
options.why_wrong: QUIC drops cause fallback to TCP, not a hard failure, for most apps.

options.text: The banking category is blocked in the web filter profile on that policy
options.why_wrong: Browsers reach the bank fine, so the category isn't blocked.

quiz.explanation: Pinned apps accept only their own certificate; exempt the bank by category or address.

quiz.output:
# diagnose sys session filter dport 443
# diagnose sys session list | grep -E "proto=|policy"
session info: proto=17 proto_state=00 duration=41 expire=138
policy_id=4 ...
session info: proto=17 proto_state=00 duration=12 expire=167
policy_id=4 ...
quiz.stem: Deep inspection is on for policy 4, yet web filter logs show almost no Chrome traffic. What is the first step?

options.text: Block UDP 443 for that traffic so Chrome falls back from QUIC to TLS over TCP
Reinstall the inspection CA on the clients because Chrome uses its own store
options.why_wrong: A trust problem shows certificate errors; the sessions here are UDP, which bypass TLS inspection.

options.text: Switch policy 4 to certificate inspection so the sessions match the profile
options.why_wrong: That inspects less, not more; the issue is the protocol.

options.text: Find the policy above 4 that Chrome's sessions match without the inspection profile
options.why_wrong: A sensible check, but the output already shows policy_id=4; the sessions are UDP, which TLS inspection skips.

quiz.explanation: proto=17 to 443 is QUIC. Blocking it (or using QUIC inspection where supported) brings the traffic into TLS-over-TCP.

quiz.stem: A hospital wants deep inspection for all staff next month. What do you settle first?

options.text: Scope and exemptions with legal and HR, including how staff get informed
The FortiGate model, using the SSL inspection throughput at peak hours of use
options.why_wrong: Sizing matters, but scope decides what traffic is decrypted at all.

options.text: The CA distribution method for managed laptops and the medical devices
options.why_wrong: Needed early, but which devices are in scope comes from the agreed policy.

options.text: A list of pinned applications to exempt, taken from vendor documentation
options.why_wrong: Exemptions should come from pilot evidence, after scope is agreed.

quiz.explanation: Decrypting staff traffic is a legal and privacy decision first; technical steps follow scope.

quiz.stem: Which traffic usually needs an exemption from deep inspection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apps that pin their server certificate
Services that require a client certificate
Health and finance categories, for privacy
Sites using TLS 1.3 rather than TLS 1.2
options.why_wrong: TLS 1.3 is inspected normally; it hides the certificate only from passive devices.

options.text: Sites whose certificates use ECDSA keys
options.why_wrong: The key type doesn't matter; the FortiGate re-signs either way.

quiz.explanation: Pinning, mutual TLS and privacy categories are the classic exemptions.

scenarios.title: The CIO wants everything decrypted by Friday
scenarios.situation: A logistics CIO read about malware in encrypted traffic and wants deep inspection for everyone by Friday. No CA is deployed, no pilot group exists and the FortiGate is at 60% CPU.
scenarios.ask: How do you respond?
right_thinking: Agree with the goal, reset the timeline with reasons
Propose certificate inspection now for quick value, deep inspection in phases
Name the three blockers: CA distribution, exemptions from a pilot, capacity
scenarios.what: Yes to the goal, phased plan for the how.
scenarios.why: A rushed rollout breaks apps and the business loses trust in security.
scenarios.model_answer: "The goal is right, and I can give you visibility this week with certificate inspection. Full decryption by Friday would break apps for people, because the CA isn't on the laptops yet, we don't know which apps pin, and the box is at 60% CPU before decrypting anything. So: certificate inspection now, CA push and a pilot group next week, then waves with an exemption list built from what we see."
scenarios.best_way: Agree with the goal, give a quick win, phase the risky part.

interview.question: What can a firewall see in HTTPS traffic without decrypting it?
interview.model_answer: "The SNI in the ClientHello in both versions, and in TLS 1.2 also the server certificate. That's enough for a category and a decent application guess. In TLS 1.3 the certificate is encrypted, and with Encrypted Client Hello even the SNI goes. Content, URLs and files need full inspection."
interview.best_way: SNI always, certificate only in 1.2, content needs decryption.

modules.title: VPN theory: IPsec phases, IKEv1 vs IKEv2, NAT-T, and TLS-based remote access
modules.stage_title: S3 · Security, crypto, identity and the threat landscape
objectives: Explain IKE phase 1 and phase 2 (IKE SA vs IPsec SAs) and what each negotiates
Compare IKEv1 and IKEv2, and route-based vs policy-based tunnels
Explain NAT traversal, ESP vs AH, and why MTU problems follow tunnels
Read a failing negotiation and name the mismatch from the log
sources: RFC 7296 (IKEv2), RFC 4303 (ESP), RFC 3948 (UDP encapsulation of ESP)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Administration Guide: IPsec VPN (phase 1 / phase 2 settings, NAT traversal)

units.title: Two phases, three SAs
units.body:
**Phase 1** builds the **IKE SA**: the peers authenticate (pre-shared key or certificates), agree on encryption,
integrity, a **DH group** and a lifetime. It's the secure control channel.

**Phase 2** (IKEv2: CHILD_SA) builds a pair of **IPsec SAs**, one per direction, each with its own **SPI**. It
negotiates the protected networks (**selectors / traffic selectors**), ESP ciphers, optional **PFS** group and
lifetime.

| | Phase 1 | Phase 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Result | 1 IKE SA | 2 IPsec SAs (in + out) |
| Must match | Auth, proposal, DH group, peer ID | Selectors, proposal, PFS group |
| Port | UDP 500 (4500 with NAT-T) | Rides inside phase 1 |

**ESP** (IP protocol 50) encrypts and authenticates; **AH** (51) only authenticates and breaks with NAT, so it's
rare.

:::recall
Q: How many IPsec SAs does one working phase 2 create?
A: Two, one per direction, each with its own SPI.
:::

units.title: IKEv1 vs IKEv2, route vs policy
units.body:
| | IKEv1 | IKEv2 |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | Main mode (6 msgs) or aggressive (3) + quick mode | 4 messages for the first CHILD_SA |
| Remote access | Needs XAuth / mode-config add-ons | EAP and config payload built in |
| Reliability | Optional DPD | Liveness checks and retransmission built in |
| Selector mismatch | Fails | Responder can narrow the selectors |

**Route-based** tunnels (FortiGate's default) create a tunnel interface: routing decides what goes in, policies
control it, and dynamic routing (BGP/OSPF) can run over it. **Policy-based** tunnels match traffic by policy;
easier to describe, harder to scale. Interop with older third-party gear often depends on matching **selectors**
exactly (one phase 2 per subnet pair) and **NAT-T** behaviour.

**NAT-T**: when NAT is detected between peers, IKE moves to UDP 4500 and ESP is wrapped in UDP 4500, because
plain ESP has no ports for PAT to track.

:::why
Q: Why does plain ESP break behind a PAT device?
A: ESP has no port numbers, so PAT can't map return traffic; NAT-T wraps it in UDP 4500.
:::

units.title: Reading a failed negotiation
units.body:
Map the symptom to the phase:
- **Nothing comes back on UDP 500**: reachability, ISP filtering, wrong peer IP.
- **"no proposal chosen" in phase 1**: cipher, hash or DH group differ.
- **Phase 1 up, phase 2 "no matching selector" / TS_UNACCEPTABLE**: subnets differ between ends.
- **Tunnel up, no traffic**: missing route or policy, or the remote side lacks a return route.
- **Tunnel up, small packets pass, big ones hang**: MTU / fragmentation → lower the TCP MSS.

On a FortiGate: `diagnose vpn ike log-filter dst-addr4 <peer>` then `diagnose debug application ike -1`;
`diagnose vpn tunnel list` shows SAs, SPIs and counters.

:::recall
Q: Phase 1 up, phase 2 fails with TS_UNACCEPTABLE. Where is the mismatch?
A: The traffic selectors (protected subnets) differ between the peers.
:::

cards.back: One IKE SA: authenticated control channel.
Two IPsec SAs, one per direction, each with its SPI.
ESP (50) encrypts + authenticates; AH (51) authenticates only and breaks with NAT.
UDP 4500 for IKE and UDP-wrapped ESP.
Fewer messages, EAP built in, liveness, selector narrowing.
Phase 1 or 2 algorithms or DH group differ.

cards.front: Big packets hang in the tunnel
cards.back: MTU: lower TCP MSS on the tunnel policy or interface.

quiz.stem: Why does a site-to-site tunnel switch from UDP 500 to UDP 4500 when a branch sits behind a home router?

options.text: The peers detected NAT and wrap ESP in UDP so the router can track the flows
UDP 4500 carries phase 2 traffic, while UDP 500 keeps carrying the phase 1 SA
options.why_wrong: With NAT-T both IKE and ESP move to 4500; the port isn't split by phase.

options.text: The router blocks UDP 500, so the peers retry on the alternate IKE port 4500
options.why_wrong: The move follows NAT detection inside IKE, not a blocked port.

options.text: IKEv2 uses UDP 4500 by default, while IKEv1 keeps UDP 500 for the exchange
options.why_wrong: Both versions start on 500 and move to 4500 when NAT is detected.

quiz.explanation: ESP has no ports; NAT-T wraps it in UDP 4500 so PAT can map it.

quiz.output:
ike 0:to-lima:4512: responder received SA_INIT
ike 0:to-lima:4512: negotiation result: OK
ike 0:to-lima:4512: IKE SA established
ike 0:to-lima:4512: received AUTH ... TSi 10.30.0.0/16 TSr 10.10.0.0/24
ike 0:to-lima:4512: no matching phase2 found
ike 0:to-lima:4512: sending TS_UNACCEPTABLE
quiz.stem: The Lima peer is a third-party firewall. Where is the mismatch, and why?

options.text: Phase 2 selectors: Lima proposes 10.30.0.0/16, the local side expects another range
Phase 1 proposal: the DH groups differ, so the IKE SA can't finish authentication
options.why_wrong: The log says the IKE SA was established; phase 1 is fine.

options.text: Phase 2 proposal: the ESP ciphers differ, which IKEv2 then reports as TS_UNACCEPTABLE
options.why_wrong: Cipher mismatches give NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN; TS_UNACCEPTABLE is about selectors.

options.text: Routing: the local side has no route to 10.30.0.0/16 through the to-lima interface
options.why_wrong: Routes matter after the SA exists; this fails during negotiation.

quiz.explanation: The IKE SA is up; the CHILD_SA fails on traffic selectors. Make the subnets match on both ends.

quiz.stem: A tunnel is up. Pings and SSH work, but file copies and web pages over the tunnel hang. First fix to try?

options.text: Lower the TCP MSS for traffic through the tunnel to fit under the path MTU
Enable PFS on phase 2 so each data transfer is protected by its own key
options.why_wrong: PFS changes keying, not packet size.

options.text: Shorten the phase 2 lifetime so that the stuck SAs get renegotiated more often
options.why_wrong: Rekeys don't change packet size; small packets already work.

options.text: Allow ICMP 'fragmentation needed' end to end so path MTU discovery works
options.why_wrong: Can help, but often outside your control; clamping MSS fixes TCP right away.

quiz.explanation: Small packets fine, large ones hang = MTU. Clamping MSS fixes TCP immediately.

quiz.stem: A customer wants BGP between HQ and 30 branches over IPsec. Which tunnel style fits?

options.text: Route-based tunnels, giving each peer a tunnel interface for its BGP session
Policy-based tunnels with one phase 2 per subnet pair for each of the branches
options.why_wrong: Works for static designs but can't run dynamic routing and doesn't scale to 30 sites.

options.text: IKEv1 aggressive mode, since branches with dynamic IPs need its speed
options.why_wrong: Aggressive mode is about identity with dynamic peers, not routing, and it's weaker.

options.text: Transport-mode ESP between loopbacks with BGP on top of the hosts
options.why_wrong: Not how FortiGate site-to-site is built; tunnel interfaces do the job.

quiz.explanation: Dynamic routing needs an interface; route-based tunnels give one per peer (or per overlay).

scenarios.title: The tunnel to the partner's Palo Alto
scenarios.situation: You're building a tunnel from a customer FortiGate to a partner's Palo Alto. The partner's engineer sends a PDF with phase 1/2 settings and two /24 subnets. Phase 1 comes up; only one of the two subnets works.
scenarios.ask: What do you check and how do you work with the partner?
right_thinking: One phase 2 per subnet pair on both ends; the second pair is likely missing or mismatched
Compare proxy IDs on their side with selectors on ours
Agree on a shared worksheet and test plan with the partner
scenarios.what: Selector per subnet pair; verify jointly.
scenarios.why: Third-party interop fails most often on selectors.
scenarios.model_answer: "Phase 1 is fine, so I'd look at phase 2. With third-party firewalls each subnet pair often needs its own phase 2, matching their proxy IDs exactly. I'd run the IKE debug, see what they propose for the second subnet, and then agree a one-page worksheet with their engineer — both ends' selectors, ciphers, PFS and lifetimes — so we change things once, together."
scenarios.best_way: Selectors per pair, one shared worksheet.

interview.question: Walk me through how an IPsec tunnel comes up.
interview.testing: Clear model of the two phases
interview.model_answer: "First the peers build the IKE SA on UDP 500: they authenticate with a key or certificates and agree on ciphers and a DH group. Inside that channel they negotiate phase 2: the subnets to protect, ESP ciphers and optional PFS, which creates two IPsec SAs, one per direction. Then data flows in ESP, or in UDP 4500 if NAT was detected. When it fails I ask which phase broke: proposals, identity, or selectors."
interview.best_way: IKE SA first, two IPsec SAs second, then data.

modules.title: Identity and access: directories, AAA, federation and MFA
modules.stage_title: S3 · Security, crypto, identity and the threat landscape
objectives: Tell authentication, authorization and accounting apart and map them to RADIUS, TACACS+ and LDAP
Explain SAML and OIDC flows and which party trusts which
Explain how 802.1X with EAP controls access at the port or SSID
Choose MFA factors and explain why phishing-resistant MFA matters
Explain SCIM provisioning and where it fits next to SAML
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: User & Authentication overview (p. 3905), SAML (pp. 3994–4040), TACACS+ (p. 4041), SCIM (p. 4043)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: FortiTokens (pp. 4054–4084), 802.1X status (p. 3986), RADSEC (p. 3987)
Protocol knowledge: RADIUS (RFC 2865/2866), LDAP (RFC 4511), SAML 2.0 (OASIS), OpenID Connect Core 1.0, SCIM (RFC 7643/7644), 802.1X/EAP (IEEE 802.1X, RFC 3748)

units.title: AAA and the three classic protocols
units.body:
**Authentication** proves who you are. **Authorization** decides what you may do. **Accounting** records what you
did. Every access design answers all three.

| Protocol | Transport | Strengths | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LDAP** | TCP 389, LDAPS 636 | A directory: users, groups, attributes | Look up users and group membership in AD |
| **RADIUS** | UDP 1812 auth, 1813 accounting | AAA for network access, vendor attributes (VSAs) | VPN, Wi-Fi, 802.1X, firewall auth via NPS or a NAC |
| **TACACS+** | TCP 49 | Separates authn, authz and accounting; per-command authorization | Network device administration |

## Details that come up in interviews

- RADIUS only obscures the **password** with the shared secret; the rest of the packet is in clear. That's why
  Fortinet recommends **RADSEC** (RADIUS over TLS) for untrusted paths (pp. 3905, 3987).
- TACACS+ encrypts the whole payload and can authorize **each command** an admin types: the usual choice for
  managing switches, routers and firewalls.
- LDAP is a **directory protocol**, not an AAA protocol: the firewall uses it to check a password with a bind
  and read groups, but the policy decision stays on the firewall.

:::recall
Q: Which protocol would you choose to control which commands each network admin may run?
A: TACACS+, because it authorizes per command and encrypts the whole session.
:::

units.title: Federation with SAML and OIDC
units.body:
Federation lets one **identity provider (IdP)** (Entra ID, Okta, FortiAuthenticator) vouch for users to many
**service providers (SPs)**. The SP never sees the password; it trusts a **signed assertion** from the IdP.

## SAML 2.0, SP-initiated (as FortiOS uses it, pp. 3994–4008)

1. The user opens a resource on the SP (for example, browses through an identity-based firewall policy).
2. The SP redirects the browser to the IdP with an authentication request. On FortiGate the captive portal port
   (1003 by default) does this redirect.
3. The user authenticates at the IdP, MFA included.
4. The IdP returns a **signed XML assertion** with the username and group attributes, through the browser.
5. The SP checks the signature with the IdP's certificate, reads the group, and applies the policy.

Configuration is an exchange of **metadata**: entity IDs, URLs and the IdP signing certificate.

## OIDC

**OpenID Connect** is an identity layer on **OAuth 2.0**: JSON tokens instead of XML, the **ID token** (a signed
JWT) carries who the user is, and an access token is for APIs. It's the modern default for web and mobile apps;
SAML still dominates enterprise SSO for older apps and network devices.

:::why
Q: Why is MFA usually configured at the IdP rather than on each firewall or app?
A: Federation centralizes authentication. One strong policy at the IdP (MFA, conditional access) then protects every SP that trusts it.
:::

:::pitfall
SAML depends on **clocks** (assertions have validity windows) and on the **certificate** the SP trusts. An IdP
certificate rollover that nobody copied to the SP breaks every login at once.
:::

units.title: 802.1X, EAP and network access control
units.body:
**802.1X** controls access at the **switch port or SSID** before the device gets a network:

| Role | Who | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Supplicant | The laptop or phone | Sends credentials |
| Authenticator | Switch or AP (or FortiGate/FortiSwitch/FortiAP) | Relays EAP inside RADIUS; opens the port |
| Authentication server | RADIUS (NPS, FortiAuthenticator, a NAC) | Decides, can return a VLAN |

**EAP** carries the actual method:

- **EAP-TLS:** certificates on both sides. The strongest common choice, no passwords to phish.
- **PEAP-MSCHAPv2:** a TLS tunnel protecting a username and password. Common, weaker if clients don't validate
  the server certificate.
- **MAB** (MAC authentication bypass) for printers and cameras that can't do 802.1X; a MAC is easy to spoof, so
  pair it with a restricted VLAN.

On FortiOS, `diagnose sys 802-1x status` shows the 802.1X state of switch members (p. 3986).

:::recall
Q: In 802.1X, which device talks RADIUS to the server?
A: The authenticator (the switch or AP), not the laptop.
:::

units.title: MFA, phishing resistance and provisioning
units.body:
## Factors

Something you **know** (password), **have** (token, phone, key), **are** (biometric). MFA combines two different
kinds.

| Factor | Phishing-resistant? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| SMS or email code | No | Can be intercepted or relayed |
| TOTP app (FortiToken Mobile) | No | A fake page can relay the code in real time |
| Push approval | No | Push fatigue: attackers spam prompts until one is approved |
| FIDO2 / passkeys, certificates | **Yes** | Bound to the real site's origin or to a private key |

FortiOS supports FortiToken hardware and mobile tokens and FortiIdentity Cloud for MFA on local and remote users
(pp. 3907, 4054).

## Provisioning with SCIM

SAML answers "who is logging in now". **SCIM** answers "which users and groups exist": the IdP pushes users and
group changes to the SP over a REST API, so a user disabled in the IdP disappears from the app too. FortiOS can act
as a SCIM server for this (p. 4043).

:::ps
In an access project, always ask about the **joiner-mover-leaver** process: how a leaver's access is removed
everywhere. SCIM, FSSO with AD, or RADIUS to a central directory all solve it; local accounts on every firewall
don't.
:::

cards.back: Who you are · what you may do · what you did.
UDP 1812 (authentication), 1813 (accounting).

cards.front: TACACS+ port and its big advantage
cards.back: TCP 49. Encrypts the whole payload and authorizes per command.

cards.front: What part of a RADIUS packet is protected by the shared secret?
cards.back: Only the password attribute. Use RADSEC (TLS) for the rest.

cards.front: SAML: who signs the assertion, who verifies it?
cards.back: The IdP signs; the SP verifies with the IdP's certificate.
An identity layer on OAuth 2.0: a signed JWT ID token says who the user is.

cards.front: Two things that break all SAML logins at once
cards.back: IdP signing certificate rollover not copied to the SP; clock skew.
Supplicant (client), authenticator (switch/AP), authentication server (RADIUS).
EAP-TLS: certificates on both sides.
MAC authentication bypass for devices without 802.1X; MACs can be spoofed, so restrict the VLAN.
FIDO2 security keys and passkeys; certificate-based authentication.
Attackers send repeated push prompts until a tired user approves one.
SAML authenticates a login; SCIM provisions and deprovisions users and groups.

quiz.stem: Which protocol lets you authorize each CLI command a network admin runs?

options.text: TACACS+
RADIUS
options.why_wrong: RADIUS combines authentication and authorization in one exchange, not per command.

options.text: LDAPS
options.why_wrong: A directory protocol; it doesn't authorize commands.

options.text: Kerberos
options.why_wrong: Authenticates users; command authorization isn't part of it.

quiz.explanation: TACACS+ separates AAA and supports command authorization.

quiz.stem: In SAML SP-initiated login, where does the user type the password?

options.text: At the IdP's sign-in page
At the SP, which relays it
options.why_wrong: The SP never sees the password.

options.text: Inside the signed assertion
options.why_wrong: The assertion carries identity and attributes, not the password.

options.text: On the FortiGate portal form
options.why_wrong: The portal redirects to the IdP for the password.

quiz.explanation: The SP redirects to the IdP, which authenticates and returns a signed assertion.

quiz.stem: Which MFA methods are phishing-resistant? Select all that apply.

options.text: A FIDO2 security key
A synced passkey
A TOTP app code
options.why_wrong: A fake page can relay the code in real time.

options.text: An SMS one-time code
options.why_wrong: Can be intercepted or relayed.

options.text: A push with number match
options.why_wrong: Number matching stops fatigue attacks, but a proxy page can still relay the session.

quiz.explanation: Origin-bound or key-bound methods resist phishing.

quiz.stem: In 802.1X, the laptop is the…

options.text: Supplicant
Authenticator
options.why_wrong: That's the switch or AP.

options.text: Auth server
options.why_wrong: That role belongs to the RADIUS server.

options.text: Relay agent
options.why_wrong: A DHCP term, not an 802.1X role.

quiz.explanation: Supplicant ↔ authenticator (EAPOL) ↔ RADIUS server.

quiz.stem: Order the SAML SP-initiated flow.
items: User requests a resource at the SP
SP redirects the browser to the IdP
User authenticates at the IdP (with MFA)
IdP returns a signed assertion via the browser
SP validates the signature and applies the policy
quiz.explanation: Redirect out, authenticate, assertion back, validate.

quiz.stem: A user is disabled in Entra ID but still exists in an app's local user list. What solves this class of problem?

options.text: SCIM provisioning from the IdP
A shorter SAML session lifetime
options.why_wrong: Limits how long a session lasts, but the local account stays.

options.text: RADIUS accounting for the app
options.why_wrong: Records usage; it doesn't deprovision accounts.

options.text: A nightly LDAP sync to the app
options.why_wrong: Works for LDAP-capable apps, but Entra ID SaaS apps use SCIM.

quiz.explanation: SCIM pushes joins, changes and removals from the IdP to the SP.

quiz.stem: Which EAP method uses certificates on both client and server?
quiz.explanation: EAP-TLS.

quiz.stem: Why does Fortinet suggest RADSEC for RADIUS?

options.text: Classic RADIUS protects the password alone; RADSEC wraps it all in TLS
RADIUS can't carry group attributes, which RADSEC then adds through VSAs
options.why_wrong: Vendor-specific attributes already carry groups in RADIUS.

options.text: RADSEC is faster, because it runs over UDP with fewer retransmissions
options.why_wrong: RADSEC runs over TLS on TCP, for security, not speed.

options.text: RADSEC adds server failover, which plain RADIUS doesn't offer at all today
options.why_wrong: RADIUS already supports several servers; RADSEC is about protecting the exchange.

quiz.explanation: Confidentiality and integrity for the whole exchange.

quiz.stem: Users intermittently get 'assertion not yet valid' errors signing in to an SP through SAML. What do you check first?

options.text: Clock sync between the IdP and the SP, as assertions carry validity times
The IdP's signing certificate, which may be close to its expiry date
options.why_wrong: An expired cert fails every login with a signature error, not intermittently on time.

options.text: A longer assertion lifetime on the IdP so that the late arrivals still pass
options.why_wrong: 'Not yet valid' means the assertion looks early; lifetime doesn't fix skew.

options.text: Switching to IdP-initiated login so the SP stops checking the times
options.why_wrong: The SP validates times in both flows.

quiz.explanation: NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter are checked against the SP's clock; skew makes fresh assertions look early or expired.

labs.title: Draw the access design for a hybrid company
labs.goal: Choose the identity protocol for each access path at Andes Logistics and justify it.

worked.config:
# Access path                     → protocol / method            → why
# Staff Wi-Fi (corporate laptops) → 802.1X EAP-TLS to NPS        → certificates, no passwords to phish
# Printers and cameras            → MAB + isolated VLAN          → can't do 802.1X; MAC is spoofable
# Remote access VPN               → SAML to Entra ID with MFA    → central MFA and conditional access
# Firewall user policies (HQ)     → FSSO collector agent         → transparent identity from AD logons
# Network device admin            → TACACS+ (or RADIUS + MFA)    → per-command authorization, accounting
# SaaS apps                       → OIDC/SAML SSO + SCIM         → SSO plus automatic deprovisioning
notes: Every path names authn, authz and how a leaver loses access.
Phishing-resistant MFA where the risk is highest: remote access and admin.

solo.prompt: Name the protocol for each, one per line: device admin per-command control, web SSO with signed XML assertions, JSON ID tokens on OAuth 2.0, user provisioning API.
solo.solution:
TACACS+
SAML
OIDC
SCIM
solo.notes: LDAP and RADIUS cover the rest of most designs.

scenarios.title: "We have MFA, we're safe"
scenarios.situation:
A customer's CISO says remote access is solved: "Everyone has push MFA." Last month a contractor approved a push
at 2 a.m. after twenty prompts.
scenarios.ask: How do you respond in the design review?
right_thinking: Acknowledge MFA is a big improvement
Explain push fatigue and that push/TOTP aren't phishing-resistant
Propose number matching as a quick win and FIDO2/certificates for admins and high-risk users
scenarios.what: A respectful upgrade path, not a lecture.
scenarios.why: Credibility comes from specific, proportionate advice.
scenarios.model_answer:
"MFA was the right move, and it stops most password attacks. The 2 a.m. approval shows its limit: push and codes
can be fatigued or relayed. Quick win: number matching and alerts on repeated prompts. Target state: FIDO2 keys
or certificates for admins and contractors, enforced at the IdP so the VPN and every app inherit it."
scenarios.best_way: Credit, gap, quick win, target.

interview.question: RADIUS or TACACS+ for administering 200 FortiGates and switches?
interview.model_answer:
"For admin access I prefer TACACS+: it encrypts the whole session, separates authentication from authorization,
and can authorize and account per command. RADIUS works too, especially with MFA through FortiAuthenticator, but
it only protects the password and has no per-command control. Either way, local break-glass accounts stay, vaulted."
interview.best_way: Pick one, give the reason, mention break-glass.

interview.question: Explain SAML to a customer who only knows usernames and passwords.
interview.model_answer:
"Think of a passport. Your company's identity system, the IdP, checks who you are once, with MFA, and gives the
app a signed pass saying 'this is Juan from Finance'. The app trusts the signature and never sees your password.
You get one strong login for everything, and when HR disables you, every app stops trusting you."
interview.best_way: One analogy, then the benefit.

modules.title: Defense concepts and the threat landscape: kill chains, ATT&CK, zero trust and how attacks really unfold
modules.stage_title: S3 · Security, crypto, identity and the threat landscape
objectives: Use the kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK to place a control or a detection on an attack path
Explain defense in depth, least privilege, segmentation and zero trust without buzzwords
Describe how ransomware and initial-access campaigns unfold today, and where FortiGate, EDR and SIEM each break the chain
Turn a threat into a prioritised control list for a customer
sources: MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise matrix (tactics and techniques, v15+)
NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture; CISA #StopRansomware advisories (public)

units.title: Models for talking about attacks
units.body:
The **kill chain** (recon → weaponise → deliver → exploit → install → command and control → actions on
objectives) is good for explaining to managers that you can break an attack at several points.

**MITRE ATT&CK** is the working vocabulary: **tactics** are the attacker's goals (Initial Access, Execution,
Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection,
Command and Control, Exfiltration, Impact), **techniques** are how (T1558.003 Kerberoasting, T1003.001 LSASS
memory). Detections and controls are mapped to techniques; coverage gaps show up as empty cells.

The **pyramid of pain**: blocking hashes and IPs costs the attacker little; detecting tools and **behaviours
(TTPs)** costs them a lot. Good detection aims high on the pyramid.

:::recall
Q: Why are behaviour-based detections worth more than IOC blocks?
A: Attackers change hashes and IPs cheaply; changing their technique is expensive.
:::

units.title: Defense principles in plain words
units.body:
- **Defense in depth**: several independent controls, so one failure isn't a breach (email filter + EDR +
  segmentation + backups).
- **Least privilege**: accounts and systems get only what they need; tiered admin accounts stop one phished
  helpdesk user from becoming domain admin.
- **Segmentation**: limit what a compromised host can reach; FortiGate internal segmentation, FortiSwitch/NAC
  for the access layer.
- **Zero trust** (NIST 800-207): no implicit trust from network location; every access is decided per request
  from identity, device posture and context, through a policy enforcement point (ZTNA proxy, FortiGate).
- **Assume breach**: design detection and response as if the attacker is already inside.

:::why
Q: What's the difference between segmentation and zero trust?
A: Segmentation limits reach by network zone; zero trust decides each access by identity and posture, wherever the user is.
:::

units.title: How a modern intrusion unfolds
units.body:
A typical human-operated ransomware case, with where each product can break it:

| Step | Typical technique | Who can stop or see it |
|---|---|---|
| Initial access | Phishing, exposed VPN without MFA, unpatched edge device | Email security, MFA, patching, FortiGate IPS |
| Foothold | Loader, remote management tool | EDR, application control, DNS filter |
| Credential access | LSASS dump, Kerberoasting | EDR, SIEM rules on 4769 / Sysmon 10 |
| Lateral movement | PsExec, RDP, WMI with stolen admin | Segmentation, SIEM on 4624 type 3 + 7045 |
| Exfiltration | Cloud storage upload, rclone | DLP, application control, egress filtering |
| Impact | Encrypt, delete backups | EDR rollback, immutable / offline backups |

Edge devices (VPN gateways, firewalls) are a top initial-access target: keep them patched, restrict their
management interfaces, and log admin access.

:::recall
Q: Which control most often turns a ransomware attack into a recoverable incident?
A: Immutable or offline backups that the attacker can't delete.
:::

cards.back: Tactic = goal (Credential Access); technique = how (Kerberoasting).
Hashes/IPs cheap for attackers to change; TTPs expensive. Detect high.
No implicit trust from location; per-request decision on identity, posture, context.
Least privilege that stops one phished account becoming domain admin.
Patch, restrict management access, log admin sessions.
Immutable or offline backups.

quiz.stem: A SOC lead wants detections that stay useful after the attacker swaps tools. What should they target?

options.text: Behaviours such as LSASS reads by unusual processes, mapped to ATT&CK techniques
File hashes from the last incident's malware, fed into the EDR and the FortiGate
options.why_wrong: A recompile changes the hash; it's the bottom of the pyramid.

options.text: Command-and-control IP addresses from threat feeds, refreshed hourly on the FortiGate
options.why_wrong: Useful but cheap for attackers to rotate; low on the pyramid of pain.

options.text: Tool names like mimikatz.exe in process creation events across the workstations
options.why_wrong: Higher than hashes, but renaming the binary defeats it.

quiz.explanation: Behaviours (TTPs) are expensive for attackers to change; detect the technique, not the artifact.

quiz.stem: Remote staff reach internal apps over SSL VPN with full network access. What makes this design zero trust?

options.text: Per-app access decided by identity and device posture through a ZTNA proxy
Adding MFA to the SSL VPN login while keeping the full network access rule
options.why_wrong: Better authentication, but trust is still implicit once connected.

options.text: Splitting the internal network into VLANs for servers, users and the printers
options.why_wrong: Segmentation helps, but access still depends on network location.

options.text: Moving the VPN gateway into the cloud so that it's closer to remote staff
options.why_wrong: Location of the gateway doesn't change the trust model.

quiz.explanation: Zero trust removes implicit network trust: each app access is decided on identity and posture.

quiz.stem: Put these steps of a human-operated ransomware case in their usual order.
items: PsExec moves to the file servers
Data is uploaded to cloud storage
Backups are deleted and files encrypted
quiz.explanation: Access → credentials → lateral movement → exfiltration → impact. Double extortion takes the data before encrypting.

quiz.stem: A manufacturer with a flat network, no EDR and nightly backups to a mapped drive asks for your top priority against ransomware. What do you recommend first?

options.text: Make backups immutable or offline, out of reach of an attacker holding domain admin rights
Deploy EDR to the endpoints and servers, then tune it over the next few months of operation
options.why_wrong: Important, but if it fails, deletable backups mean no recovery.

options.text: Segment the flat network into zones with FortiGate internal segmentation firewall policies
options.why_wrong: Valuable and slower to roll out; recovery comes first.

options.text: Subscribe to threat intelligence feeds and block the latest ransomware IOCs at the edge
options.why_wrong: IOCs rotate quickly and do nothing for recovery.

quiz.explanation: Backups on a mapped drive get encrypted with everything else. Recoverability first, then prevention and detection.

quiz.stem: Which controls reduce the risk of an edge VPN gateway becoming the initial access point? Select all that apply.

options.text: Patching quickly after vendor security advisories
Restricting management access to trusted hosts
Requiring MFA for remote access logins
Raising the IPsec phase 1 DH group to 21 or so
options.why_wrong: Stronger crypto doesn't stop exploited vulnerabilities or stolen passwords.

options.text: Moving SSL VPN to a non-standard TCP port number
options.why_wrong: Scanners find it anyway; obscurity isn't a control.

quiz.explanation: Patch, restrict management, MFA. Crypto strength and port changes don't address how edges get breached.

scenarios.title: The board asks: are we ready for ransomware?
scenarios.situation: A retail chain's CFO asks you, in a 10-minute slot with the board, whether they're ready for ransomware. You've seen: MFA on VPN, no EDR on servers, flat store networks, backups on the same domain.
scenarios.ask: What do you say?
right_thinking: Answer in business terms: could we recover, how long, what's exposed
Name the two biggest gaps (backups on the domain, flat networks) and one strength (MFA)
Give a 90-day plan with costs ranked
scenarios.what: Honest answer, two gaps, a plan.
scenarios.why: Boards decide budget; they need risk and options, not product names.
scenarios.model_answer: "Partly. You've closed the most common door with MFA on the VPN. The two gaps that would turn an incident into weeks of downtime are backups that an attacker on the domain can delete, and flat store networks that let one infected PC reach everything. In 90 days I'd make backups immutable first, then segment the stores, then put EDR on the servers. I can bring rough costs for each next week."
scenarios.best_way: Partly ready, two gaps, a ranked 90-day plan.

interview.question: How would you explain zero trust to a customer who already has a firewall?
interview.framework: Old model → new decision → Fortinet pieces
interview.model_answer: "Your firewall trusts whoever is inside the network. Zero trust stops trusting location: every time someone opens an app, we check who they are, whether their device is healthy, and only then open that one app — not the whole network. With Fortinet that's FortiClient sending posture to EMS, and the FortiGate or FortiSASE acting as the ZTNA proxy."
interview.best_way: Stop trusting location; decide each app access on identity and device.

interview.question: You have a red-team background. How does that help you as a defender in a PS role?
interview.framework: What I learned → how I use it → limits
interview.model_answer: "From labs and certification work I know what attackers look for: weak service accounts, flat networks, edge devices without patches. So when I design a deployment I ask how I'd attack it, and I write detections for the steps I'd take, like Kerberoasting or LSASS reads. I'm careful to say this is lab and certification experience, not years in a SOC, and I test my detections against replays before I trust them."
interview.best_way: Attacker's eye for design and detection, framed honestly.

modules.title: OSPF: neighbors, LSAs, areas and SPF
objectives: Walk through the OSPF neighbor states and name what each mismatch breaks
Explain DR/BDR election and why it exists on broadcast segments
Explain the main LSA types, areas, ABRs and ASBRs
Predict intra-area, inter-area and external routes and their metrics
Choose stub, totally stubby or NSSA areas for a branch design
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Dynamic routing overview and OSPF (pp. 675–716), basic OSPF example and outputs (pp. 699–707)
Protocol knowledge: OSPFv2 (RFC 2328), NSSA (RFC 3101)

units.title: How two routers become neighbors
units.body:
OSPF is a **link-state** IGP: every router floods descriptions of its links (LSAs), builds the same map (the
LSDB), and runs Dijkstra's **SPF** algorithm to find shortest paths. Metric = **cost**, summed along the path.

## Neighbor states

| State | What happened |
|---|---|
| Down | No hellos heard |
| Init | I hear your hellos, but I'm not in yours yet |
| 2-Way | We see each other. On broadcast segments, DROthers stop here with each other |
| ExStart / Exchange | Master/slave chosen, database description (DBD) packets exchanged |
| Loading | Requesting the LSAs I'm missing |
| **Full** | Databases synchronized |

## What must match in the hello

Area ID, subnet and mask, **hello and dead intervals**, authentication, the stub/NSSA flags, and the router IDs
must differ. A mismatch here means **no neighbor at all**.

**MTU** is checked later, in the DBD exchange: a mismatch leaves the pair stuck in **ExStart/Exchange**. That's
why someone can "see the neighbor" and still have no routes.

:::recall
Q: One side says hello 10/dead 40, the other 2/8. Which state do they reach?
A: None: the hellos are discarded, so the neighbor never appears.
:::

:::pitfall
Duplicate router IDs (often from cloned VM configs) cause flapping and odd SPF results. Set router IDs
explicitly, usually from a loopback.
:::

units.title: DR/BDR and network types
units.body:
On a **broadcast** segment with many routers, full adjacency between every pair would flood the same LSA many
times. So routers elect a **Designated Router** and a **Backup DR**; everyone forms Full adjacencies only with them
and stays **2-Way** with the other DROthers.

Election: highest **priority** (default 1; 0 means "never DR"), then highest router ID. It's **not preemptive**: a
better router joining later doesn't take over until the DR fails.

**Point-to-point** network type skips the election: faster, and the right choice on /30 or /31 transit links,
tunnels and most WAN links. Both sides must agree: one side broadcast and the other point-to-point usually
breaks the adjacency or the routes.

In FortiOS output, `Full/DR`, `Full/Backup` or `Full/DROther` is the **neighbor's** role (p. 705).

:::why
Q: Why set the network type to point-to-point on a FortiGate-to-core transit /29 with only two routers?
A: There's nothing to gain from a DR with two routers, and skipping the election and wait timer speeds up adjacency and failover.
:::

units.title: LSAs, areas and route types
units.body:
| LSA | Name | Generated by | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Router | Every router | Its area |
| 2 | Network | The DR | Its area |
| 3 | Summary | ABR | Other areas |
| 4 | ASBR summary | ABR | How to reach an ASBR in another area |
| 5 | AS external | ASBR | Whole domain (not stub areas) |
| 7 | NSSA external | ASBR inside an NSSA | Its NSSA; the ABR translates it to type 5 |

- **Area 0** is the backbone; every other area attaches to it through an **ABR**.
- An **ASBR** redistributes routes from outside OSPF (static, connected, BGP).

## Route types in a routing table

- **O** intra-area: from type 1/2 in your area.
- **O IA** inter-area: from type 3.
- **O E2** external type 2 (the default): the metric is the external metric only and doesn't grow inside OSPF.
- **O E1** external type 1: external metric **plus** the internal cost.

Preference: intra-area > inter-area > E1 > E2, regardless of metric.

:::recall
Q: A redistributed default route shows as O*E2 0.0.0.0/0 [110/10] on every router, whatever the distance from the ASBR. Why the same metric everywhere?
A: E2 routes carry only the external metric; internal cost isn't added.
:::

units.title: Stub areas and branch designs
units.body:
| Area type | Blocks | Branch gets |
|---|---|---|
| Stub | Type 5 externals | Inter-area routes + a default from the ABR |
| Totally stubby | Type 3 and 5 | Only a default route |
| NSSA | Type 5, but allows local redistribution (type 7) | Inter-area routes, its own externals |

Smaller areas mean smaller LSDBs and less SPF churn, useful for many small branches. On the other hand, a
branch that only sees a default can't pick the best exit per prefix.

## Summarization

Only at the edges: ABRs (`area range`) and ASBRs (summary addresses). One summary hides the flapping of every
subnet behind it.

:::ps
Most FortiGate designs today use OSPF inside the campus or data center and BGP over the WAN or SD-WAN overlays.
When a customer asks for OSPF across 200 branches, ask what problem it solves first: BGP with ADVPN or SD-WAN
usually scales better.
:::

cards.back: Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, Full.
Area, subnet/mask, hello and dead intervals, authentication, stub/NSSA flags (router IDs must differ).

cards.front: Neighbor stuck in ExStart/Exchange: classic cause
cards.back: MTU mismatch.
Cost, summed along the path.
Highest priority (0 = never), then highest router ID. Not preemptive.

cards.front: Why DROthers stay in 2-Way with each other
cards.back: They only need Full adjacencies with the DR/BDR, which reduces flooding.

cards.front: Network type for a two-router transit link
cards.back: Point-to-point: no DR election, faster adjacency.
Summary LSA, generated by an ABR for other areas.
5: AS external from an ASBR, domain-wide. 7: NSSA external, translated to 5 by the ABR.
E1 adds internal cost; E2 (default) keeps only the external metric.
Intra-area > inter-area > E1 > E2.
Stub blocks type 5; totally stubby also blocks type 3. Both get a default from the ABR.
Only at ABRs (area ranges) and ASBRs (external summaries).

quiz.stem: Two routers see each other as neighbors but stay in ExStart. Most likely cause?

options.text: An interface MTU mismatch
Mismatched hello intervals
options.why_wrong: They wouldn't become neighbours at all.

options.text: Different OSPF process IDs
options.why_wrong: Process IDs are local and never compared.

options.text: Duplicate router IDs on them
options.why_wrong: Duplicate RIDs cause flapping and odd LSDB behaviour, not a stall at ExStart.

quiz.explanation: MTU is checked in DBD packets during ExStart/Exchange.

quiz.stem: Router A (priority 1, RID 10.0.0.9) is DR. Router B (priority 200) joins the segment. What happens?

options.text: A stays DR until it fails or restarts
B becomes DR at once on higher priority
options.why_wrong: DR election in OSPF isn't preemptive.

options.text: B becomes BDR now and DR at A's failure
options.why_wrong: Only if the BDR role is free; and B takes over only when A fails.

options.text: B becomes DR if its RID is also higher
options.why_wrong: Priority beats RID, but election still isn't preemptive.

quiz.explanation: DR election isn't preemptive.

quiz.stem: Order OSPF route preference.
quiz.explanation: Type beats metric.

quiz.stem: Which must match for two routers to become OSPF neighbors? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hello and dead intervals
The area ID on the link
Authentication settings
The router IDs of both
options.why_wrong: Router IDs must differ, not match.

options.text: The interface OSPF cost
options.why_wrong: Costs are local and can differ per side.

quiz.explanation: Cost is local; router IDs must be unique.

quiz.stem: Which area type lets a branch redistribute its local static routes while blocking type 5 LSAs?

options.text: NSSA
Stub
options.why_wrong: Stub areas block type 5 but allow no ASBR inside.

options.text: Totally stubby
options.why_wrong: Blocks externals and summaries, still with no ASBR.

options.text: Backbone
options.why_wrong: Area 0 carries type 5 LSAs.

quiz.explanation: NSSA uses type 7 for local externals.

quiz.stem: Which LSA type number does the DR generate for a broadcast segment?
quiz.explanation: Type 2, the network LSA.

quiz.output:
FGT-BR3 # get router info routing-table ospf
O*E2    0.0.0.0/0 [110/10] via 10.0.13.1, port3, 00:41:12
FGT-BR9 # get router info routing-table ospf
O*E2    0.0.0.0/0 [110/10] via 10.0.19.1, port3, 00:41:09
quiz.stem: BR3 is one hop from the ASBR, BR9 is four hops away. Why do both show [110/10]?

options.text: It's an E2 route, so the internal path cost isn't added
The links all have cost 0 in this area, so totals match
options.why_wrong: OSPF costs are at least 1.

options.text: It's an E1 route, and E1 keeps the metric set at the ASBR
options.why_wrong: Reversed: E1 adds internal cost, E2 doesn't.

options.text: It's an inter-area summary, so each ABR resets the cost
options.why_wrong: A redistributed default from an ASBR is external, not inter-area.

quiz.explanation: E2 doesn't add internal cost; E1 does.

labs.title: Diagnose an adjacency from the state alone
labs.goal: Map each neighbor symptom to its most likely cause.

scenarios.title: "OSPF is up, so it's not the network"
scenarios.situation:
After a core switch swap, an integrator says OSPF is fine because "the FortiGate is in the neighbor list". The
warehouse has no routes. The neighbor state is EXSTART.
scenarios.ask: Explain to the integrator and the customer.
right_thinking: Neighbor listed ≠ adjacency Full
ExStart points at MTU (jumbo on the new switch)
Short-term mtu-ignore or match MTU; long-term consistent MTU
scenarios.what: A clear explanation and a fix plan.
scenarios.why: Precise language avoids blame games.
scenarios.model_answer:
"The FortiGate hears the switch's hellos, so it's listed, but they're stuck in ExStart, which means they never
exchanged databases, so no routes. That state points at an MTU mismatch: the new switch uses jumbo frames on the
uplink. We can set mtu-ignore now to restore service and align MTUs in the next window."
scenarios.best_way: State, cause, now, later.

interview.question: An OSPF neighbor is stuck in ExStart. What do you check?
interview.model_answer:
"ExStart means hellos match but the database description exchange fails, and the classic cause is an MTU
mismatch between the two interfaces. I'd compare MTUs, run the OSPF debug, and either align the MTU or set
mtu-ignore as a temporary fix."
interview.best_way: Name the state's meaning first.

interview.question: Explain E1 vs E2 routes.
interview.model_answer:
"Both are external routes from an ASBR. E2, the default, keeps only the external metric, so every router sees
the same cost. E1 adds the internal cost to reach the ASBR, so with two ASBRs advertising the same prefix, E1
lets each router pick the closest exit."
interview.best_way: Definition plus the two-ASBR case.

units.title: Sessions and the finite-state machine
units.body:
BGP is a **path-vector** protocol between configured neighbors over **TCP 179**. Neighbors in different ASes are
**eBGP**; in the same AS, **iBGP**.

| State | Meaning | Usual cause when stuck |
|---|---|---|
| Idle | Not trying, or reset after an error | Admin shutdown, NOTIFICATION (e.g., Bad Peer AS) |
| Connect / Active | Trying to open TCP | No route, wrong IP, wrong update-source, TCP 179 blocked, MD5 mismatch |
| OpenSent / OpenConfirm | OPEN messages exchanged | AS or router-ID problems |
| **Established** | Exchanging routes | — |

In `get router info bgp summary` the last column shows the **state**, or the **number of prefixes received** once
Established.

## eBGP vs iBGP rules

- eBGP peers are expected to be **directly connected** (TTL 1). Loopback peering needs multihop
  (`ebgp-enforce-multihop` on FortiOS).
- iBGP usually peers between **loopbacks** with `update-source`, reached through the IGP.
- Both sides need a neighbor statement for the other's **exact source IP** and the right remote AS.

:::recall
Q: The session is Idle and the neighbor log says "Bad Peer AS". Where's the error?
A: A remote-as value on one side doesn't match the other side's local AS.
:::

units.title: What gets advertised, and to whom
units.body:
## Origination

- `network` statements: on FortiOS, with **network-import-check** (enabled by default) the exact prefix must be
  in the routing table, or nothing is advertised (p. 749).
- Redistribution: connected, static, OSPF into BGP (origin incomplete, `?`).
- Aggregates: summaries, often anchored by a blackhole static route.

## The rules of propagation

- eBGP: prepend your AS, set the **next hop to yourself**.
- iBGP: **don't** change the AS path, **don't** change the next hop (by default), and **never pass an iBGP-learned
  route to another iBGP peer** (split horizon). Hence full mesh, or **route reflectors**: a RR may reflect routes
  between clients and non-clients.
- Loop prevention: a router drops a route whose AS path contains its own AS.

## The next-hop trap

An HQ router learns an Internet prefix from its ISP via eBGP and passes it by iBGP to a second router. The next
hop is still the ISP's IP. If the second router has no route to it, the BGP route is **invalid**: present in the
table, not installed. Fix: `next-hop-self` on the iBGP neighbor, or advertise the link into the IGP.

:::why
Q: Why doesn't iBGP just forward iBGP-learned routes like eBGP does?
A: iBGP doesn't modify the AS path, so the AS path can't detect loops inside the AS. Split horizon prevents them instead.
:::

units.title: Best-path selection
units.body:
When several paths exist for the same prefix, the first difference decides:

1. Highest **weight** (local to the router; FortiOS gives locally originated routes 32768)
2. Highest **local preference** (default 100, shared across the AS)
3. Locally originated
4. Shortest **AS path**
5. Lowest **origin** (IGP < EGP < incomplete)
6. Lowest **MED** (compared only between paths from the same neighbor AS by default)
7. **eBGP over iBGP**
8. Lowest IGP metric to the next hop
9. Oldest path / lowest router ID / lowest neighbor IP

## Influencing traffic

| You want to control | Attribute | Where |
|---|---|---|
| How **you** leave (outbound) | Local preference (AS-wide) or weight (one router) | Inbound route map on your routers |
| How **others** come in (inbound) | AS-path prepend, MED | Outbound route map toward the provider |

:::recall
Q: Two ISPs. You want all outbound traffic through ISP-A, and inbound to prefer ISP-A too. What do you set?
A: Higher local preference on routes from ISP-A (inbound route map), and prepend your AS a few times toward ISP-B (outbound route map).
:::

units.title: Filtering with prefix lists and route maps
units.body:
## Prefix lists

Ordered rules: `permit`/`deny` a prefix with optional `ge`/`le`. Without ge/le a rule matches **only that exact
prefix**; `10.20.0.0/16 le 24` matches the /16 and anything more specific down to /24. The end has an **implicit
deny**.

## Route maps

Ordered rules that **match** (a prefix list, AS path, community…) and **set** (local preference, weight, MED,
AS-path prepend, community). A route map with no matching rule denies the route.

:::cli
config router route-map
    edit "FROM-ISP-A"
        config rule
            edit 1
                set set-local-preference 200
            next
        end
    next
end
config router bgp
    config neighbor
        edit "203.0.113.1"
            set route-map-in "FROM-ISP-A"
        next
    end
end
:::

Apply filter changes without dropping the session: `execute router clear bgp ip <peer> soft in|out`.

:::pitfall
Always filter what you accept from a provider and what you announce to it. A FortiGate announcing a full
table it learned from ISP-A to ISP-B makes your company a transit AS, and a route leak with your name on it.
:::

cards.back: TCP 179.

scenarios.title: The carrier leaked someone else's routes
scenarios.situation:
During a BGP migration you notice the carrier's PE announces 172.16.40.0/24 into Andes's MPLS VRF. It doesn't
belong to Andes. The carrier's NOC says they'll look into it "this week".

right_thinking: Protect the customer now: inbound prefix list with only Andes ranges
Document evidence (bgp network output) for the carrier ticket
Explain the risk calmly: traffic to those prefixes could be misrouted or intercepted
scenarios.what: A filter in place, evidence sent, customer informed.
scenarios.why: Accepting everything a provider sends is how leaks become incidents.
scenarios.model_answer:
"I'd apply an inbound prefix list on both FortiGates that only accepts Andes's 10.20/16 and 10.30/16 ranges,
soft-clear the sessions, and confirm the routing tables. I'd send the carrier the bgp network output as evidence.
To the customer: the carrier made a configuration mistake that could have sent some traffic to another company's
network; we've filtered it on our side, so Andes is protected while they fix it."
scenarios.best_way: Protect, evidence, explain.

interview.question: Walk me through BGP best-path selection.
interview.framework: List the order, then one example
interview.model_answer:
"Highest weight, which is local; highest local preference, AS-wide; locally originated; shortest AS path;
lowest origin; lowest MED from the same neighbor AS; eBGP over iBGP; lowest IGP cost to the next hop; then
tie-breakers like router ID. In practice I use local preference to control how we leave and AS-path
prepending to influence how traffic comes in."
interview.best_way: Order, then how you use it.

interview.question: An iBGP route is in the BGP table but not in the routing table. Why?
interview.model_answer:
"Most likely the next hop isn't reachable: iBGP keeps the eBGP next hop, the ISP's IP, and this router has no
route to it. next-hop-self on the edge router, or advertising the link into the IGP, fixes it. I'd confirm with
the BGP table output, which shows the path isn't marked valid."
interview.best_way: Name the next-hop rule.

modules.title: Routing on FortiGate: static, policy routes, ECMP and the routing database
objectives: Read the routing table and the routing database and explain why a route is or isn't active
Use distance and priority for primary/backup and ECMP designs
Configure policy routes and know where they sit in the lookup order
Build dual-Internet failover with a link health monitor
