scenarios.title: Design review: twenty minutes with their architect
scenarios.situation:
You present the HLD to Andes' architect and CIO. The architect challenges: "Why FortiManager if we only have 40
sites?", "Why not keep MPLS for the warehouses?", "What happens to the tracking app if AWS us-east has an
outage?" The CIO asks: "Can we be live in 4 months?"
scenarios.ask: Answer the four questions.
right_thinking: FortiManager: templates, ZTP, consistent policy and audit across 40 sites and two hubs
MPLS for warehouses: a valid option; compare cost and SLA; SD-WAN SLA rules plus LTE can meet scanner needs if tested
AWS region outage: out of scope of the network design unless the app is multi-region; say so and flag it as a risk
4 months: yes for wave 1 (10 branches) with conditions: circuits ordered now, templates in month 2, pilot branch in month 3
scenarios.what: Answer with reasons, accept good alternatives, name risks.
scenarios.why: A review rewards honest trade-offs over defending every choice.
scenarios.model_answer:
"FortiManager because 40 sites and two hubs by hand drift apart within months; templates and zero-touch
give the same config everywhere and an audit trail. Keeping MPLS at warehouses is a fair option: if the
pilot shows the scanners miss their latency target on broadband plus LTE, we keep MPLS there and the cost case
changes for those sites. An AWS region outage takes the app down regardless of our network; that needs a
multi-region app, so I'll put it in the risk register for the app owner. And yes to 4 months for the first 10
branches, if circuits are ordered this month — that lead time is the critical path."
scenarios.best_way: Reason, concede what's fair, register what's out of scope, conditional yes.

interview.question: Design a WAN for 40 branches and two data centres on a whiteboard. Talk me through it.
interview.framework: Requirements → topology → routing → steering → management → security → test
interview.model_answer: "First I'd confirm the requirements: survive a DC loss, latency-sensitive apps, cost. Then dual hub with two underlays per branch, IPsec overlays to both hubs, BGP on loopbacks and ADVPN for branch-to-branch. SD-WAN SLA rules for the critical apps, broadband for bulk, LTE as backup. FortiManager templates and zero-touch for 40 sites, FortiAnalyzer for logs. And I'd prove it with a DC-loss drill in the acceptance tests."
interview.best_way: Requirements first, then dual hub, routing, steering, management, and a test.

modules.title: Exam simulations: mixed-track timed sets and how to take them
modules.stage_title: S12 · Capstone: design, exams and mock interviews
objectives: Answer mixed FortiGate, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, Enterprise Firewall, FortiSIEM and FortiEDR items under time

objectives.Use an exam routine: read the last line first, eliminate, flag and return

objectives: Spot your weak tracks from the results and feed them back into review
sources: Everything before this stage; FortiOS 8.0.2 Administration Guide (debug flow, HA election, BGP)
FortiSIEM and FortiEDR admin guides (architecture, policy modes)

units.title: An exam routine
units.body:
1. **Read the last line of the stem first**: what is actually asked (cause? first step? which would NOT work?).
2. **Look for the deciding detail**: a mode (central NAT, override), a version, an output line.
3. **Eliminate** what contradicts the evidence, then choose between the two that remain.
4. **Flag and move** after 90 seconds; come back with fresh eyes.
5. **Don't change** an answer without a concrete reason you missed the first time.

Use the sets below as timed runs: about 75 seconds per item. After each run, the review queue picks up what you
missed; the progress view shows which track it came from.

:::recall
Q: What do you read first in a long scenario question?
A: The last line of the stem, to know what is asked.
:::

cards.back: About 75 seconds per item; flag and move after 90.
Only with a concrete reason you missed before.
Monitored interfaces → uptime → priority → serial.
Monitored interfaces → priority → uptime → serial.
Highest weight (local to the router), then local preference.

quiz.output:
id=20085 trace_id=1 func=print_pkt_detail msg="vd-root:0 received a packet(proto=6, 10.1.1.10:51514->93.184.216.34:443) from port2. flag [S]"
id=20085 trace_id=1 func=init_ip_session_common msg="allocate a new session-0001a2b3"
id=20085 trace_id=1 func=vf_ip_route_input_common msg="find a route: flag=04000000 gw-203.0.113.1 via port1"
id=20085 trace_id=1 func=fw_forward_handler msg="Denied by forward policy check (policy 0)"
quiz.stem: [FGT Admin] What is the cause of the drop?

options.text: No policy matches port2 to port1 for this traffic, so the implicit deny drops it
There's no route back to 10.1.1.10, so the reverse path check drops the session
options.why_wrong: RPF failures log 'reverse path check fail'; here the policy check denies.

options.text: Source NAT is disabled on the matching policy, so the packet can't leave port1
options.why_wrong: Missing NAT doesn't produce a policy deny; the session would pass and fail upstream.

options.text: The route lookup found no gateway, so the packet was dropped before policy
options.why_wrong: The route was found (gw 203.0.113.1 via port1); policy 0 is the implicit deny.

quiz.explanation: 'policy 0' is the implicit deny: route found, no matching policy.

quiz.stem: [FGT Admin] Order the FGCP primary election criteria with override disabled.
quiz.explanation: With override disabled, uptime beats priority. Enabling override moves priority above uptime.

quiz.stem: [FGT Admin] After a firmware upgrade, the unit with HA priority 200 isn't primary again. Override is disabled. Why?

options.text: The peer has run longer since the upgrade, and age is compared before the priority
Priority set on a unit takes effect after the cluster is rebooted together
options.why_wrong: Priority is evaluated at each election; the order of criteria is the issue.

options.text: The other unit has a higher serial number, which is checked before device priority
options.why_wrong: Serial number is the last tie-breaker, after priority.

options.text: A monitored interface on the priority-200 unit is down, so it lost the first criterion
options.why_wrong: Possible in general, but nothing indicates a link failure here; uptime explains it after an upgrade.

quiz.explanation: With override disabled, uptime (age) wins over priority. Enable override if priority must decide.

quiz.stem: [Enterprise Firewall] Two BGP paths reach 10.50.0.0/16. Path A has local preference 200; path B has weight 100 and local preference 100. Which does the FortiGate prefer?

options.text: Path B, since FortiOS compares its weight ahead of LP values
Path A, as higher local preference is the first attribute compared
options.why_wrong: Weight is checked first on FortiOS; local preference comes second.

options.text: Path A, as weight is ignored for paths learned over iBGP sessions
options.why_wrong: Weight is local to the router and applies to any path, iBGP or eBGP.

options.text: The path with the shorter AS path, as it's compared ahead of the other two
options.why_wrong: AS path is reached after weight and local preference tie.

quiz.explanation: Best path: weight → local preference → locally originated → AS path → origin → MED...

quiz.stem: [FGT Admin] How many usable host addresses does a /27 subnet have?
quiz.explanation: 2^5 = 32 addresses, minus network and broadcast = 30.

quiz.stem: [FortiSIEM Analyst] Ingest is growing past what the Supervisor can process. Which component do you add first?

options.text: Workers, which take over event processing and queries from the Supervisor
Collectors at each site, which parse and analyse events before they upload
options.why_wrong: Collectors collect and forward; processing load is handled by Workers.

options.text: A second Supervisor in active-active mode to split the processing load
options.why_wrong: Supervisor HA is for availability, not to scale event processing.

options.text: Faster event database storage, since disk writes are the usual bottleneck
options.why_wrong: Storage can matter, but processing load is scaled with Workers.

quiz.explanation: Scale processing horizontally with Workers; Collectors handle collection at remote sites.

quiz.stem: [FortiEDR Admin] During rollout, the customer wants to see what FortiEDR would block without disrupting users. Which setting?

options.text: Security policies in Simulation mode, so events are logged but not blocked
Collectors in a group with the policies unassigned until the pilot is done
options.why_wrong: With no policy assigned you don't see what would be blocked.

options.text: Prevention mode with exceptions for the processes seen in the first week
options.why_wrong: Mass exceptions hide real threats; simulation gives the same visibility safely.

options.text: Prevention mode on a pilot group of volunteers who accept some disruption
options.why_wrong: A sound later step, but it still blocks; the ask is to see blocks without disruption.

quiz.explanation: Simulation mode records what Prevention would block, so you can tune before enforcing.

quiz.stem: [FortiAnalyzer Analyst] Reports on last month's traffic are empty, but the logs exist on disk. What is the likely reason?

options.text: Analytics retention ended; archive copies remain, but reports don't read those
The ADOM's disk quota was reached, so FortiAnalyzer stopped writing any new logs
options.why_wrong: A full quota affects new logs; here last month's logs exist but aren't queryable.

options.text: Log forwarding to the SIEM removed the logs from FortiAnalyzer after sending
options.why_wrong: Forwarding copies logs; it doesn't delete them.

options.text: The report's time zone differs from the device's, so it filters out the period
options.why_wrong: Could shift hours, not empty a whole month.

quiz.explanation: Analytics (indexed) and archive (compressed) logs have separate retention. Reports need analytics logs; import archive logs back if needed.

quiz.stem: [FortiManager Admin] A FortiGate's local change keeps getting overwritten. Which would NOT keep the change?

options.text: Leaving it on the FortiGate and installing the policy package again from FMG
Retrieving the device config into FMG and then importing it into the package
options.why_wrong: This brings the change into FortiManager, so the next install keeps it.

options.text: Making the same change in FMG's policy package and installing it to the device
options.why_wrong: Configuring it in FortiManager is the normal way to keep it.

options.text: Adding it through a CLI script in FMG run against the device database first
options.why_wrong: A script on the device database stores it in FortiManager, so installs keep it.

quiz.explanation: FortiManager installs its own copy; a change that exists only on the FortiGate is overwritten.

interview.question: How do you read a debug flow when traffic is dropped?
interview.testing: Fluency with the main FortiGate tool
interview.framework: Filter → run → read the last line → map to stage
interview.model_answer: "I set a filter on the host and port, run a few packets, and read top to bottom: received on which interface, session allocated, route found or not, then the policy check. The last line tells me the stage: 'policy 0' is the implicit deny, 'reverse path check fail' is routing back, no route is a routing gap. Then I fix that stage and run it again."
interview.best_way: Filter, run, read the last line, map it to the stage.

modules.title: Mock interview gauntlet: recruiter, hiring manager and a SecOps-heavy technical panel
modules.stage_title: S12 · Capstone: design, exams and mock interviews
objectives: Run three full mock interviews back to back, timed and self-scored on rubrics
Answer SOC, SecOps and SASE questions with the honest framing of where your experience comes from
Recover from a question you can't answer without bluffing
Close each interview with questions that show you think like a consultant
sources: Your evidence: super-cv (Fortinet TAC P3, Netskope CSM and Scale CSM, SYKES), certifications, portfolio joseacostasec.com
I1–I3 and the S13/S14 modules

units.title: How to run the gauntlet
units.body:
Three rounds, recorded (voice capture or phone), with a break between:
1. **Recruiter (15 min):** pitch at 90 seconds, why Fortinet again, logistics, two questions back.
2. **Hiring manager (30 min):** delivery stories (STAR), customer handling, a 30-60-90 plan, the hard questions.
3. **Technical panel (45 min):** one design (this stage's case), one troubleshooting walk-through, then a
   SecOps block: SOC stack design, a detection, an incident, a FortiSASE question.

Score each answer on the rubric right after, while you remember it. Re-run the two weakest answers the next day.

**The honesty frame** for SOC and SecOps: what you did (TAC cases on FortiSIEM and FortiEDR, SIEM log streaming
at Netskope), what you studied and built (certifications, red-team labs, these capstones), and what you'd do in
the first months. Interviewers forgive gaps; they don't forgive bluffing.

:::recall
Q: Three parts of the honesty frame for an area where you lack production experience?
A: What you did hands-on, what you studied and built, and how you'll close the gap.
:::

units.title: When you don't know
units.body:
A good "I don't know" has four parts: say it plainly, reason out loud from what you do know, say how you'd find
out (docs, lab, TAC, a colleague), and offer to follow up. Example:

> "I haven't configured that FortiSASE feature in production. From the architecture, I'd expect it to work
> through the SPA hub, so I'd check the admin guide for the supported topology and test it in a lab before the
> customer window. I can send you what I find."

What fails: guessing a number, naming a command you're unsure of, or talking for two minutes to hide the gap.

:::why
Q: Why reason out loud instead of just saying "I don't know"?
A: It shows how you think, which is what the panel is testing.
:::

cards.back: Recruiter 15 min, hiring manager 30, technical panel 45.
What I did, what I studied and built, how I'll close the gap.
Say it, reason out loud, how you'd find out, offer to follow up.

quiz.stem: The panel asks: 'How many FortiSIEM deployments have you done?' Which answer is strongest?

options.text: "None as lead. I worked FortiSIEM cases at TAC and built the detections in my labs; here's one."
"Several, through TAC: I troubleshot many customer deployments, which is close to deploying them."
options.why_wrong: Stretching TAC cases into deployments falls apart on the first follow-up question.

options.text: "None yet, but I'm a fast learner, and I'm sure I can pick it up in the first weeks on the job."
options.why_wrong: Honest, but gives no evidence; the strong answer adds what you have done.

options.text: "It depends on what you count as a deployment; can you tell me what scope you have in mind?"
options.why_wrong: Clarifying can help, but here it reads as evasion of a simple question.

quiz.explanation: Plain fact, then real evidence, then an offer to go deeper.

quiz.stem: Asked about a FortiSASE feature you haven't used, which response works best?

options.text: Say so, reason from the architecture, explain how you'd verify, and offer to follow up
Describe how a competitor's SSE does it, since the concepts transfer between vendors
options.why_wrong: Transferable knowledge helps, but without saying you don't know the Fortinet side it sounds like a dodge.

options.text: Give the closest command you remember and say the syntax may differ in this version
options.why_wrong: Guessing a command invites the next question you can't answer.

options.text: Say plainly that you don't know it and move on, so the panel's time goes to other questions
options.why_wrong: Honest, but it skips the reasoning and the path to an answer, which is what they're testing.

quiz.explanation: Honest, reasoned and with a path to the answer; that's what a consultant does with a customer too.

quiz.stem: Order a strong answer to 'Tell me about a difficult customer escalation.'
items: Situation and stakes in two sentences
Your specific task and what made it hard
The actions you took, in order
The result, with a number if you have one
What you'd do differently or reused later
quiz.explanation: STAR plus a lesson: the panel wants judgement, not just a happy ending.

quiz.stem: In the technical panel, you're handed a vague design question: 'Build us a SOC.' What do you do first?

options.text: Ask about size, log sources, staff, compliance needs and whether they want 24/7 cover
Draw the FortiSIEM, FortiEDR and FortiSOAR stack and explain how the data flows between them
options.why_wrong: A fine second step; drawing before scoping misses the consultant part.

options.text: Describe the SOC tiers (L1, L2, L3) and a hiring plan for the analyst roles in each tier
options.why_wrong: People matter, but you don't know yet whether they want in-house or managed.

options.text: State which SIEM you'd pick and why it beats the alternatives on the market
options.why_wrong: A product pick without requirements is sales, not design.

quiz.explanation: Scope first: size, sources, staff, compliance, hours. Then design.

scenarios.title: Round 3, minute 30: 'Walk me through an incident you handled'
scenarios.situation: The SecOps panellist asks you to walk through an incident you handled end to end. You've worked many incidents at TAC and Netskope escalations, but not as a SOC incident lead.
scenarios.ask: Answer in two minutes.
right_thinking: Pick a real case where you owned a part (a TAC escalation with a security impact, a Netskope customer escalation)
Be clear about your role in it
Bridge to how you'd lead one: the K6.01 capstone flow (triage, scope, contain together, communicate)
scenarios.what: Real case, clear role, bridge to the lead role.
scenarios.why: Honest evidence plus a method beats an invented story.
scenarios.model_answer: "I haven't led a SOC incident, so let me give you one I worked and then how I'd lead one. At TAC I handled an escalation where [real case from your STAR bank]: my part was [your part], and the result was [result]. Leading an incident, I'd follow the same discipline I practised in my capstone labs: triage and severity, scope by account and host before blocking, contain all footholds together, and give the executive an update with facts, actions, unknowns and the next update time."
scenarios.best_way: Real case and role, then the method you'd lead with.

interview.question: This role leans on SOC, SecOps and SASE. Where are you strongest and where are you still building?
interview.framework: Strength with evidence → gap with plan
interview.model_answer: "Strongest on the FortiGate and network-security side from TAC, and on SASE from two years at Netskope plus FortiSASE study and labs. In SOC I have the attacker's view from OSCP and red-team labs, and FortiSIEM and FortiEDR cases from TAC; what I'm building is production SOC delivery, which is why I've been working through detection and incident-response capstones."
interview.best_way: Strength with evidence, gap with a plan already running.

interview.question: Your first customer wants FortiSIEM live in six weeks. What do you do in week one?
interview.model_answer: "Week one is scoping: which log sources matter most, the EPS estimate, who in their team owns the SIEM after we leave, and the top ten use cases they care about. Then I'd agree a phased plan: core sources and a few high-value rules in the first weeks, tuning against their baseline, then handover with runbooks. Six weeks works if the sources and access are ready in week two."
interview.best_way: Scope, priority sources and use cases, phased plan, conditions.

interview.question: Write me a detection for Kerberoasting and tell me how you'd tune it.
interview.model_answer: "On the DCs, event 4769 with ticket encryption type 0x17, RC4, for service accounts. I'd group by requesting account and count distinct service names, alerting at a threshold over a short window — a burst is the tell. To tune, I'd replay a normal week: exclude known legacy services that still use RC4 and the machine accounts, and long term push AES on service accounts so the rule gets quieter on its own."
interview.best_way: 4769 + RC4, distinct SPNs per account, tune on a baseline.

interview.question: A customer moving from Netskope to FortiSASE asks what changes for their users. What do you tell them?
interview.model_answer: "For users, the experience is similar: an agent that steers traffic to a cloud security service. What changes is the agent — FortiClient managed from FortiSASE instead of the Netskope client — and how policies are expressed. I'd map their steering and policies first, pilot a group, and run both agents' tunnels carefully so they don't conflict. I know the Netskope side from two years there; the FortiSASE side from study and labs, so I'd validate the mapping in a lab before rollout."
interview.best_way: Similar experience, different agent and policy model, phased with a lab check.
